Trick to save money on flights  – the “inverted return flight”! Replace two return flights from A to B, with one return flight from A to B and one return flight from B to A in-between.

Example of how I saved 20% on my last booking 👇 

---

 [2/5] I want to book a return flight from Munich to Sofia in April and then again in August. Normally, you would book like this:

MUC-SOF from April 10 to April 19 (274 €)
MUC-SOF from August 8 to August 16 (344 €)
Total: 618 € 

---

 [3/5] Instead, you can book the same flights like this:

MUC-SOF from April 10 to August 16 (314 €)
SOF-MUC from April 19 to August 8 (200 €)
Total: 514 €

That’s 20% cheaper (105 €), for the exact same flights – same airline, same dates, same times! 

---

 [4/5] This works in cases, where one of the destinations is in a cheaper country than the other. In this case Bulgaria is much cheaper than Germany, so booking flights starting from Sofia is usually much cheaper. 

---

 [5/5] The example above contains real prices from Lufthansa from 2 days ago. I ended up booking slightly different dates, but I still used that trick and saved around 20%, on those otherwise really expensive flights...

Client or server side analytics? I've been playing around with different analytics options on my blog - @Netlify on the server and @PlausibleHQ  on the client side. The results from the last 7 days are quite different. Why? How are the two approaches different? A Thread (1/8)  

---

 Server side analytics have several native advantages: 
- No overhead on your website, because no external resources are loaded 
- Not affected by content blockers 
- Can track resources other than web pages, like images or redirects
- Show resources that could not be found (2/8) 

---

 Client side analytics on the other hand:
- Can capture more data about the user, like device size, browser and OS 
- Better track user behavior, like time spent on each page 
- Provide real-time feedback about visitors
- Usually easier to setup (3/8) 

---

 The difference in page views is interesting - the server side tool shows much more views across all pages in my blog. I think this is because the pages are accessed many times from automated systems that don't run JavaScript and are therefore not counted on the client side. (4/8) 

---

 This happens when you post a link on Twitter or WhatsApp for example, because their websites or clients then make a request to fetch the metadata of the page and display a card preview. Therefore, it counts on the server, but not on the client side. (5/8) 

---

 A perfect example is the draft article, which I only sent per WhatsApp to my wife for proof reading. The difference there is just 2 views (I guess one preview each on my and on her phone). I sent all other links to several people and posted them on Twitter and Reddit. (6/8) 

---

 You can also somewhat see this effect in the referrers. The server side tool counted many hits from a RSS reader and Google Translate (my parents in law reading my blog in Bulgarian 😂). The preview requests from Twitter and WhatsApp are probably counted as direct traffic. (7/8)  

---

 In conclusion, I think client side analytics more realistically count the number of people reading my blog (even if not many). However, there are cases that can be captured only on the server side (for example Google Translate). I guess I will stick with both for now... 😃 (8/8) 

---

💡 When you have an idea, try to validate it by build a prototype with as little effort as possible. 

When I started writing my blog I had an idea for a tool to help me decide what to write about next. Read below how I hacked Netlify Analytics to build a first prototype.

👇 

---

 The idea 💡

I wanted to include voting links in the text at places touching on a topic that I could write more about. If somebody was interested in reading about it, they could just click the link to vote for it. Based on the votes I would decide what my next article would be.  

---

 So how to quickly build a prototype? 🤔

I host my site on @Netlify where you can easily create redirects. I created a URL for each topic and redirected it to an empty page. Clicking a voting link would send a GET request to the corresponding voting URL in the background. 

---

 How it works? ⚙️

While the user only sees a message that the vote was sent, the access to the URL is recorded in the logs and displayed in the Analytics tool. Looking at the number of times each voting URL was accessed, I would know which topic is most interesting to my readers.  

---

 It works! 🔥

People were clicking the voting links! Sometimes I was surprised that they wanted to read about topics that I didn't prioritized very high initially.

Since the idea worked for my blog, I decided to turn it into a product and started building  

---

Why use a static site generator? 🤔

When creating a website with mostly static content (product page, blog or personal site), using a static site generator may be a good idea. Static sites have several advantages compared to Content Management Systems (CMS).

Read more below 👇 

---

 How it works? ⚙️

Static site generators allow you to define the structure of your site as templates, while keeping the content separately (usually in Markdown files). They are then combined to generate the final HTML pages. 

Static sites have several big advantages 👇 

---

 Static sites are fast 🏎️

When the web server needs to serve a page, it just needs to open the HTML file and send its content over the network. This is simple and fast.

CMS usually need to query a database first and generate the HTML before serving the request, which takes time. 

---

 Static sites are cheap 💰

You don't need a database and you don't need to run a script on you server. This makes hosting cheap, so services like GitHub Pages or @Netlify offer generous free tiers. CMS hosting is usually more expensive or the free tier is more restricted. 

---

 Static sites are scalable 📈

Again, because of the simple web server needed, static sites can be scaled easily. The hosting provider usually takes care of this fully automatically through their edge network. You will be able to easily handle millions of requests! 

---

 Static sites are secure 🛡️

Since there is no dynamically generated content, there are much less opportunities for exploits. The server needs to run less software so it is more secure as well. This makes development easier and let's you focus on your content. 

---

 Trade-offs ☝️

Okay, not everything is 🌈 and 🦄 - there are some trade-offs you need to be aware of.

Static sites are, well... static. However, you can add dynamic functionality using JavaScript. There are many popular frameworks that can help you, like React, Vue and Angular. 

---

 Static site generators can also be a bit difficult to setup and configure, compared to an already installed CMS. However, once everything is ready, publishing new content is easy. Most generators also have large collections of themes to help you start. 

---

 Here a short summary of the pros and cons of static site generators:

✅ Fast
✅ Simple
✅ Secure
✅ Cheap
✅ Scalable

⚠️ Setting things up
⚠️ Dynamic functionality

Tomorrow I will write more about how to choose a suitable static site generator from the many available options.

How to choose a static site generator? 🔎

You want to create a personal website or start a blog? Or maybe you want to create a page describing your product? Using a static site generator is a good fit for all these use-cases, but how to choose one?

Read below for some tips 👇 

---

 There are so many different static site generators (SSG), so choosing the right one may not be trivial. A great site that you can use to compare different options is StaticGen: 

Here are the criteria I used to chose one for my personal website and blog 👇 

---

 1. You know the programming language 📜

You probably won't need to write code for a simple site, but being comfortable the language of the SSG will make it easier. You will already know most tools around it and will be able to set things up and configure it faster. 

---

 2. The focus of the SSG fits your use-case 👌

Some SSG are specialized for creating blogs, others focus on project documentation. There are also many that try to be as flexible as possible. 

Choosing one suitable for your use-case will save you time when setting it up. 

---

 3.  You are familiar with the template engine ⚙️

You can start with a predefined theme, but you will probably want to customize your site. So, you will need to adapt the templates defining the structure of the site. Again, choose a template engine you are already familiar with. 

---

 4. It is widely used ⭐

All things equal, I would go for a more popular SSG. When a project has many users, you will usually be able to easily find solutions to common problems. The number of GitHub stars or Twitter followers of a project is usually a good proxy for that. 

---

 When building my personal website and my side project (both having a blog), I looked at several options and Pelican (@Getpelican) was a perfect fit for me:

1. Language - Python 🐍
2. Specialization - blogs 📖
3. Template engine - Jinja2 ⚙️
4. Popularity - almost 10000 stars 🌟 

---

How to quickly create a minimal static site with a blog using Pelican? 🚀

Pelican (@getpelican) is a static site generator written in Python, which makes it easy to create a blog or a landing page.

Read how you can quickly start with Pelican 👇

 

---

 1. Install pelican

Installing Pelican is very easy using pip. It supports both Markdown and reStructuredText for writing blog articles, but I prefer Markdown.  

---

 2. Create a Pelican project 

Create a new project by typing pelican-quickstart in the terminal. You will then need to answer a couple of questions like website and author name, URL etc. Don't worry - you can always change these settings in the config files later.  

---

 3. Check your project structure

You now have the following structure:
▪️ content - blog articles (Markdown)
▪️ themes - website templates (Jinja2)
▪️  - configuration file
▪️  - publishing configuration
▪️ output - generated files 

---

 4. Disable unneeded features

When building something I like to start with a minimal version and build on top of it. That's why I recommend leaving only the most important features turned on in the beginning. You can disable features in the  file.  

---

 5. Choose a theme

There are more than 100 predefined themes you can use to get started quickly. Browse through the gallery and see if you find something you like. You can even start with the default theme and customize the design yourself.

 

---

 6. Customizing the templates

The most important templates that you will likely want to customize in the beginning are the following:
▪️ base.html - main template used for every page
▪️ index.html - start page of your blog
▪️ article.html - template for rendering articles 

---

 7. Creating pages

By default Pelican gives you the structure for a blog. You can create static pages outside of the blog as well. I usually want the index page to be some kind of a landing page, while the blog is moved to <domain>/blog/. You can easily configure this:  

---

 8. Writing an article

Once everything is setup, writing an article is easy - just add a new .md file in the content folder. Your file should start with a header specifying some important metadata, like title, date and a short summary.  

---

 9. Publishing your site

While you are working on your site or writing articles you can start a local server to preview the changes. Once you are ready you can use the publish command to generate the production HTML files.  

---

 Static sites created with Pelican can be easily deployed on any hosting provider, but the integration with @Netlify is especially easy. I will write more about it in one of my next threads. 

---

 I have also written a more in-depth tutorial how to setup a new site with Pelican. It describes the process I used to create . You can also find the code of the site and the minimal theme I created for it on GitHub.

How I improved my Lighthouse Performance from 85 to 99 ? 🏎️

In the first version my side-project website, , I focused on the content, so it wasn't loading very fast. The Lighthouse Performance score was only 85.

Read what I did to improve it to 99 👇  

---

 1. Optimize images 🏞️

This turned out to be the biggest problem - my images were way too big. I got a nice high-quality image for my header from @unsplash, but didn't compress it properly - it was more than 1 MB 🤦‍♂️. After some optimization I got it down to 66KB 😎  

---

 2. Move big images from CSS to HTML 🔁

The big image was loaded in a CSS file as a div background. The CSS file needed to be loaded and parsed first, before the image could start loading. Inlining the image in the HTML (in the style attribute) improved the loading time.  

---

 3. Using Google Fonts 🔤

I was serving font files from my server. While you can get good performance in this way, you need to implement several tricks. Using Google Fonts is actually faster than the naive implementation!

Read more on the topic here:  

---

 4. Deferring non-critical CSS and JavaScript ⌛

The last step was to defer the loading of non-critical CSS and JavaScript files. For JS files you can just add defer or async in the script tag. For CSS you need to use some (ugly IMO) hacks like this:

How I got my Lighthouse scores to 100? 💯

The first version of my side-project  didn't score high in Lighthouse. I already wrote about improving the Performance, so now I'll focus on Accessibility, Best Practices and SEO.

Read how I got them to 100 👇  

---

 1. Accessibility (colors) ♿

The color of my links didn't have enough contrast with the background. I used the color picker in Chrome when inspecting an <a> tag, to help me select a color with a sufficient contrast ratio. I also had to bold the text of my buttons.  

---

 1. Accessibility (headings) ♿

When I used heading tags, they weren't always consistent. For example, sometimes I had <h4> coming after an <h2> or had some tags not in descending order. I cleaned up all the headings and adjusted the size of the elements using CSS. 

---

 2. Best Practices 🏅

I had links to external pages that were opened in a new window (GitHub repo and Plausible Analytics dashboard) . Lighthouse recommends adding noopener to the <a> tag to improve security. I have a lot of trust in @github  and @PlausibleHQ, but still... 😁 

---

 3. SEO 🔎

Fixing the SEO problems was easy:
▪️ Added a robot.txt file
▪️ Added ALT attributes to all images
▪️ Added aria-label to all links and buttons

Lighthouse actually complained that some links don't have descriptive names (only symbols), but aria-label worked fine. 

---

I got an idea for a nice weekend computer vision project, while listening to a podcast with @gruber and @JoannaStern. They were complaining about video calls on the iPad, because the camera is usually on your left or right. What if Apple added a second front camera? 🤔 

Thread👇  

---

 The problem is that if you put the iPad horizontally and look at the center of the screen, you appear to be looking either left or right, because the camera is on the side.

If we had cameras on both sides, we could compute a 3D model and render a view from the center. 👇  

---

 To simulate this I used my wife's iPad Pro and made her take 2 photos of me with the camera on the left and on the right.

I then used a open-source deep learning stereo algorithm called GA-Net to compute a disparity map between the two images in both directions.  

---

 The disparity value of a point in the image tells you how many pixels you need to move horizontally in order to find the same pixel in the other image.

Points closer to the camera move more between the images than points further back - this is called the parallax effect. 

---

 I actually didn't need to compute a 3D model of my face, because I just wanted to move the virtual camera halfway between the two frames. I simply used the disparity values directly dividing them by 2! 🤷‍♂️ 

---

 Some points on the face are only visible from one side,, so just taking one of the images and translating it didn't work. The occluded regions appear as black shadows in the projected image. I implemented some simple logic in Python to choose the best point from the two images.  

---

 And here is the final result! I animated the transition between the two frames to make it look better. 😀

It is far from perfect - you can see many artifacts on the face and on my left shoulder. However, I think it is enough as a proof of concept that this may work...  

---

 And as always, you can find all the code and the images I used on GitHub along with documentation how you can do it yourself.

When is a machine learning model good enough? 🤔

@AlejandroPiad and @svpino posted some great approaches to this problem from academic and business view point!

However, I would like to talk about the case where the result doesn't depend on the ML algo *directly*.  

---

 For example, a self-driving car has a ML algo do detect traffic lights. However, the car will not react directly on the output of a the classifier. It will first do fusion with other sensors and a map, before it decides what action to take: stop or drive through. 

---

 How do you decide if you should further optimize your traffic lights detection and in what direction? Reduce FP or FN?

I have an idea how to do this, but I would really love to hear some more opinions! 

---

 Here the great threads from @svpino and @AlejandroPiad  for more context on the discussion and for some great approaches.

Yesterday I asked the question below and got some very interesting answers!

@svpino suggested several approaches to focus on the end problem directly: 

@AlejandroPiad suggested using the theoretical framework  AutoML: 

My take 👇  

---

 In such situations it is difficult to tune the ML algo by evaluating its output alone. A problem of the model (a FN or a FP) may or may not cause problems in the final result. This depends on many factors and the exact implementation of the function logic. 

---

 In the self-driving car example, a FN of a red traffic light may lead to an accident if the car enters the junction on red. However, if the ML classifier misses only 1 out of 4 red traffic lights at the junction it is not a big deal. Not all FNs are equal! 

---

 One possible approach that I always found useful is to measure the performance on the application level. Did the car stop correctly at the red light (TP) or did it run the red light (FN)? This gives us a new way to measure how changes of the ML model affect the final result.

How much money is in the jar full of coins?

People are usually bad at estimating such things...  However, our guesses can often be viewed as samples from a probability distribution which is centered close to the true value. This property can be used to get a good estimate... 👇  

---

 We can ask several people to guess the amount of money in the jar. Then, we can take the average of their estimates. There is a good chance that this number will be more accurate than any individual guess.

This is called "Wisdom of the crowd". 

---

 I tried that in the office some time ago. We had a jar full of spare change from the coffee machine, so I asked my colleagues to guess how much money we had (real data here!)

The real amount was 244.39€, so the average was really the closest value. Our PM did good as well 😀.

What is Simpson's Paradox? 🤔

Understanding it will help you avoid pitfalls when evaluating changes (for example new ML algorithm version).

Imagine you come up with a new version of your software, you test it and the results are worse. So it didn't work, right? Not always... 👇 

---

 When comparing the results of two versions, they have to be evaluated on the *exact same data*. Otherwise, you may get worse results, even if the new version is better or the other way around. This is called Simpson's paradox.

There are many examples, but here my favorite one 👇 

---

 A developer at YouTube managed to reduce the size of the video watch page from 1.2MB to 100KB. He tested it with real users for a week, but the results showed that the average loading time of the page increased!

The problem was that the new version also changed the user base 👇 

---

 People on very slow internet connections had to wait for 20 min to load a video - they were mostly giving up. The new faster page took  2 min to load, so it was worth waiting. Many people on slow connections actually started using YouTube and so the average load time increased. 

---

 Read the full story by @zacman85

 

---

 Always keep the Simpson's paradox in mind when comparing different versions of your software. Make sure you test on the same data or that you understand how the underlying data changed between tests.

It's finally time for some paper review! 📜🔍🧐

I promised the other day to start posting threads with summaries of papers that had a big impact on the field of ML and CV.

Here is the first one - the AlexNet paper!  

---

 This is one of the most influential papers in Computer Vision, which spurred a lot of interest in deep learning. AlexNet combined several interesting ideas to make the CNN generalize well on the huge ImageNet dataset. It won the ILSVRC-2012 challenge by a big margin. 

---

 Architecture 🏗️

The network consists of 5 convolutional layers (some of which followed by max-pooling) and 3 fully-connected layers and has 60M parameters. The network is distributed over two GPUs with only particular layers allowed to communicate between them.  

---

 Activation function 📈

AlexNet is one of the first papers to use ReLUs instead of sigmoid or tanh. The network was able to learn much faster (about 6x) and enabled the authors to train such a large network in the first place. 

Btw. ReLU is a complicated way to say max(0,x) 😉  

---

 Normalization 🗜️

AlexNet uses Local Response Normalization to improve generalization. It is similar to lateral inhibition in biology, where neurons try to increase contrast to their neighbors. Example image - A and B are the same color, but your brain sees them differently.  

---

 Pooling 🔲

Pooling reduces the resolution of the feature maps and adds some translational invariance. Contrary to the traditional non-overlapping pooling methods, AlexNet allows neighbor regions to overlap. This further improves generalization.

Image:   

---

 Dropout ⛔

Dropout was a new technique in 2012, but it turns out to be crucial for good generalization in AlexNet. During training, the output of random 50% of the neurons in the first 2 fully-connected layers is set to 0, which reduces co-adaptation of neurons and overfitting. 

---

 Results 🏆

The results that AlexNet achieved vastly superior to any other method at that time. They won the ILSVRC-2012 challenge with 15.3% top-5 error rate with the second-best method being 26.2%. 

---

 Feature maps 🌠

A very interesting result is how the two GPUs learned fundamentally different filters in the first convolutional layer. GPU 1 learned frequency and orientation filters, while GPU 2 focused on color. This happened in every run, independent on the initialization.  

---

 Even though, CNNs weren't a new thing in 2012, AlexNet was the first method that managed to train such a large network. It employing several techniques that made it possible without severe overfitting.

It is considered by many as the paper that started it all... 

---

Confirmation bias - an important type of cognitive bias! 🧐

When we have a theory about something, we often start looking for information that confirms it, without testing if it could be wrong.

Confirmation bias has real impact on our lives so we need to be aware of it👇  

---

 Example when coding 💻

When we write tests for our code, we often focus on creating test cases that show the intended behavior of the code, but we often forget to write negative tests. That's why it is a good idea to do TDD (it won't always be a solution, but it helps). 

---

 Example when shopping 🛍️

When we want to buy some product that you like, we start looking for reviews where the product performs well. If we see a negative review, we usually find a reason, why it is not representative. 

---

 Example when driving a car 🚗

When in traffic jam, we always seem to be stuck in the slowest lane, right? This is because we focus on a particular moment when it was true, but ignore all the other time that we are actually moving faster. 

---

 Example when we have an idea 💡

We want the idea to be good so we start looking for facts that support it. It is useful to put ourselves in the shoes of somebody that thinks the idea is bad and try to find arguments against it. 

---

 Not being aware of confirmation bias in our choices, often leads us to take wrong decisions. It is useful to consciously think about it and try to avoid it by looking at things from different sides. 👍👎

Time for another ML paper review - generating synthetic ground truth data from video games! 🎮

I love this paper, because it pushes the boundaries of creating realistic synthetic ground truth data and shows that you can use it for training and improve your model. 

Details 👇  

---

 The Problem 🤬

Creating ground truth for semantic segmentation is very slow and expensive - somebody needs to annotate every pixel in an image!

Labeling a single image takes between 60 and 90 minutes. Scale AI will charge you $6.40 (while a bounding box costs only $0.08).  

---

 Idea 💡

The authors used GTA V to capture highly realistic images of traffic scenes in different weather and lighting conditions. They managed to extract a lot of information from the game, so that the labeling process could be accelerated almost 800 times!  

---

 How? ⁉️

The authors didn't have access to the source code of GTA V, which could have made everything much easier...

However, they managed to intercept the communication between the CPU and the GPU and capture the rendering commands send by the Direct3D driver. 

---

 Details ⚙️

They extracted the information from which mesh, texture and shader each pixel was rendered and generated a unique ID from it. When a pixel was annotated, the label could be propagated to all other pixels with the same ID in the image and even across frames.  

---

 Labeling Tool ⚒️

The authors created an efficient labeling tool using this method. While images in the beginning took more time, the labeling speed kept increasing, as the existing annotations could be propagated of the other images. On average it took only 7 second per image!  

---

 Dataset 💽

The authors created a dataset containing almost 25.000 annotated images, which was much bigger than any dataset containing semantic segmentation ground truth at that time. Labeling took only 49 hours!  

---

 Training with synthetic data 🤖

The authors trained a CNN with both synthetic and real data for 2 benchmarks and achieved much better results, than training only with real data.

Even more, they could reduce the amount of real data to 1/3 and still get comparable results!  

---

 Conclusion 🏁

Training on synthetic data is already done in several domains like human pose estimation from depth data (Microsoft Kinect) and optical flow, but is still not fully possible for camera images. However, it has a lot of potential to unlock many new applications! 

---

Another paper review, but a little different this time... 🤷‍♂️ 

The paper is not published yet, but is submitted for review at ICLR 2021. It is getting a lot of attention from the CV/ML community, though, and many speculate that it is the end of CNNs... 👇

  

---

 The paper successfully applies the Transformer deep learning model to the image classification problem. 

Transformers are dominating the field of natural language processing, just look at GPT-3...

However, they have found only limited application in Computer Vision so far... 

---

 Image as input 🏞️

Transformers take a series of tokens as input - usually the words of a sentence. But what about images? 🤔
 
Treating each pixel as a token would be too computationally expensive 🚫

Taking only a local neighborhood of a pixel will only provide local context 👎 

---

 Here, the image is split into patches of 16x16 pixels, which are fed in the Transformer (more accurately a linear transformation of the patch + positional information).

This allows this so called Vision Transformer (ViT) to capture global context, while still being effiecient.  

---

 Model ⚙️

What's interesting is that the network itself is a standard Transformer, exactly as used for NLP! 🤯  

It takes as input the sequence of image patches and outputs a classification, which is the Transformer's output for the special [class] token, as done in other models  

---

 Results 🏆

Results are impressive! Evaluated on 7 different datasets, ViT achieves results comparable to the state-of-the-art CNN with 15x less computational resources. A deeper version of ViT outperforms the CNN, while still being 4x faster.

It needs 2500 TPU days, though...  

---

 Analysis 🔍

Looking at the learned linear transformation of the input patches, we can see that they resemble the first layer of a CNN. The Transformer learned to capture frequency and color information, without any convolutions. This speaks for its good generalization ability!  

---

 Analysis  🔍🔍

Even in the first layers, ViT learns to pay attention to almost the whole image and not only to a local neighborhood of each pixel. This is something that CNNs can only do in the deeper layers - in the beginning the receptive fields of the neurons are limited.  

---

 Analysis 🔍🔍🔍

The authors also tried using features from the initial layers of a CNN as input to the Transformer instead of the patches. While this showed better results for smaller models, a deeper version of ViT was able to generalize just as good using the images directly. 

---

 Conclusion 🏁

It is impressive that a very general model (Transformer) is able to outperform a more specialized one (CNN), while being more efficient.

The authors note, though, that this is only possible when training on huge amount of data - 300M images (the JFT-300M dataset). 

---

 Considering that JFT-300M is a non-public dataset by Google and that it takes 2500 TPUv3 days to train the model, it will not be easy to apply it in practice...

The Curse of Knowledge 🏴‍☠️

This is another type of cognitive bias that prevents us seeing things from the position of others, who don't have the same knowledge as us.

To demonstrate it I asked you to put yourself in the shoes of a kindergarten child:  

---

 The answer ✅

The correct approach is to "see" just the shapes of the numbers and don't interpret their meaning. Remember, the kids cannot read, but only count to 10!

Then just count the number of circles! The correct answer is 2, because the 8 has two circles. 

---

 The facepalm moment‍ 🤦

Many people struggled to see the answer (including myself when I first saw this 🤷‍♂️). 

The problem is that we are all used to reading numbers and it is hard to "unsee" them, so we can put ourselves in the shoes of the kids. Complex math won't help here... 

---

 Another example 🎨

Try to look at this image and quickly say out loud the color of each word, not the word itself. It is not easy, right? You just cannot not read the words!  

---

 Watch out for the Curse of Knowledge 🔭

We need to be aware of this bias when communicating with other people that have less knowledge about a certain topic. We often unconsciously assume they know things that seem easy for us, but we forgot how difficult they were to learn. 

---

 How to avoid if? 🤔

When explaining something, try to consciously think about what the other person knows and try to adapt your explanation to that. Then you will be able to communicate your ideas more clearly and become a better teacher. It's easier said than done, though...

ML paper review time - DenseNet! 🕸️

This paper won the Best Paper Award at the 2017 Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) - the best conference for computer vision problems.

It introduces a new CNN architecture where the layers are densely connected.  

---

 I attended a talk by Prof. Weinberger at GCPR 2017. He compared traditional CNNs to playing a game of Chinese Whispers - every layer passes what it learned to the next one. If the some information is wrong, though, it will propagate to the end without being corrected. 🤷‍♂️  

---

 The Idea 💡

The main idea of DenseNet is to connect each layer not only to the previous layer, but also to all other layers before that. In this way, the layers will be able to directly access all features that were computed in the chain before.  

---

 Details ⚙️

Creating "shortcuts" between layers has been done before DenseNet - important for training very deep networks.

The interesting point here is that the connectivity is dense and that the feature maps from all layers are concatenated and not summed up as in ResNet. 

---

 Details (2) ⚙️

Sharing feature maps is not possible when the resolution is reduced by pooling, so in practice there are 3-4 dense blocks connected by so called transition layers. The layers in each block are densely connected.  

---

 Growth rate 📈

An important hyper parameter is the growth rate - it specifies the number of feature maps that is added after each layer. In contrast to other architectures, DenseNet can use very narrow layers, typically containing only 12 feature maps. 

---

 Training 🏋️‍♂️

A big advantage of DenseNet is that it is easy and fast to train, because it avoids the Vanishing Gradients problem. During backpropagation, the gradients are free to flow directly to each layer because of the dense connections. It's much faster to train than ResNet.  

---

 Size ⭕

Sharing the feature maps between layers also means that the overall size of the network can be reduced. Indeed, DenseNet is able to achieve accuracy similar to ResNet with half of the number of parameters.  

---

 Generalization ✅

An nice side effect of having a smaller network is that it is less prone to overfitting. Especially when no data augmentation is performed, DenseNet achieves significantly better results than other methods. 

---

 Results 🏆

DenseNet is tested on several benchmark datasets (including ImageNet) and either beats all other methods or achieves results comparable to the state-of-the-art, but using much less computational resources. 

---

 Conclusion 🏁

DenseNet is an architecture where each layer is able to reuse the information in all previous layer. This results in a network that is smaller, faster to train and generalizes better. 

It is implemented in all major DL frameworks: PyTorch, Keras, Tensorflow etc.

Machine Learning Paper Reviews 🔎📜

Check out this thread for short reviews of some interesting Machine Learning and Computer Vision papers. I explain the basic ideas and main takeaways of each paper in a Twitter thread.

👇 I'm adding new reviews all the time! 👇 

---

 AlexNet - the paper that started the deep learning revolution in Computer Vision! 🏃‍♂️

 

---

 DenseNet - reducing the size and complexity of CNNs by adding dense connections between layers. 🕸️

 

---

 Playing for data - generating synthetic GT from a video game (GTA V) and using it to improving semantic segmentation models. 🕹️

 

---

 Transformers for image recognition - a new paper with the potential to replace convolutions with a transformer. 🔁

 

---

 ResNet allowed to train very deep and simpler networks for the first time. ↩️

Here comes a review of one of the fundamental papers in CV and ML - ResNet ↩️

Formulating the classical CNN network as a residual network allowed training much deeper (but simpler) networks. ResNet won the first place in the ILSVRC and COCO 2015 challenges.

Thread 👇  

---

 Deeper is not always better 🚫

The authors give several examples how adding more layers to a CNN makes the network perform worse on the testing dataset. I hear you saying overfitting...? 🤔 

Actually no! The network also shows both worse test and training error...  

---

 When the network gets deeper, it becomes harder to train! In theory, you could just add 36 identity layers to a 20-layer net and get a 56-layer net with the same performance, but the optimizers have problems with the complexity.

Here the authors have an important insight 👇 

---

 Residual network ↩️

The idea is to train several layers to learn a residual function H(x) - x instead of the function H(x) itself (as traditional networks do). 

This is achieved elegantly with a simple shortcut connection that adds the input of the layer block to its output.  

---

 Think about it - the network now only needs to focus on learning the difference between its input and the final output - the residual.

This modification of the network architecture requires no additional parameters, practically no runtime overhead and is very easy to implement. 

---

 But why does it work? 🤔

You can now easily create identity mappings - just set all parameters to 0! This is not what we want of course, but it turns out in practice many useful functions are close to the identity mapping - they are much easier to learn in this setting! 

---

 It does work! 🌟

A comparison between an 18 layer and 34 layer variants of a standard CNN (plain) and ResNet shows that going deeper is beneficial for ResNet, but actually leads to worse results for the classical CNN.  

---

 Bottleneck Architecture🍶

The authors also introduce a bottleneck variant that decreases the number of parameters. A 1x1 conv first reduces the number of features and after a regular 3x3 conv another 1x1 is applied to increase it back. The shortcut connections are critical here.  

---

 Results 🏆

ResNet is compared to the state-of-the-art methods and a classical CNN with the same architecture apart from the shortcut connections.

It achieve *significantly* better results with *less parameters* on several datasets: ImageNet, CIFAR, MS COCO and PASCAL VOC. 🥇  

---

 Going very deep ⏬

An interesting experiment is to go much deeper on the CIFAR dataset - from 110 to 1202 layers... 😲

Impressively, the authors report no difficulties in training the network and getting a very small training error. However, they run into overfitting problems.  

---

 Conclusion 🏁

ResNet show that reformulating the CNN architecture to learn residual functions allows to train much deeper and simpler networks that perform much better than their regular counterparts. Great work by Microsoft! 🎖️

Self-driving car approaches 🧠🚗

Some interesting self-driving news lately:
- Waymo launching test fleet without safety driver
- Tesla launching a beta of their Full Self-Driving
- Mercedes announcing a level 3 traffic jam pilot for 2021

There are 3 very different approaches 👇 \n\n---\n\n 1️⃣  "Everything that fits" approach.

This is Waymo's approach, but other companies like Cruise, Argo, Aurora, Uber, Zoox have a similar strategy.

Fit as much sensors as possible on the car,  build high-definition maps of the environment and throw in lots of compute power. \n\n---\n\n Check out some images of these cars - they all have multiple lidars, cameras and radars all around the car. Waymo now has 29 cameras! 😲

They are not really integrated in a consumer oriented way, but it should be fine for a robotaxi.  \n\n---\n\n The strategy here is to try to find the fastest (and also most expensive) way to self-driving, usually directly to level 5. 

Since all these companies strive to remove the safety driver, they want the system to be extremely safe, but also handle all scenarios. \n\n---\n\n Summary of the "Everything that fits" approach:

✅ Lots of sensor redundancy for a safe system
✅ Fast development by taking all "shortcuts"
✅ Straight to L5

❌ Very expensive (both development and product)
❌ Difficult to scale
❌ Difficult to collect massive amounts of data \n\n---\n\n 2️⃣  "Ask for permission" approach.

This is the strategy of Mercedes and also many of the other traditional car manufacturers. They prefer to start with a very safe system (automotive safety standards are very hard), but in limited scenarios, like level 3 or only in traffic jams. \n\n---\n\n The sensors are nicely integrated and not really visible if you aren't looking for them. Can you spot the lidars, the cameras and the radars in these cars? 🤔Computation power is more limited.

The goal is to be on the safe side and scale the system slowly as regulations allow.  \n\n---\n\n Summary of the "Ask for permission" approach:

✅ Very safe approach
✅ Not too expensive
✅ Easily scalable and can provide lots of data

❌ Slow development
❌ Only limited use cases in the beginning 
❌ Not clear if it can easily scale to level 5 \n\n---\n\n 3️⃣  "Ask for forgiveness" approach.

This is where Tesla is going - launch as quickly as possible to the end users and let them test and provide feedback and data. This is not the safest approach, but the one that provides the fastest feedback loop and most data 🤷‍♂️ \n\n---\n\n Tesla famously rejects the use of lidar and HD maps and goes all in using cameras (plus radar) and lots of compute power.

While their system is level 2, it seems that they want to show that it is statistically safer than a regular driver in order to get regulatory approval.  \n\n---\n\n Summary of the "Ask for forgiveness" approach:

✅ Cheap
✅ Scalable and provides massive amount of feedback and data
✅ Very fast development

❌ Dangerous (end user testing)
❌ Bets on CV/ML reaching human like performance 
❌ Not clear if it can easily scale to level 5 \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁

It is difficult to tell which approach will be most successful. All approaches have somewhat difference goals and bet on different strategies. Very interesting times are coming...

Self-driving car engineer roles - Software Engineer 💻

Some problems that software developers work on to build a self-driving car (the list is not exhaustive):

You will most probably need good C++ knowledge. If you are writing code for an ECU, other languages are not very common, because you usually need full control on the software. If you are more focused on tooling the choice is even bigger... \n\n---\n\n Who is it for? 👫

The tasks for software devs are so diverse that most software developers will find something suitable for their background!

While C++ and embedded knowledge will increase your chances, don't let anybody tell you that you need to be a math genius or have a PhD! \n\n---\n\n Next, I'll start looking into some of the more specialized roles.

Self-driving car engineer roles - Computer Vision Engineer 👀

The camera is one of the most important sensors! It is not always the most accurate one, but it can provide much more data than a lidar or radar. Extracting this data is the job of the CV engineer.

Thread 👇 \n\n---\n\n Problems to work on 🤔

Here some typical object classes that need to be detected and classified.

🛑 Traffic signs
🚦 Traffic lights
🚘 Vehicles
🚶 Pedestrians
🦌 Animals
🛣️ Lane markings
🏔️ Landmarks
🚧 Construction zones
🧱 Obstacles
🚔 Police cars \n\n---\n\n Distance estimation 📏

Detecting an object is not enough, though. You also want to know how far the object is from the car.  While the detection part is dominated by deep learning, the traditional CV methods (e.g. Kalman Filter) are still very useful for distance estimation. \n\n---\n\n Semantic segmentation 🎨

Semantic segmentation is useful for detecting objects and areas in the image that don't have a well defined shape, like buildings, trees, the free space on the road and so on. It can also serve as a basis for object detection algorithms.  \n\n---\n\n Depth estimation 🔭

A self-driving car needs a good 3D model of the surrounding. While lidar (and to some extent radar) can provide that, the camera can be seen as a redundant sensor.

There are different approaches:
- Stereo cameras
- Structure-from-motion
- Single frame depth  \n\n---\n\n Relevance ⁉️

Another important aspect is how relevant is an object:
- Is the car in my lane or not?
- Is the red or the green traffic light relevant for my lane?
- Is the pedestrian going to jump on the road in front of the car?

Here, fusion with other sensors can help as well. \n\n---\n\n Required knowledge 📚

Nowadays, deep learning and CNNs are a must for a computer vision engineer. However, don't underestimate the importance of traditional CV methods, especially around tracking, distance estimation and depth estimation! \n\n---\n\n Programming language 💻

Computer vision is very computationally intensive, so good C++ skills are required. However, for training and evaluation CNNs you usually only need Python! \n\n---\n\n Getting started 🏎️

There are again many ways to enter the industry as a CV engineer. Pick one of the problems above and focus on it to gain knowledge and experience!

Self-driving car engineer roles - Safety Engineer  🚧

Let's talk about a role that I think many people don't realize exists, but is extremely important! When we program a 2 ton metal box driving 130 km/h on the highway, we better be sure it is safe! 

---

 Problems to work on 🤔

There are two main safety aspects that need to be covered, in order to ensure that a system is safe enough.

1️⃣ Functional safety - doing things right
2️⃣ Safety in use - doing the right things 

---

 1️⃣ Functional safety

The goal is to identify all possible problems that may cause a failure of a particular system and define measures to handle them. 

For example, a defect may cause the camera to malfunction, rendering the car "blind". Not a good idea when driving fast!  

---

 The safety engineers need to study all possible failure modes, define and implement measures according to a very strict standard (ISO 26262).

In the example above a good measure can be to have a redundant camera or another sensor, like a lidar or a radar. 

---

 2️⃣ Safety in use

No system works correctly in 100% of the time. This is especially true for machine learning  algorithms!

The safety engineer needs to analyze what are the cases in which the system has a problem and how to deal with it. 

---

 For example, we know that a ML model for detecting stop signs will have False Negatives. Ignoring a stop sign can cause a severe accident, so we need so minimize the risk. 

For example, we can have a map where we mark the positions of all stop signs as a redundancy.  

---

 Required knowledge 📚

You will need knowledge in designing safe systems. If you have similar experience in other industries, you may be able to get into self-driving with such a role!

There are also many open topics for  designing safe Machine Learning systems... 

---

 Resources 📖

There are not so many resources as for CV or ML for example, but there are companies offering certification for the topic. You can also take a look at the automotive standards:
- ISO 26262 (Functional Safety)
- ISO 21448 (Safety of the Intended Functionality)

Self-driving car engineer roles - Test Engineer  📝

Test and validation is a very important part of building a self-driving vehicle. You want to make sure that it can reliably handle all kinds of situations it will encounter on the road.

Thread 👇 

---

 The job of the testing engineer is to design, implement and evaluate testing campaigns to validate the performance of the self-driving car in the field.

This comes on top of the standard software dev testing procedures like unit, acceptance, integration, fuzzing testing etc. 

---

 Testing on the road 🛣️

Testing on the real roads is important - there is a huge variety of situations that the car will get into. The goal is to collect large amounts of data in order to make statistical evaluations and find hard edge cases. A trained safety driver is essential! 

---

 The test engineer needs to design such campaigns so that all kind of environment variations are covered well enough:
🌧️ Weather conditions (sun, clouds, rain, snow...)
🌒 Day and night driving
🛣️ Road types
🗺️ Countries or states
🚦 Traffic scenarios
🚒 Rare events 

---

 Test tracks 🚧

It is difficult to test all kind of situations in the real world, so testing on dedicated test tracks is important. Examples:
🚶 Emergency braking on pedestrians and kids
🚗 Emergency cross traffic tests
🏎 ️Tests requiring high vehicle dynamics  

---

 All companies invest heavily in testing facilities where they can play out different scenarios in controlled conditions. Here some examples:
- The BMW test track in Miramas
- Waymo's Castle 
- The Mcity Test Facility

The test engineer needs to plan and execute the tests there.  

---

 And here is why you want to test some things with dummies on the test track - sometimes things go wrong...  

---

 Required knowledge 📚

The testing engineer needs to have knowledge in testing methodologies and be able to organize large scale campaigns. The test tooling development is also an important part in order to process the scenarios in an efficient way. 

---

 A big challenge there is the huge amounts of data that the car generates from all of its sensors while driving. Data rates of more than 1 GB per second are quite common! 

---

 Programming language 💻

Python is a very popular language for developing evaluation tools. When things need to be scaled up for handling huge amounts of data, languages as C++ and Java/Scala come into play as well.

What is FJCVTZS?

It's a special instruction in the ARM architecture that stands for "Floating-point Javascript Convert to Signed fixed-point, rounding toward Zero".

Yes, the ARM compiler had  create a special instruction, because  JavaScript only supports   float numbers 🤦‍♂️ \n\n---\n\n This instruction helps  convert from double-precision floating-point values to  integer value in order to  help with bitwise operations.

This really is a testimony how important JavaScript performance has become...

Your software is crashing? Maybe you can blame it on the cosmic rays next time... 🤔

Cosmic rays are high-energy  protons or atomic nuclei  traveling trough space. They have enough energy to corrupt data if they hit an electronic circuit.

 \n\n---\n\n Unlikely to happen?  ☝️

A study from IBM in the 90s shows that computers typically experience  one cosmic-ray-induced error per 256 MB of RAM per month. This is probably even worse with the much smaller transistor sizes today.

This is a real problem for data centers. \n\n---\n\n Popular accidents that are probably caused  by cosmic rays:

🗒️ One candidate getting 4096 additional votes in a Belgian election (2003)

Cognitive bias time - the IKEA effect 🛏️

People tend to place a unrealistically high value on things they helped create. 

Studies show that people would value IKEA furniture they assembled themselves 63% more than similar pre-assembled items!

There are real implications 👇  \n\n---\n\n Selling 💰

When we are selling things that we invested effort building or maintaining (like a car or a house), we tend to value it higher than the potential buyers. \n\n---\n\n Ideas 💡

We often think that ideas we have thought a lot about are brilliant, while they may not seem particularly interesting to others. \n\n---\n\n Working on projects 💻

Even worse, people (and especially managers) often continue pouring work and resources into projects they helped develop, even if much better alternatives become available.

A website that shows tweets anonymously. It would work like this:

▪️ One account may submit only once per week (or month).

Inattentional blindness 🙈

Sometimes when we are focused on a particular task, we  are likely to ignore unexpected sensory inputs. 

I asked you to play a game last week to demonstrate this phenomenon, so here is a more detailed explanation.

Thread 👇

 \n\n---\n\n It is really amazing! Looking at this video, about half of the people don't see the gorilla! I didn't see it the first time I watched the video as well...

 \n\n---\n\n While I was looking for a nice example to post last week I found a similar video (that I also posted). I was expecting the gorilla, but didn't see the curtain changing color 🤦‍♂️

It is a good way to troll somebody that knows about the first video...

 \n\n---\n\n In real life  🏙️

If you think about it, you will find examples in real life as well. I'm sure it happened to you that you met somebody you know in a unfamiliar situation (for example a colleague from work somewhere in the city). It is likely that you "don't see" them... \n\n---\n\n Extreme case ⚠️

In 1995 an officer chasing a subject didn't see another officer shooting the wrong person. He was convicted for lying to protect his colleague. An experiment later showed that this was likely a case of inattentional blindness and he was probably not guilty. \n\n---\n\n Why it happens ⁉️

There are different theories, including limited congitive capacity, dominance of what we expect, saturation of attention etc. It is a limitation of our perception and attention system. \n\n---\n\n How to avoid it 🤔

Inattentional blindness may be difficult to avoid, since it happens if something is unexpected.

However, we can avoid distractions when doing important tasks, like for example looking at our phones when walking and especially when driving! \n\n---\n\n Further reading 📖

Check out the website of @cfchabris and @profsimons who did a lot of work in this direction and also designed the invisible gorilla experiment.

@elonmusk famously said that lidar is a crutch. Tesla is bringing autonomy to consumer vehicles where lidar comes with  trade-offs (cost, integration).

Tesla bet on the massive  amounts of video data they have  and improvements in CV.

The traditional OEMs like Audi, BMW and Mercedes all announced using lidar for their L3-4 efforts.

They are not using the big 360° lidars like many other companies. They are going for smaller lidars integrated in the front, for increased redundancy.

Machine Learning Interview Question #1 🧠🤖🧐

Let's start with an easy question...

❓ What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning❓

❓BONUS QUESTION: What other types of machine learning do you know ❓

Answer in the replies. Read the rules 👇 \n\n---\n\n  \n\n---\n\n Lots of great answers in the replies! Thanks you all for your contribution! 👍

Here is my answer for reference, but you should really go through all others, because there are some great ones there as well! \n\n---\n\n The most distinguishing difference between supervised and unsupervised learning is if we have access to ground truth data during training.

This means, can we tell our model when it is right or wrong or not. \n\n---\n\n Supervised learning 🧑‍🏫

Supervised models learn to predict a certain output from the input data, based on many example input/output pairs.

Typical example is classification - is this an image of a car or not. We train a model using lots of examples of cars and not-cars. \n\n---\n\n Unsupervised learning ⁉️

Here we don't have ground truth, so the model needs to find patterns in the data by itself. 

Typical examples
▪️ Clustering
▪️ Dimensionality reduction
▪️ Anomaly detection
▪️ Autoencoders \n\n---\n\n Other types of learning 🤔

▪️ Reinforcement - learn trough interaction with an environment

What are typical challenges when training a deep neural networks ⁉️

▪️ Overfitting
▪️ Underfitting
▪️ Lack of training data
▪️ Vanishing gradients
▪️ Exploding gradients
▪️ Dead ReLUs
▪️ Network architecture design
▪️ Hyperparameter tuning

How to solve them 👇 \n\n---\n\n Overfitting 🐘

Your model performs well during training, but poorly during test.

Possible solutions:
- Reduce the size of your model
- Add more data
- Increase dropout
- Stop the training early
- Add regularization to your loss
- Decrease batch size \n\n---\n\n Underfitting 🐁

You model performs poorly both during training and test.

Possible solutions:
- Increase the size of your model
- Add more data
- Train for a longer time
- Start with a pre-trained network \n\n---\n\n Lack of training data 🤷‍♂️

Deep learning algorithms are hungry for data compared to classical ML methods.

Possible solutions:
- Get more data (😂)
- Use data augmentation
- Use a pre-trained network and fine tune for your problem
- Try transfer learning \n\n---\n\n Vanishing Gradients 📉

During training the gradients in the first layers become small or 0. Learning is slow or the net doesn't learn at all.

Possible solutions:
- Use ReLU, which doesn't saturate in the positive direction
- Add residual/skip connections
- Batch normalization \n\n---\n\n Exploding Gradients 📈

Gradients become too big, training is unstable.

Possible solutions:
- Decrease the learning rate
- Use saturating activation functions, like sigmoid or tanh
- Gradient clipping
- Batch normalization \n\n---\n\n Dead ReLUs 😵

When using ReLU as activation function, a large gradient can knock off the weight of certain neurons so that they output 0 for all input data. They become useless.

Possible solutions:
- Decrease learning rate
- Use Leaky ReLU, ELU or some other variant \n\n---\n\n Network Architecture Design 🕸️

What and how many layers? How many neurons? Designing a network architecture may not be trivial.

Possible approaches:
- Find existing architectures for similar problems
- Trail and error
- User Network Architecture Search () \n\n---\n\n Hyperparameter Tuning 🔧

Finding the right hyperparameters for your problem is not easy.

Possible approaches:
- Check out existing parametrizations for similar problems
- Inspect your data and play around
- Grid search
- Bayesian optimization
- User Auto ML \n\n---\n\n If you wan to get better at training neural networks, this article by @karpathy is a must read!

What is backpropagation? ◀️◀️◀️

Backpropagation is an algorithm used to train neural networks. 

It adjusts the weights of the network in a way that minimizes the difference between the predictions of the net and the ground truth labels - the loss function.

More 👇 \n\n---\n\n The math 📐

The math behind it is essentially taking every weight in the network and computing the partial derivative of the loss function for it.

We can then adapt this weight according to the computed gradient and the learning rate - this is called Gradient Descend. \n\n---\n\n How it works? 1️⃣

A naive implementation of this will be super slow - here comes backpropagation.

We start from the last layer where we can directly compute the loss and the effect of every weight on it, so we can do the adaptation easily. \n\n---\n\n How it works?  2️⃣

Then we use the chain rule to move back 
to the previous layer and reuse the computations we did just before that to compute the gradients and update the weights.

We continue until we reach the first trainable layer. \n\n---\n\n It is fast! 🐇

Backpropagation avoids redundant computation of the intermediate terms and therefore is very efficient.

It is a great example of dynamic programming! \n\n---\n\n And here is one nice visualization of the chain rule 😆 Credits to @Khoa_NguyenTuan

Learning Rate 📉

During training of a neural network, we minimize a loss function using gradient descent.

In each iteration we adapt the weights by changing them a little in the direction of the gradient. How large this change is is defined by the learning rate.

Details 👇 \n\n---\n\n Imagine you are on the top of a mountain and want to get down to the lodge in the valley. The learning rate defines the speed at which you will be going down. ⛷️

A high speed means that you may breeze past the lodge and need to go back. Going to slow will cost you lots of time. \n\n---\n\n It is similar with the learning rate...

🐘 If it is too high, the optimization will be unstable jumping around the optimum.

🐁 It if is too low, the optimization will take too long to converge.

So how to find the best learning rate... 🤔

You have several options 👇 \n\n---\n\n As usual, for hyperparameter tuning, it will require some trail and error. You will try different approaches on your training dataset and check how good it was on the validation set.

You can use the following strategies:
- Parameter search
- Schedule
- Adaptive learning rate \n\n---\n\n Parameter search 🔎

The easiest way is to just try different values and see how it goes. You should select them in a exponential manner: 1, 0.1, 0.01, 0.001... you get the idea...

If the loss goes down, but slowly - increase ⬆️

If the loss starts oscillating - decrease ⬇️ \n\n---\n\n Schedule ⏰

The schedule allows you to apply a decay of the learning rate. You start with a high rate to get close to the optimum fast, but decrease it after that to be more precise.

The LR can be reduced based on the epoch or based on another criteria, like hitting a plateau. \n\n---\n\n Momentum 🎢

You can also apply momentum. Just like a ball rolling down a hill, the optimization will accelerate if it is steadily going down.

Momentum will also help the optimizer jump over small local minima and find a better optimum. \n\n---\n\n Adaptive Learning Rate 📉

There are also optimizers that adapt the learning rate automatically based on the gradients. They introduce other hyperparameters (e.g. the forgetting factor), but they are usually easier to tune.

Prominent examples:
- Adagrad
- RMSProp
- Adam ⭐️

How to add new classes to your ML model? 🍏🍎🍊... 🍌?

You have a large multi-class NN in production.

You discover a new important class and want to add support for it *quickly* and with *low* risk.

Example: traffic signs recognition for self-driving cars 🛑🚗

Thread 👇 \n\n---\n\n The naive approach 🤷‍♂️

Collect examples of the new class (for example a new traffic sign), label them and retrain the whole NN.

✅ It will probably work

❌ It will be time consuming, especially for big models.
❌ Risk for unintended regressions \n\n---\n\n Freezing the first layers 🥶

Typical CNNs learn generic image features in the initial layers and they will likely apply to the new sign as well.

You can freeze the weights of the initial layers and only retrain the last fully connected layer(s). \n\n---\n\n ✅ Faster retrain, because only the last layers are updated
✅ Lower risk for regressions

❌ For signs that look very differently, the CNN may lack the required features, leading to poor performance
❌ Still some risk for regression, because we touch all classes. \n\n---\n\n Extracting high-level features ⭕️⚪️6⃣

Train the NN to extract high-level features suitable for traffic signs, like shape, color, text or digits.

Define rules to classify each sign based on these features.

(Special credits to @ernestomancebo and @KwasiRansom for this idea) \n\n---\n\n ✅ No need to retrain
✅ Low risk because classes can be separated well
✅ Will work well for speed limits

❌ Won't work for some sign categories, like for example warning signs that only differ by their pictogram
❌ Won't work for signs with new shapes \n\n---\n\n One-shot learning 🛑▶️🔢

Transform sign images into a latent space, where they can be compared. Each class image is then described by a feature vector.

Siamese NNs can trained to transform images of the same class to very similar feature vectors in a latent space. \n\n---\n\n How it works?

1⃣ Choose examples for the known classes and precompute their feature vectors
2⃣ Transform new images to the latent space and find the best match to a known class
3⃣ When a new class is found, simply add an example image to the set of known classes. \n\n---\n\n ✅ No retrain needed
✅ Low risk for regression
✅ Only few examples of the new class needed

❌ May not work well if the new sign is very different and not supported well by the encoder \n\n---\n\n And finally some examples of traffic signs that you may not think exist until you encounter them... 😁

Is this formula difficult? 🤔

This is the formula for Gradient Descent with Momentum as presented in Wikipedia. 

It may look intimidating at first, but I promise you that by the end of this thread it will be easy to understand!

Thread 👇  \n\n---\n\n The Basis ◻️

Let's break it down! The basis is this simple formula describing an iterative optimization method.

We have some weights (parameters) and we iteratively update them in some way to reach a goal.

Iterative methods are used when we cannot compute the solution directly  \n\n---\n\n Gradient Decent Update 📉

We define a loss function describing how good our model is. We want to find the weights that minimize the loss (make the model better).

We compute the gradient of the loss and update the weights by a small amount (learning rate) against the gradient.  \n\n---\n\n Here is an illustration how it works. 

The gradient tells us if the loss will decrease (negative gradient) or increase (positive gradient) if we increase the weight.

The learning rate defines how far along the gradient we will jump in the current step of the optimization.  \n\n---\n\n Momentum ⚽️

Now we add the momentum. It is defined as the weight update in the previous step times a decay factor.

The decay factor is just a number between 0 and 1 defining how much of the previous update will be taken into account. α = 0 means no momentum and α = 1 is a lot.  \n\n---\n\n A useful analogy is a ball rolling down a hill. If the hill is steep, the ball will accelerate (we update the weights more).

This will help the ball jump over small local minima and continue down the hill (to a smaller loss).

More momentum means a heavier ball with high inertia  \n\n---\n\n Putting it all together 🏁

So, in the original formula we update the weights using two terms.

The *gradient descent* term pushes us down the slope of the loss function.

The *momentum* term helps us accelerate and jump over small local minima.

Not that hard, right? 😃

How to choose your batch size during training of a deep neural network? 🤔

There are reasons to use both larger and smaller batch sizes and you need to find the right *balance* for your  dataset.

Thread 👇 \n\n---\n\n Why use *larger* batch sizes? 🐘

▪️ Computing the gradients on more data leads to less noise that can be caused by outliers.
▪️  Increase training speed, by avoiding the optimization jumping in different directions.
▪️  Reduce oscillation of the loss function. \n\n---\n\n Why use *smaller* batch sizes? 📉

▪️  You training data likely doesn't sample the problem space perfectly. You actually want some noise to avoid overfitting.
▪️   Smaller batches act as a regularization mechanism.
▪️  You can't fit all the data in the GPU memory. \n\n---\n\n Why do smaller batch sizes improve generalization? 🤔

There may be multiple reasons. Smaller batches mean that the net will look only on a part of the data, which adds some noise. This forces the network to learn more generic features and specialize too much. \n\n---\n\n Small batch size reduces the network capacity? 😳

This is a very interesting paper by @mehtadushy.

In some common NN setups, many specialized filters are pruned and the effective network capacity is reduced, which leads to better generalization.

 \n\n---\n\n The reason is that specialized filters will not get updates during training from many of the batches (no relevant data). At the same time, their weights will be pushed down by the regularization every time.

This imbalance basically kills (or prunes) the filter. \n\n---\n\n In summary, you want your batch size to not be too large, but also not be too small.

This is a hyper parameter that you will need to tune for your *specific* problem!

Machine Learning Formulas Explained 👨‍🏫

This is the formula for Mean Squared Error (MSE) as defined in WikiPedia. It represents a very simple concept, but may not be easy to read if you are just starting with ML.

Read below and it will be a piece of cake! 🍰

Thread 👇  \n\n---\n\n The core ⚫

Let's unpack from the inside out. MSE calculates how close are your model's predictions Ŷ to the ground truth labels Y. You want the error to go to 0.

If you are predicting house prices, the error could be the difference between the predicted and the actual price.  \n\n---\n\n Why squared? 2️⃣

Subtracting the prediction from the label won't work. The error may be negative or positive, which is a problem when summing up samples.

You can take the absolute value or the square of the error. The square has the property that it punished bigger errors more.  \n\n---\n\n Why squared? Example 2️⃣

Imagine your pediction for the price of two houses is like this:

🏡 House 1: actual 120K, predicted 100K -> error 20K
🏠 House 2: actual 60K, predicted 80K -> error -20K

If you sum these up the error will be 0, which is obviously wrong... \n\n---\n\n Summing up all samples ➕

When training your model you will have many samples (n) in your batch. We need to calculate the error for each one and sum it up.

Again, having the error be always ≥ 0 is important here.  \n\n---\n\n Taking the average ➗

You are good to go how!

However, if you want to compare the errors of batches of different sizes, you need to normalize for the number of samples - you take the average.

For example, you may want to see which batch size produces a lower error.  \n\n---\n\n Mean Squared Error 📉

Now it should be easier to understand the formula!

MSE is a commonly used statistical measure and loss function in ML regression models (e.g. linear regression).

You should look into the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as well, which handles outliers better.  \n\n---\n\n For the people that can "think" better in code, here a small Python example for calculating the Mean Square Error. 👨‍💻

This is mind-blowing 🤯

Dealing with imbalanced datasets 🐁 ⚖️ 🐘

Real world datasets are often imbalanced - some of the classes appear much more often in your data than others.

The problem? You ML model will likely learn to only predict the dominant classes.

What can you do about it? 🤔

Thread 👇 \n\n---\n\n Example 🚦

We will be dealing with a ML model to detect traffic lights for a self-driving car 🤖🚗

Traffic lights are small so you will have much more parts of the image that are not traffic lights. 

Furthermore, yellow lights 🟡 are much rarer than green 🟢 or red 🔴. \n\n---\n\n The problem ⚡

Imagine we train a model to classify the color of the traffic light. A typical distribution will be:
🔴 - 56%
🟡 -    3%
🟢 -  41%

So, your model can get to 97% accuracy just by learning to distinguish red from green.

How can we deal with this? 🤔 \n\n---\n\n Evaluation measures 📐

First, you need to start using a different evaluation measure than accuracy:
- Precision per class
- Recall per class
- F1 score per class

I also like to look at the confusion matrix to get an overview. Always look at examples from the data as well! \n\n---\n\n In the traffic lights example above, we will see very poor recall for 🟡 (most real examples were not recognized), while precision will likely be high.

At the same time, the precision of 🟢 and 🔴 will be lower (🟡 will be classified as 🟢 or 🔴). \n\n---\n\n Get more data 🔢

The best thing you can do is to collect more data of the underrepresented classes. This may be hard or even impossible...

You can imagine ways to record more yellow lights, but imagine you want to detect a very rare disease in CT images? \n\n---\n\n Balance your data 🔀

The idea is to resample your dataset so it is better balanced.

▪️Undersampling - throw away some examples of the dominant classes

▪️ Oversampling - get more samples of the underrepresented class \n\n---\n\n Undersampling ⏬

The easiest way is to just randomly throw away samples from the dominant class.

Even better, you can use some unsupervised clustering method and throw out only samples from the big clusters.

The problem of course is that you are throwing out valuable data... \n\n---\n\n Oversampling ⏫

This is more difficult. You can just repeat sample, but it won't work very good.

You can use methods like SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) to generate new samples interpolating between existing ones. This may not be easy for complex images. \n\n---\n\n Oversampling ⏫

If you are dealing with images, you can use data augmentation techniques to create new samples by modifying the existing ones (rotation, flipping, skewing, color filters...)

You can also use GANs or simulation the synthesize completely new images. \n\n---\n\n Adapting your loss 📉

Another strategy is to modify your loss function to penalize misclassification of the underrepresented classes more than the dominant ones.

In the 🚦 example we can set them like this (proportionally to the distribution)
🔴 -     1.8
🟡 - 33.3
🟢 -    2.4 \n\n---\n\n If you are training a neural network with TensorFlow or PyTorch you can do this very easily:

▪️ TensorFlow - use the class_weights parameter in the fit() function ()

▪️PyTorch - use the weight parameter in the CrossEntropyLoss () \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁

In practice, you will likely need to combine all of the strategies above to achieve good performance.

Look at different evaluation metrics and start playing with the parameters to find a good balance (pun intended) 😀

Prisoner's Dilemma 🤔

Time for some game theory! 👨‍🏫

Prisoner's Dilemma (PD) is an interesting game that explains how two rational individuals may make decisions that seem irrational.

The game has lots of examples and applications in real life!

Thread 👇 

---

 There are different examples of PD, but this is the one I like most.

You want to buy something from another person. You exchange closed bags one containing the money and one the goods. 

Both you and the other person can choose to honor the deal ✅ or to give an empty bag ❌. 

---

 If you both honor the deal ✅ ✅ (cooperate), you both gain something.

If you both exchange empty bags ❌ ❌ (defect), at least nobody loses.

If you leave the bag empty, but get a full bag ✅ ❌, you gain a lot, while the other person is screwed.

Image source: Wikipedia  

---

 The optimal move? 💯

If you play only ones, than the only rational move is to defect:

▪️ If the other side cooperates ✅, it is better to defect ❌, get the goods and keep the money.
▪️ If the other side defects ❌, it is better to also give an empty bag ❌ to not lose money. 

---

 The dilemma 🤔

But wait, if both people think in this way, the deal will never happen, right? This is obviously suboptimal, because you both actually want to do the dael!

Both sides individuallt act rationally, but the final result seems irrational - this is the dilemma! 

---

 Playing multiple times 1️⃣, 2️⃣, 3️⃣...

This changes if the game is played multiple times (Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma). Now, people actually start to cooperate more, even if the Nash euqilibrium of the system is still to always defect! People start acting superrationaly! 

---

 Both sides always cooperating is the optimal strategy, but it is not a stable state. One side will always have the incentive to screw the other side by defecting and increasing its gain in the short term.

IPD is a very interesting psyhological problem! 😀 

---

 Real world example - climate change ☀️

All contries agree that they have to cut CO2 emissions, because they need a stable climate. However, every country is hesitant to invest in measures to actually reduce CO2. It is better if everybody else reduces CO2 except you... 

---

 Real world example - doping 💉

If all atheltes are clean than they stay healthy an dcompete on a level playing field. When somebody starts doping they get an advantage. However, if everybody is doping, the advantage disappears, but everybody incurs the negative side effects. 

---

 Real world example - advertising 💰

If one of two competing companies starts advertizing, it will make some of the customers of the other company switch and gain an advantage. However, if both companies advertise a lot, they will both have high expenses without any gain. 

---

 Look around you and I'm sure you will find examples of Prisoner's Dilemma all around you. The question now is how to make the other person always wanting to cooperate? 😄
