What are Convolutional Neural Networks? 🏞️ ⏭️ ⛰️

CNNs are an important class of deep artificial neural networks that are particularly well suited for images.

If you want to learn the important concepts of CNNs and understand why they work so well, this thread is for you!

🧵👇 \n\n---\n\n What is a CNN? 🤔

A CNN is a deep neural network that contains at least one convolutional layer. A typical CNN has a structure like this:
▪️ Image as input
▪️ Several convolutional layers
▪️ Several interleaved pooling layers
▪️ One/more fully connected layers

Example: AlexNet  \n\n---\n\n A good example - AlexNet 

Throughout the thread I will be giving examples based on AlexNet - this is the net architecture that arguably started the whole deep learning revolution in computer vision!

I've written more about AlexNet here:
 \n\n---\n\n Convolutional Layer *️⃣ ⏸️

Each convolutional layer is defined by a set of filters which are used on the input to transform it into some other representation.

A typical filter may detect horizontal edges or some specific color in the image.

The filters defined as convolutions. \n\n---\n\n Convolution Filter *️⃣

Here is how it works on the example of an image:

1️⃣ Take a small matrix (for example 5x5) - the filter
2️⃣ Overlay it over the image, multiply the pixel values with the matrix values and add them up
3️⃣ Slide the matrix over the whole image  \n\n---\n\n Real examples 🔬

Let's see what kind of filters AlexNet uses (it actually learns them, but will come to that in a moment). The example shows 11x11 filters that detect different features.

1️⃣ - horizontal edges
2️⃣ - vertical edges
3️⃣ - green patches
4️⃣ - blue to yellow edges  \n\n---\n\n The first Convolutional Layer *️⃣ ⏸️

The image as processed with many filters in the first layer (96 for AlexNet). 

Every filter will effectively create a new image (called feature map) telling you where the filter "found" matching patterns.

Example for edge detection filters.  \n\n---\n\n The next Convolutional Layer *️⃣ ⏸️

The next layer will have as input not the image, but the feature maps from the previous layer. Now it can combine simple features to create more complex ones.

For example, find places in the image with both horizontal and vertical edges. \n\n---\n\n Hierarchical architecture 🌲

Layer after layer the network will be combining more and more complex features giving it more expressive power. This is one of the big advantages of deep CNNs!

However, you may be wondering now - where do the filters come from??? \n\n---\n\n Feature Learning 👨‍🏫

This is the coolest thing - the optimal filters are learned automatically by the network!

In traditional ML methods the features are usually engineered by people, but this is one of the greatest advantages of CNNs - they are learned from the data!

How...? \n\n---\n\n Parametrization 🔡

In classical NNs we connect each neuron of a layer to all of the neurons in the input and assign the connection some weight.

In CNNs the weights are the values in the filter matrix and they are shared over the whole image! This is way more efficient. \n\n---\n\n Parametrization 🔡

Imagine an image of 100x100 pixels. Every neuron in the first layer will have 10000 weights. 10000 per neuron❗

For a CNN with 100 3x3 filters we need 900 weights + 100 for the bias.

Indeed, 96% of the weights of AlexNet are in the dense layers!  \n\n---\n\n Training 🏋️

As with regular neural nets, during training we can use backpropagation to find the best weights for our problem. This is how the weights of the filter matrices will be optimized and the network will learn the best filters for our problem. \n\n---\n\n Local connectivity ⭕

CNNs are very suitable for images, because they exploit the local connectivity between pixels - pixels next to each other are usually correlated.

The way the filters are applied over the image also make them invariant to translation, which is important. \n\n---\n\n Global context 🏞️

But wait, if we only look at 5x5 patches, how do we see the "big picture"? How do we use info from different parts of the image?

We scale the image down! When we make the image smaller, a 3x3 filter will correspond to a bigger patch of the original image. \n\n---\n\n Pooling 💠

While there are ways to reduce resolution with convolutions, let's focus on pooling for now.

The idea is simple:
1️⃣ Take a NxN patch of the feature map
2️⃣ Replace it with a single value - the max or average value in the patch

This will reduce the resolution by N \n\n---\n\n Pooling is useful as a way to select the strongest features and also give the network some additional translation invariance. In practice, a 2x2 pooling is usually used. \n\n---\n\n Typical architecture 🏛️

In a typical CNN, convolutional and pooling layers are alternated. The resolution of the feature maps is reduced through the network, but we usually increase the number of feature maps. The CNN will then learn more high-level features. \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁

▪️ CNNs use convolutions to compute feature maps describing the image
▪️ The filters share the weights over the image reducing the number of parameters
▪️ CNNs exploit the local relationships between pixels
▪️ CNNs can learn high-level image features and concepts \n\n---\n\n Further reading 📖

Make sure that you also read this great thread on the topic by @svpino!

Machine Learning Interview Question #11 🤖🧠🧐

Let's stay with CNNs for a while longer.

❓ How do you choose the size of your convolutions? What tricks can you apply here❓

Answer in the replies. Read the rules 👇 \n\n---\n\n  \n\n---\n\n Here is my answer... with a meme 😁

How do you choose the kernel size in a CNN? 🤔

Choose 3×3 and go deeper...

Let me explain. Thread 👇  \n\n---\n\n Receptive field 📣👁️

The receptive field of a neuron in a CNN is the size of the original image that contributes to the input of the neuron.

In the first convolutional layer the receptive field equals the kernel size. Going deeper in the network, the receptive field increases. \n\n---\n\n Deeper instead of Wider ↕️ vs ↔️

You can replace a layer with 5×5 convolution filters with two layers of 3×3 convolutional filters.

Look at the image to see how the receptive field remains the same.

Taking 3 layers of 3×3 will give you a 7×7 receptive field and so on.  \n\n---\n\n Parameters count 🔡

The big advantage? Much less parameters!

▪️ 5×5 convolution will require 25 parameters.
▪️ Two 3×3 convolutions require 2*9 = 18 parameters.

This is a reduction of 28% 📉

For 7×7 the reduction is 45% and for 11×11 we save 70% of the parameters. \n\n---\n\n Different architectures 🏛️

AlexNet used fairly big convolutions (11×11), but after VGG in 2014 3×3 kernels became much more popular. 

Many of the problems of training very deep networks are solved nowadays, so this is a good option. \n\n---\n\n There are network architectures that try to combine different kernel sizes (Inception net) or create feature pyramids (Retina net), but 3×3 seems to work very well enough if you can use more layers... 🤷‍♂️

How to detect objects using CNNs? 🎥 🕸 🌻

Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are very good at classifying images. 

But how can we use them to detect the presence, class and location of multiple objects in the image? 🤔

Thread 🧵  \n\n---\n\n Naive Approach 🤷‍♂️

The simplest way is to use a sliding window approach and check for each position of the image if it contains one of the objects we are interested in.

▪️ Take an image patch
▪️ Scale it and run it through the CNN
▪️ Check if some class has high probability \n\n---\n\n Since objects may appear big or small, we need to process the image at different scales.

This whole process is very slow! The image patches will have a lot of overlap, so the CNN will compute the same features over and over and over again.

There is a better way... 👇 \n\n---\n\n Region Based Convolutional Neural Networks (R-CNN) 🔲

R-CNN, Fast R-CNN and Faster R-CNN are examples of this family of models. The idea:

▪️ Generate many region proposals
▪️ Pass each region through the CNN
▪️ Classify each region
▪️ (optional) regress a tighter bounding box  \n\n---\n\n Region proposals 🔲 🔲 🔲

Region proposals are image patches that are likely to contain objects. We need to generate many of them so that we don't miss some object in the later stage.

Faster R-CNN actually integrates the region proposal finding (selective search) in the net. \n\n---\n\n Bounding box regression ➡️ 🔲 ⬅️

Fast and Faster CNN not only classify the path, but also use a regression to better fit the bounding box around the object.

They estimate the center point, width and height of the bounding box. \n\n---\n\n The problem with region based methods is that they don't look at the whole image - If there is no region proposal covering the object you are looking for it cannot be detected... ❌

We can improve here 👇 \n\n---\n\n You Only Look Once (YOLO) 😎🤙

YOLO (v5) is one of the best performing methods and it is also very fast. The idea:

▪️ Divide the image in a grid (for example 7×7)
▪️ Each cell predicts a class
▪️ Each cell predicts several bounding boxes
▪️ Predictions are combined  \n\n---\n\n Bounding box prediction 🔲

Each cell of the grid is responsible for predicting several bounding boxes (center, width, height) that have their centers in the cell. The amount is usually small though - the original paper uses 2 boxes per cell.

These are examples from YOLO  \n\n---\n\n Non-Maximum Suppression 📉

There may be multiple bounding boxes covering the same object. Non-maximum suppression chooses the best bounding box from all the overlapping ones. \n\n---\n\n If you want to try out YOLO yourself it is actually really easy! Check out this GitHub repository and follow the instructions.

I created the examples in this thread using this lib and some photos from @unsplash.

 \n\n---\n\n Semantic Segmentation 🏞

There are also methods based on Fully Convolutional Nets (consisting only of convolutional layers) that classify each pixel of the image.

They are very powerful, but much slower than object detection methods. I will write about this another time...

What is the best Prisoner's Dilemma strategy? ♟

Robert Axelrod, professor at the University of Michigan, wanted to find this out in 1980.

He organized a tournament and invited well known game theory researchers to submit a program playing Prisoner's Dilemma. 

Thread 🧵  \n\n---\n\n The Rules 📜 

The rules of the tournament were simple.

▪️ Programs are paired to play against each other for 200 moves
▪️ Each program plays in a round robin against each other
▪️ Each program plays against itself
▪️ Each program plays against a random generator \n\n---\n\n The Winner 🏅 

Surprisingly, one of the simplest programs won the tournament - tit-for-tat.

Tit-for-tat always starts by cooperating and then repeats its opponent's move. \n\n---\n\n Why? 🤔 

Tit-for-tat can be beaten by strategies - like one that always defects. However, on average it performs very well!

In fact, tit-for-tat can never win, because it will never defect first! However, it will never lose by more than one move. 🤯 \n\n---\n\n So, tit-for-tat managed to beat much more complicated strategies submitted by over 60 other researchers from all over the world...

The 5 Levels of Autonomous Driving  🧠 🚙 

There is a lot of talk about level 2, 3, 5 self-driving cars, but what do these levels mean? Which level is Tesla at? What about Waymo?

Let me walk you through the different levels in this thread 👇  \n\n---\n\n Level 0️⃣ - No Automation

Just old fashioned cars here - there are no systems assisting during driving. The human driver needs to do all the work.

▪️ Driving -🧍
▪️ Monitoring -🧍
▪️ Fallback -🧍 \n\n---\n\n Level 1️⃣ - Hands-on

The car takes over part of the driving.

Example: adaptive cruise control - the car accelerates and breaks automatically, but the driver needs to steer.

L1 cars have been around for more than 20 years!

▪️ Driving -🧍/🚙
▪️ Monitoring -🧍
▪️ Fallback -🧍 \n\n---\n\n Level 2️⃣ - Hands-off

The car takes over both steering and acceleration/breaking, but the driver needs to be able to take over at any time.

All car companies now offer L2 systems as an option.

▪️ Driving - 🚙
▪️ Monitoring -🧍
▪️ Fallback -🧍 \n\n---\n\n Going from L2 to L3 📈

The big difference is that the responsibility in case of an accident is transferred from the driver to the car.

This increases complexity significantly, because the car needs to handle all possible edge cases.

Regulations still don't allow L3 systems... \n\n---\n\n Level 3️⃣ - Eyes off

The car does the driving in specific situations (e.g. on the highway). The car may hand back control to the driver, but it needs to give couple of seconds warning, because he may be distracted.

▪️ Driving - 🚙
▪️ Monitoring - 🚙
▪️ Fallback -🧍 \n\n---\n\n There are not L3 cars yet.

Many companies are working on L3 systems and BMW, Mercedes and Honda already announced specific plans. However, there are still regulatory hurdles that need to be overcome.

The FSD Beta of Tesla are still a L2 system! \n\n---\n\n Level 4️⃣ - Mind off

The car drives itself and doesn't rely on a human as a fallback - there may be no one behind the steering wheel.

However, the car can only drive in certain areas and conditions, which it supports.

▪️ Driving - 🚙
▪️ Monitoring - 🚙
▪️ Fallback -🚙 \n\n---\n\n Objective Design Domain (ODD)

These restrictions are called ODD. Example: Waymo's service in Phoenix, which is geofenced and the safety driver is present if the environmental conditions are challenging.

Another company that is allowed to drive without safety driver is Cruise. \n\n---\n\n Level 5️⃣ - Steering Wheel Optional

The ultimate stage of self-driving - the car can handle all situations under all conditions on its own. At this stage, you don't really need a steering wheel anymore.

However, we are still quite far from this... 🤷‍♂️ \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁 

So now you know that almost all systems that are today on the market are sill L2. Yes, even Tesla...

The only comany that arguably has a true L4 system is Waymo, but it still operates in very limited situations under optimal conditions. \n\n---\n\n If you liked this thread and want to read more about self-driving cars and machine learning give me a follow! 👍

There are different ways to detect concept drift for computer vision, depending on the application.

You will need to set up monitoring of your model in production and continuously evaluate it.

1/6  \n\n---\n\n You can do spot checks on production data by labeling some small amounts and comparing the performance to the performance on the test dataset.

This is of course a very expensive and error prone approach (see Simpson's paradox).

2/6 \n\n---\n\n You can evaluate some high-level statistics about the performance of your application. Usually the CV model is not the last part of the pipeline.

For example, a car recognizing speed limits may check if the driver actually drives at a speed close to the speed limit.

3/6 \n\n---\n\n Another example - you are building a web tool that removes the background from images. You can measure how many corrections the user makes manually after that.

In general, check if your customer uses your model output directly or corrects it somehow.

4/6 \n\n---\n\n Another way is to train an autoencoder on the original dataset and note the reconstruction loss. After that, pass a dataset collected from production and see if the reconstruction loss is larger. This would indicate concept drift.

More on this here: 

5/6 \n\n---\n\n In summary, try to get as much information as possible from your end application. In the end, only issues that affect your final product are worth looking into!

6/6

How Does a Self-Driving Car Work? 🔧 🧠 🚙 

This is classical self-driving car software stack. Nowadays, all steps in the pipeline are dominated by machine learning.

Read below for details on each step 👇  \n\n---\n\n Sensors 🎥 

There are 3 main sensors for environment perception 360° around the car:
▪️ Cameras
▪️ Lidars
▪️ Radars

Each sensor has different advantages and disadvantages, so combining all 3 is the best strategy to achieve maximum robustness.  \n\n---\n\n Perception 🖼️ 

The perception module processes all the sensor raw data to detect different objects, drivable space, lane boundaries, measure distance etc.

Fusing the information from different sensors usually increases the quality of the data significantly.  \n\n---\n\n Localization 🗺️ 

Most self-driving cars use a HD map. The map provides information about the geometry of the road, traffic rules and position of interesting objects (e.g. traffic lights).

Localization in the map is done using GPS and landmarks detected by the sensors.  \n\n---\n\n Prediction 🔮 

The goal of this module is to predict the actions and trajectories of other traffic participants.

Will the car in front break?
Will the car cut in front of me?
Will the pedestrian cross the street? 

This is crucial for the car to plan its own trajectory!  \n\n---\n\n Planning 🔀 

In this step the car plans its own trajectory and actions. It needs to consider all other traffic participants, their intentions and the surrounding infrastructure.

One of the main objectives when planning is to maximize safety, but also to drive naturally.  \n\n---\n\n Control 🚙 

The final step is controlling the throttle, breaks and steering so that the car actually drives the planned trajectory.

Here, it is important to have a smooth and natural control and not a steering wheel that twitches all the time.  \n\n---\n\n If you liked this thread and want to read more about self-driving cars and machine learning give me a follow! 👍

End-to-end approach to self-driving 🎥 🕸️ 🕹️ 

I recently wrote about the classical software architecture for a self-driving car. The end-to-end approach is an interesting alternative.

The idea is to go directly from images to the control commands.

Let me tell you more... 👇  

---

 This approach is actually very old, dating back to 1989 and the ALVINN model by CMU. It is a 3-layer neural network using camera images and a laser range finder.

Again, this was back in 1989... 🤯 

  

---

 A modern example is Nvidia's PilotNet - a Convolutional Neural Network with 250M parameters, which takes as input the raw camera image and predicts directly the steering angle of the car.

No explicit lane boundary or freespace detection needed!

  

---

 How to train such network?

Easy! When a human drives the car, we can record the camera images and the actual steering angle as ground truth 🤷‍♂️ 

The network will then learn to predict a steering angle similar to what the human driver chose - this is called immitation learning. 

---

 Take a look at this video to see the system in action. Around 8 minutes you can see what the network actually "sees".

 

---

 Now, to be clear - this is not really a full self-driving car, but only a model that does the steering! There is much more you need to do to actually let the car drive by itself:

▪️ Longitudinal control (acceleration and breaking)
▪️ Lane changes
▪️ Emergency maneuvers 

---

 A similar approach is implemented by Comma AI in their newest version of Openpilot.

They train a version of EfficientNet combined with a network that predicts the trajectory the car needs to drive.

  

---

 The good ✅ 

The advantage of end-to-end networks is that you can get small and efficient models. The net will only focus on solving the final task and no intermediate representations.

Collecting of training data is fairly easy as well - no manual labeling! 

---

 The bad ❌ 

The disadvantage is that it will be very difficult to understand why the net makes some mistakes - we don't have any explicit intermediate representations, like lane boundaries.

It will also need lots of data to cover all possible scenarios on the road. 

---

 There is an interesting paper by Prof. Shashua, CEO of Mobileye, arguing that in order to reach very high accuracy, end-to-end methods will require exponentially more training samples, than the more modular approaches.

 

---

 The truth lies somewhere in the middle...

There are now approaches that try to combine the advantages of both the modular and the end-to-end approaches. I recommend watching this great talk by Prof. Raquel Urtasun from Uber ATG.

Sensors for self-driving cars  🎥 🧠 🚙 

There are 3 main sensors types used in self-driving cars for environment perception:
▪️ Camera
▪️ Radar
▪️ Lidar

They all have different advantages and disadvantages. Read below to learn more about them.

Thread 👇 \n\n---\n\n 1️⃣ Camera

The camera is arguably the most important sensor - the camera images contain the most information compared to the other sensors.

Modern cars across all self-driving levels have many cameras for a 360° coverage:
▪️ BMW 8 series - 7
▪️ Tesla - 8
▪️ Waymo - 29  \n\n---\n\n This is an example from Tesla of what a typical camera sees and detects in the scene. Videos from other companies look very similar.

 \n\n---\n\n 2️⃣ Radar

The radar is one of the oldest sensors used for automation - it is used since 1999 for adaptive cruise control.

It uses the Doppler effect to measure distance and relative velocity to other objects and is very accurate.

Again, modern cars usually have several radars.  \n\n---\n\n Classical radars have fairly low resolution and the raw data is difficult to interpret visually. There is a new generation of imaging radars that promise much better resolution!

Take a look at this video to get an intuition what a radar "sees".

 \n\n---\n\n 3️⃣ Lidar

This is the hot topic in self-driving cars currently!

A laser scanner shoots multiple rays measuring distance to objects and they do this very accurately.

360° lidars are typical for L4 cars, but smaller lidars are already being integrated into production cars.  \n\n---\n\n There are many companies now working on solid state lidars that can be easily integrated in the grill of a car.

Take a look at this video to see how the point cloud from such a lidar looks like.

 \n\n---\n\n Comparison 🔀 

There is no perfect sensor - each of them has its own advantages and disadvantages! Take a look the the table below for a comparison.

The best way is to combine all of them for maximum redundancy and robustness! No everybody agrees to that, though... 🤷‍♂️  \n\n---\n\n If you liked this thread and want to read more about self-driving cars and machine learning follow me @haltakov!

Let's do a small experiment! 🧐 

Look at the image below. The roof is supported only by one pillar and if you put a brick on it it will collapse killing the figure.

How will you make the stucture more stable, so the roof doesn't fall? Every added block costs 10 cents.  \n\n---\n\n Read some more information on the topic here:

Interesting results from the small experiment... 😄 

This was actually a study reported in a Nature paper. Most people offer additive solutions (adding bricks) instead of substractive solutions (removing the pillar).

More details 👇 

 

---

 In this example, the most elegant solution is to remove the pillar completely and let the roof lie on the block. It will be simpler, more stable and won't cost anything.

Some people quickly dismiss this option assuming this is not allowed, but it actualy is 😃 

---

 This isn't because people don't recognize the value, but because many don't consider the substractive solution at all. Me included 🙋‍♂️ 

The paper shows that this happens a lot in real life, especially in regulation. People tend to add new rules, instead of removing old ones. 

---

 I see this a lot in software development as well. People often tend to start adding new features, instead of refactoring the existing functionality and throwing away a big part that is not needed anymore.

Always think about the substractive solution! 

---

Computer vision for self-driving cars 🧠 🚙 

There are different computer vision problems you need to solve in a self-driving car.

▪️ Object detection
▪️ Lane detection
▪️ Drivable space detection
▪️ Semantic segmentation
▪️ Depth estimation
▪️ Visual odometry

Details 👇  \n\n---\n\n Object Detection 🚗🚶‍♂️🚦🛑 

One of the most fundamental tasks - we need to know where other cars and people are, what signs, traffic lights and road markings need to be considered. Objects are identified by 2D or 3D bounding boxes.

Relevant methods: R-CNN, Fast(er) R-CNN, YOLO  \n\n---\n\n Distance Estimation 📏 

After you know what objects are present and where they are in the image, you need to know where they are in the 3D world.

Since the camera is a 2D sensor you need to first estimate the distance to the objects.

Relevant methods: Kalman Filter, Deep SORT  \n\n---\n\n Lane Detection 🛣️ 

Another critical information the car needs to know is where the lane boundaries are. You need to detect not only lane markings, but also curbs, grass edges etc.

There are different methods to do that - from traditional edge detection based methods to CNNs.  \n\n---\n\n Driving Path Prediction ⤴️ 

An alternative is to train a neural network that will directly output the trajectory that the car needs to drive. This can be used as a substitute to centering between the lane markings if they are not visible for example.  \n\n---\n\n Drivable Space Detection ⭕️

The goal here is to detect which parts of the image represent the space where the car can physically drive onto.

The methods here are usually very similar to the semantic segmentation methods (see below).  \n\n---\n\n Semantic Segmentation 🎨

Not all parts of the image can be described by a bounding box or a lane model, e.g. trees, buildings, the sky. Semantic segmentation methods classify each pixel in the image.

Relevant methods: Fully Convolutional NN, UNet, PSPNet  \n\n---\n\n Depth Estimation 📐

The goal is to estimate the distance to every pixel in the image, in order to have a better 3D model of the surrounding.

Methods like stereo and structure-from-motion are now being replaces by self-supervised deep learning models working on single images.  \n\n---\n\n Visual Odometry 🎥 

While we know the movement of the car from the wheel sensors and IMU, determining the actual movement in the camera can be more accurate to get the pitch angle for example.

The visual odometry estimates the 6 DoF movement of the camera between two frames.  \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁 

There are of course many other computer vision problems that may be helpful, but this thread will give you an overview of the most important ones.

As you see, nowadays, deep learning methods (and especially CNNs) dominate all aspects of computer vision... \n\n---\n\n If you liked this thread and want to read more about self-driving cars and machine learning follow me @haltakov!

Karma is a real dog trained to detect drugs. However, he would fail the simplest tests we apply in ML...

Let me take you through this story from the eyes of an ML engineer.



Thread 🧵 \n\n---\n\n Story TLDR 🔖 

The story is about police dogs trained to sniff drugs. The problem is that the dogs often signal drugs even if there are none. Then innocent people land in jail for days.

The cops even joke about the “probable cause on four legs”.

Let's see why is that 👇 \n\n---\n\n 1. Sampling Bias 🤏

Drugs were found in 64% of the cars Karma identified, which was praised by the police as very good. In the end, most people don't carry drugs in their cars, so 64% seems solid.

There was a sampling problem though... 👇 \n\n---\n\n The cars were not sampled at random! The police only did the sniff test if there was a serious suspicion that something is wrong. 

The chance there are drugs in the car is much higher in this case! \n\n---\n\n 2. Evaluation Metrics 🔍

The police referred to a 2014 study from Poland measuring the efficacy of sniffer dogs. The problem was that every test actually contained drugs!

This means there was no chance to measure false positives from the dogs! Only recall, not precision 🤦‍♂️ \n\n---\n\n 3. Leaking Training Data 🚰

Another study found that the dogs learned to recognize the emotions of their handlers during tests. They felt that their human wanted them to find drugs in the specific test scenario, so they did.

The trainer leaked the ground truth during testing. \n\n---\n\n 4. Overfitting ➿

Similar to the one above, in many cases, the dog saw that their handler wanted to find drugs in a car during a traffic stop. So it would raise an alarm.

The dog was rewarded before the car was actually searched! It found an easy signal giving it a reward. \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁 

It is fascinating how many problems there are with the sniffer dogs that are well known to machine learning engineers (and of course mathematicians). Some of them are even common sense...

Avoid these problems not only when training your model, but also in life 😃 \n\n---\n\n If you liked this thread and want to read more about self-driving cars and machine learning follow me @haltakov!

A short lesson on object tracking 🧑🏻‍🏫 

Look at this video from a @Tesla Model 3 driving on the highway. The display shows multiple traffic lights coming out of the truck in front towards the car. What's going on? 🤔

This is a typical case of a 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗹𝗼𝘀𝘀!

Thread 👇  \n\n---\n\n The problem 🤔

The truck in front carries 3 real traffic lights. The problem is that the computer vision system on the Tesla assumes that traffic lights are static (which is a good assumption in general 😄). In this case, though, the traffic lights are moving at 120 km/h...

👇  \n\n---\n\n Object detection 🚦 

A typical object detection system takes a single camera frame and detects all kinds of objects in it. 

One of the best models for object detection is YOLO. I just ran this image through it and sure enough, it detects 2 of the traffic lights!

👇  \n\n---\n\n If you want to learn more about how deep learning based object detection works, check out this thread.



👇 \n\n---\n\n Object tracking 📏

We now want to track an object over multiple frames. In this way, we can more accurately determine the position of the object. 

Given the detections in two frames, we need to associate each object in the first frame to an object in the second frame.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Static object assumption 🚦 

For traffic lights, it is reasonable to assume they are static. Therefore, the change of its position in the second frame only depends on the speed of our own car.

Since we know it, we can predict where the light will be in the next frame.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Track loss 🤚

The problem is that these 🚦 are actually moving, so the prediction is wrong. The Tesla cannot associate them anymore, so:

1️⃣ The light from the previous frame is counted as lost
2️⃣ The light from this frame is regarded as a new object seen for the first time

👇 \n\n---\n\n Tracking 🚗

What happens to the lost object? The Tesla assumes the light can't be detected for some reason. Instead, It shows on the display the expected position of the light based on the vehicle speed.

That's why the lights come "flying" towards the car in the display. \n\n---\n\n As you can see in the video, this happens all the time. This is what happens when we make assumptions about the real world, that fail in some situations... 🤷‍♂️

Can you detect COVID-19 using Machine Learning? 🤔

You have an X-ray or CT scan and the task is to detect if the patient has COVID-19 or not. Sounds doable, right?

None of the 415 ML papers published on the subject in 2020 was usable. Not a single one!

Let's see why 👇  \n\n---\n\n Researchers from Cambridge took all papers on the topic published from January to October 2020.

▪️ 2212 papers
▪️ 415 after initial screening
▪️ 62 chosen for detailed analysis
▪️ 0 with potential for clinical use



There are important lessons here 👇 \n\n---\n\n Small datasets 🐁 

Getting medical data is hard, because of privacy concerns, and at the beginning of the pandemic, there was just not much data in general.

Many papers were using very small datasets often collected from a single hospital - not enough for real evaluation.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Biased datasets 🧒🧑‍🦲

Some papers used a dataset that contained non-COVID images from children and COVID images from adults. These methods probably learned to distinguish children from adults... 🤷‍♂️

👇 \n\n---\n\n Training and testing on the same data ❌

OK, you just never do that! Never!

👇 \n\n---\n\n Unbalanced datasets ⚖️

There are much more non-COVID scans than real COVID cases, but not all papers managed to adequately balance their dataset to account for that.

Check out this thread for more details on how to deal with imbalanced data:


👇 \n\n---\n\n Unclear evaluation methodology ⁉️

Many papers failed to disclose the amount of data they were tested or important aspects of how their models work leading to poor reproducibility and biased results.

👇 \n\n---\n\n The problem is in the data 💽

The big problem for most methods was the availability of high-quality data and a deep understanding of the problem - many papers didn't even consult with radiologists.

👇 \n\n---\n\n A high-quality and diverse dataset is more important than your fancy model! \n\n---\n\n References 🗒️

More detailed coverage:

I think the important point is that rushing to publish results based on small and bad quality datasets undermines the credibility of ML...

 \n\n---\n\n There are already much better datasets and I'm sure this problem will get solved at some point. There is also a promising Kaggle challenge:



The point is that it needs to be done right and the Nature paper gives some guidance how.

 \n\n---\n\n Yes, this is a common problem with such datasets/competitions. At some point people start figuring out how to fine tune on the test set...

The Kernel Trick

The kernel trick is a cool method that helps efficiently solve some classes of machine learning problems and is used a lot with SVMs.

Here a short intuition without going deep into the math...

Thread 👇  \n\n---\n\n Imagine you have points belonging to 2 classes, which you can't separate by a line - this is basically what SVM does.

(Image source: Wikipedia)

However, you could do something here... 👇  \n\n---\n\n You can transform the points in a 3D space, where the 3rd coordinate is the distance of the point from the center (x^2 + y^2).

Now it is easy to draw a plane here and separate the points - problem solved!

(Image source: Wikipedia)

So far so good, but it gets better... 👇  \n\n---\n\n Transforming all points in another space may be computationally expensive - the Kernel Trick comes to the rescue!

It allows us to draw such decision boundaries in higher dimensional spaces (even infinite ones) without explicitly transforming the data!

How? 👇 \n\n---\n\n In SVMs we need to compute the dot product between points. There is a clever mathematical way to directly compute the dot product of the points in another space without explicitly transforming them!

We can apply a kernel that does that!

😲 👇 \n\n---\n\n Without kernel trick - explicit conversion ❌

1⃣ We have points 𝘅𝟭 and 𝘅𝟮
2⃣ We transform them into another space using junction 𝗳: 𝗳(𝘅𝟭), 𝗳(𝘅𝟮)
3⃣ We compute the dot product of the transformed points: 𝗳(𝘅𝟭) · 𝗳(𝘅𝟮)

👇 \n\n---\n\n With kernel trick - implicit conversion ✅

1⃣ We have points 𝘅𝟭 and 𝘅𝟮
2⃣ We want to implicitly transform them into another space using junction 𝗳
3⃣ We use the kernel 𝗸 of function f to directly compute the dot product of the transformed points: 𝗸(𝘅𝟭, 𝘅𝟮)

👇 \n\n---\n\n Coming up with the kernel of a specific function may not be trivial and requires some maths, but it is possible for many useful functions!

Scikit-learn for example offers you implementations of different kernels for SVM:



👇 \n\n---\n\n Conclusion

The kernel trick allows us to efficiently compute the dot product of points that we want to transform in another space, without doing the transformation explicitly.

This helps us solve machine learning problems that can otherwise not be separated by a line/plane. \n\n---\n\n If you liked this thread and want to read more about self-driving cars and machine learning follow me @haltakov!

Tesla is getting rid of the radar. But are cameras enough for self-driving? 👀 🧠 🚙 

While most other self-driving companies rely heavily on sensor redundancy, @Tesla now uses only 8 cameras.

Can they (safely) push the limits of computer vision enough?

A thread 🧵  \n\n---\n\n No Lidar 🚨

@elonmusk famously said that lidar is a "crutch" so Teslas never had one.

Lidars, though, are very accurate in measuring distance (and FMCW lidars also measure velocity) and have increasingly higher resolution providing redundancy and increasing safety.

👇 \n\n---\n\n No HD Map 📍 

They also don't use HD maps, which provide information about the surrounding environment that may be difficult to capture with cameras alone.

Well, they clearly do some mapping for their FSD beta, but much less than Waymo for example.



👇 \n\n---\n\n Drivers and Maps 🗺️ 

Interestingly, human drivers do create a local HD map in their heads.

When you're driving in a familiar area you know where each lane is going, what intersection is coming up, where the traffic lights are etc.

Driving there is easier and safer!

👇 \n\n---\n\n No Radar 📡

Radars are extremely accurate in measuring speed and distance to other vehicles. 

However, they have problems mostly due to their low resolution (Tesla used a fairly standard radar by Continental). This makes fusing camera and radar information tricky.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Vision is all you need 👀 

Tesla will focus on cameras only. This talk by @karpathy from CVPR explains why and how. 



Well, Tesla have a good argument because humans are able to drive only relying on their eyes.

There are some trade-offs, though 👇 \n\n---\n\n Advantages ✅ 

There are certainly many advantages in getting rid of the radar:

▪️ Reducing costs
▪️ Reducing effort to fuse radar information
▪️ Reducing effort to deal with the specific radar failure modes
▪️ Focusing the team on one technology only - vision

👇 \n\n---\n\n Disadvantages ❌

However, this strategy has drawbacks as well:

▪️ No redundancy to the vision system, potentially impacting safety
▪️ No radar available for future training data
▪️ Possibly worse performance in adverse weather conditions
▪️ Missing on new radar technology

👇 \n\n---\n\n Redundancy and safety 🦺 

Self-driving is far from solved and other companies are using every available technology to increase redundancy and safety. 

Tesla bets on advancing the state-of-the-art in Computer Vision fast enough to compensate for this, but will this work?

👇  \n\n---\n\n As Andrej says in the talk, sensor fusion is difficult, because cameras and radars have different error modes. But this is exactly why there are situations where radar can provide better data than cameras. For example in adverse weather conditions.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Training data 💪 

Tesla trained their neural network to estimate distance, speed, and acceleration on a massive 1.5 PB dataset (1M clips) sourced from the fleet. However, humans are bad at annotating these values to create ground truth...

👇 \n\n---\n\n They use the radar as one source of ground truth for training the vision system. If not available in the fleet this source will not be usable in the future. They will need to rely on object tracking during the processing of the training clips.

👇 \n\n---\n\n New radar technology 🆕

Some companies are working on imaging radars that can provide much higher resolution than the one Tesla is using. Just look at this example from Mobileye's radar!

Tesla not investing in radars will not benefit from this technological advancement.

👇  \n\n---\n\n If somebody can pull this off, this is Tesla! 🤷‍♂️

This is a challenge that they are uniquely positioned to solve, because they:

▪️ have access to huge amount of data from the fleet
▪️ control their entire stack
▪️ invest in deep learning infrastructure
▪️ are focused

👇 \n\n---\n\n Impressive Results 🏆

The results that @karpathy showed in the talk are very impressive! This shows how important it is to focus on building and curating a high-quality dataset (1.5 PB) and having the resources to use it (5th most powerful supercomputer in the world). \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁

Tesla's strategy to focus on vision only is undoubtedly very brave, but also very risky. But it could work...

They are arguably the only company in the position to do that and what they've achieved already is nothing short of amazing. \n\n---\n\n Tesla using another crutch ♿ 

And finally on a more philosophical level - Tesla's network is estimating distance, speed, and acceleration, but this is *not* how humans drive! We use vision but in quite a different way.

Is Tesla using just another crutch there...? 🤔 \n\n---\n\n I regularly post similar threads on machine learning, computer vision, and self-driving.

Follow me @haltakov for more! \n\n---\n\n This is a great question! Lidars and radars have no problem in the night.

There are camera sensors that with good low light performance, but still it may be difficult. On the front you also have the headlights, but not on the back and on the side...

 \n\n---\n\n This is true, but self-driving cars today (including Tesla) are not really driving like a human does. Why would then Tesla estimate accurate distance, speed and acceleration? People cannot do that either 😃

 \n\n---\n\n The high-level fusion between the camera data and the radar data is not very computationally expensive. The problem is rather writing robust code that can handle the different failure modes and edge cases from both sensors in a robust way.

Dataset bias strikes again! 😬

This is a great example of dataset bias! This ML method classifies skin lesions as being malignant or not.

Can you see the problem from the examples? 🤔 

Let me shortly explain 👇  \n\n---\n\n The dataset used to train the model contains images of both malignant and benign lesions. The problem is that the malignant images often contain rulers printed on the skin. They are used by doctors to assess the lesion over time.

Guess what the model learned... 👇 \n\n---\n\n The ML model learned to detect the rulers... 🤷‍♂️

"In our dataset, images with rulers were more likely to be malignant; thus the algorithm inadvertently “learned” that rulers are malignant."

 \n\n---\n\n To avoid dataset bias it is important to sample all data in the same way (and sample the whole distribution).

This would mean not having the rulers in the image. This may be difficult, though because you need them for doctors to classify correctly.

 \n\n---\n\n From the top of my head you could try the following:
▪️ Taking the images in a way that the ruler is not visible (may be impossible)
▪️ Removing the rulers with Photoshop
▪️ Adding rulers to all healthy examples 😃
▪️ Marking the ruler in the image as data that may not be used \n\n---\n\n Several people pointed this out and it is a very valid point - another bias could be the skin color!

For this dataset I couldn't find information about that, but it is another thing to consider!

 \n\n---\n\n This is a great point - inspecting what your model does internally can help you find these issues.

 \n\n---\n\n Oh, the model is not stupid at all. It always finds the shortest path to solve the problem 😀

It's up to the model designer to define the problem in such a way that the solution is useful...

How it works - changing ads in the live stream of a football game ⚽ 📺 

I asked you yesterday how you would implement such a computer vision system and there were some quite interesting answers.



Let's see how it is done now 👇 \n\n---\n\n Magenta screen 🟣

The LED screens at the stadium show each frame for 20ms in total (50 frames per second), but 2ms are used to show a magenta color, while the other 18ms show the real ad.

This is too short for the people at the stadium to see, but not for the camera... 👇  \n\n---\n\n Cameras 🎥 

The cameras at the stadium are synchronized with the system so they can shoot a frame exactly in the 2ms the magenta "screen" is shown.

Replacing the magenta color with another video is a fairly standard technique in video production (chromakey).

There's more 👇 \n\n---\n\n Camera movement ↔️

The cameras are not static though - they pan, zoom and tilt. Aligning the ad video with the screen is not trivial.

The system uses additional tracking of the cameras to determine their orientation and improve the overlaying of the ad. \n\n---\n\n Performance ⏩ 

This approach is great, because it doesn't require lots of computation ressources. This is important since the system needs to process a high-quality video stream (4K or more) in real-time! \n\n---\n\n If you are interested in more details about this system developed by the Fraunhofer Institute, read the full article:

AI Job Interviews - another good example of bias in ML 🤦‍♂️

Two journalists tested some AI tools for assessing job candidates. Even when the candidate read a Wiki article in German instead of answering questions in English, the AI systems gave them good scores 🤷‍♂️

Let's unpack 👇  \n\n---\n\n The Setup 🔬

The journalists created a fake job posting on two AI interview platforms. They specified the traits of the ideal candidate and provided the questions that need to be answered during the interview.

Then they started experimenting... 👇 \n\n---\n\n The Positive Test ✅ 

One of them did a fake interview giving all the right answers and predictably got very high scores - 8.5 out of 9 👍

Then she tried something different... 👇 \n\n---\n\n The Negative Test ❌

In a second interview, instead of answering the questions in English, she just read the article on psychometrics from the German Wikipedia 😁

One system gave her a score of 6 out of 9, while the other determined she is a 73% match for the job.

Oops... 👇 \n\n---\n\n What happened? 🔍

Interestingly, one of the systems generated a transcript which was obviously meaningless.

This means that the machine learning model behind the tool likely captured nuances of the intonation of the speaker instead of the meaning of the actual words.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Bias ⚖️

These tools are biased - they incorrectly put more weight on the intonation instead of the actual meaning of what is being said.

This is shown when one of the components is artificially removed - in this case, the meaning (German instead of English).

More examples 👇 \n\n---\n\n Bias again ⚖️

Another AI interview tool was reported to give candidates different ratings when they used different backgrounds or accessories during the interviews.

Why does this happen? 👇 \n\n---\n\n The Dataset 💽

One likely reason is the dataset used to train the machine learning models. It may not contain enough data for the model to correctly learn to discriminate important features. It overfits on some non-essential features, like the background.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Black-Box Models ⬛ 

Another common problem is the use of black-box models where it is difficult to interpret why the algorithm makes a certain decision (for example in the case of neural networks).

More work is needed to inspect what the model is paying attention to.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Lack of Testing 🧪 

Furthermore, it seems that the systems weren't tested in scenarios like this one and weren't prepared to meaningfully handle these cases. The question is then, what other cases will not be handled correctly?

👇 \n\n---\n\n Bias in Human Interviews 👤

Interestingly, human interviews are also subject to many biases and this is a known problem. The hope is that AI systems will help reduce those biases, but one needs to be careful to not just replace them with different ones. \n\n---\n\n More Details 🗒️

Machine Learning in the Real World 🧠 🤖

ML for real-world applications is much more than designing fancy networks and fine-tuning parameters.

In fact, you will spend most of your time curating a good dataset.

Let's go through the steps of the process together 👇  \n\n---\n\n Collect Data 💽

We need to represent the real world as accurately as possible. If some situations are underrepresented we are introducing Sampling Bias.

Sampling Bias is nasty because we'll have high test accuracy, but our model will perform badly when deployed.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Traffic Lights 🚦

Let's build a model to recognize traffic lights for a self-driving car. We need to collect data for different:

▪️ Lighting conditions
▪️ Weather conditions
▪️ Distances and viewpoints
▪️ Strange variants

And if we sample only 🚦 we won't detect 🚥  🤷‍♂️

👇  \n\n---\n\n Data Cleaning 🧹

Now we need to clean all corrupted and irrelevant samples. We need to remove:

▪️ Overexposed or underexposed images
▪️ Images in irrelevant situations
▪️ Faulty images

Leaving them in the dataset will hurt our model's performance!

👇  \n\n---\n\n Preprocess Data ⚙️

Most ML models like their data nicely normalized and properly scaled. Bad normalization can also lead to worse performance (I have a nice story for another time...)

▪️ Crop and resize all images
▪️ Normalize all values (usually 0 mean and 1 std. dev.)

👇 \n\n---\n\n Label Data 🏷️

Manual labeling is expensive. Try to be clever and automate as much as possible:

▪️ Generate labels from the input data
▪️ Use slow, but accurate algorithms offline
▪️ Pre-label data during collection
▪️ Develop good labeling tools
▪️ Use synthetic data?

👇 \n\n---\n\n Label Correction ❌

You will always have errors in the labels - humans make mistakes. Review and iterate!

▪️ Spot checks to find systematic problems
▪️ Improve labeling guidelines and tools
▪️ Review test results and fix labels
▪️ Label samples multiple times

👇 \n\n---\n\n The danger of label errors 🧑‍🏫

A recent study by MIT found that 10 of the most popular public datasets had 3.4% label errors on average (ImageNet had 5.8%).

This even lead authors to choose the wrong (and more complex) model as their best one!



👇 \n\n---\n\n Balance Dataset ⚖️ 

Dealing with imbalanced data can be tricky...

Let's classify the color of the 🚦 - we can get 97% just by learning to recognize 🟢 and 🔴, just because 🟡 is severely underrepresented.

I have a separate thread on this topic:


👇 \n\n---\n\n Train and Evaluate Model 💪📏

This is the part that is usually covered by ML courses. Now is the time to try out different features, network architectures, fine-tune parameters etc.

But we are not done yet... 👇 \n\n---\n\n Iterative Process 🔄

In most real-world applications the bottleneck is not the model itself, but the data. After having a first model, we need to review where it has problems and go back to:

▪️ Collecting and labeling more data
▪️ Correcting labels
▪️ Balancing the data

👇 \n\n---\n\n Deploy Model 🚢

Deploying the model in production poses some additional constraints:

▪️ Speed
▪️ Cost
▪️ Stability
▪️ Privacy
▪️ Hardware availability and integration

We have to find a good trade-off between these factors and accuracy.

Now we are done, right? No...👇 \n\n---\n\n Monitoring 🖥️

The performance of the model will start degrading over time because the world keeps changing:

▪️ Concept drift - the real-world distribution changes
▪️ Data drift - the properties of the data change

We need to detect this, retrain, and deploy again.

Example 👇 \n\n---\n\n Drift ➡️

We now have a trained model to recognize 🚦, but people keep inventing new variants - see what some creative people in Munich came up with 😄

We need a way to detect that we have a problem, collect data, label, and retrain our model.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁 

This is how a typical ML pipeline for real-world applications looks like. Please remember this:

▪️ Curating a good dataset is the most important thing
▪️ Dataset curation is an iterative process
▪️ Monitoring is critical to ensure good performance over time  \n\n---\n\n If you liked this thread you will also like the other things I post too. I regularly tweet about machine learning, computer vision, and self-driving cars.

How to evaluate your ML model? 📏

Your accuracy is 97%, so this is pretty good, right? Right? No! ❌

Just looking at the model accuracy is not enough. Let me tell you about some other metrics:
▪️ Recall
▪️ Precision
▪️ F1 score
▪️ Confusion matrix

Let's start 👇 \n\n---\n\n We'll use this example in the whole thread - classifying traffic light colors (e.g. for a self-driving car).

Yellow traffic lights appear much less often, so our dataset may look like this.

This means our model could reach 97% accuracy, by ignoring all 🟡 lights. Not good!

👇  \n\n---\n\n Let's assume now that we trained our model and we get the following predictions.

Do you think this model is good? How can we quantitatively evaluate its performance? How should it be improved?

Let's first discuss the possible error types 👇  \n\n---\n\n Let's evaluate how well our model classifies 🟡  lights. There are 3 possible cases:

✅ True Positive - our model correctly classifies the 🟡
❌ False Negative - our model classifies 🟡  as another color
❌ False Positive - our model classifies another color as 🟡 

👇  \n\n---\n\n Accuracy

We can now just take the percentage of correctly classified samples - this is called the accuracy. In this case, it is 75%.

What is the problem? 🤔 

We have no idea in which cases the model has problems and needs to be improved.

We need to look at other metrics 👇  \n\n---\n\n Recall

The recall is computed separately for each color as the percentage of samples of the color classified correctly (per class accuracy).

We now see that we have a big problem with 🟡 and we should also improve 🟢. 

On the other hand 🔴 looks perfect. But it isn't... 👇  \n\n---\n\n Precision

The precision tells us how many of the model's predictions for a certain class were correct. The precision for 🔴 is low because the model wrongly classifies 🟢 and 🟡 lights as 🔴. 

The 🟢 looks much better, while 🟡 is bad again.

Now, let's combine both 👇  \n\n---\n\n F1 Score

The problem with Recall is that it ignores False Positives (FPs), while Precision ignores False Negatives. The F1 score is another metric that considers both.

We can see that 🟡 is indeed quite bad, but we also see that both 🔴 and 🟢 need to be improved.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Confusion Matrix

We can also get an overview of both FPs and FNs by looking at the Confusion Matrix. It breaks down for each class, how it was classified.

For example, looking at the 🟡 row, we see that 67% of the 🟡 lights were classified as 🔴 , 33% as 🟡 and none as 🟢 

👇  \n\n---\n\n If you look closely, you'll see that the diagonal of the matrix is exactly the Recall.

However, in the Confusion Matrix we can also see where we have FPs - for example, the 🟡 and 🟢 lights that are classified as 🔴.

That's why I like to use the Confusion Matrix.

👇 \n\n---\n\n So, let's summarize:

▪️ Accuracy - doesn't tell us where the problems are
▪️ Recall - ignores FPs
▪️ Precision - ignores FNs
▪️ F1 score - combines Recall and Precision
▪️ Confusion matrix - overview overall error types

You need to choose the best metrics for your application! \n\n---\n\n I regularly write threads like this to help people get started with Machine Learning.

👇 \n\n---\n\n  \n\n---\n\n Yes, it is a fine distinction. You can remember it like that:
▪️ Recall looks for misses (FNs) - it counts what percentage of the real objects were detected.
▪️ Precision looks for falses (FPs) - it counts what percentage of the predictions were correct.

 \n\n---\n\n There is a trade-off between both.

I can make my model more sensitive and it will start to detect more objects (TPs), but will also detect more wrong objects (FPs) - Recall 📈, Precision 📉.

Less sensitivity means fewer FPs, but also more misses (FNs) - Recall 📉, Precision 📈.

Let's talk about a common problem in ML - imbalanced data ⚖️ 

Imagine we want to detect all pixels belonging to a traffic light from a self-driving car's camera. We train a model with 99.88% performance. Pretty cool, right?

Actually, this model is useless ❌

Let me explain 👇  \n\n---\n\n The problem is the data is severely imbalanced - the ratio between traffic light pixels and background pixels is 800:1.

If we don't take any measures, our model will learn to classify each pixel as background giving us 99.88% accuracy. But it's useless!

What can we do? 👇 \n\n---\n\n Let me tell you about 3 ways of dealing with imbalanced data:

▪️ Choose the right evaluation metric
▪️ Undersampling your dataset
▪️ Oversampling your dataset
▪️ Adapting the loss

Let's dive in 👇 \n\n---\n\n 1️⃣ Evaluation metrics 

Looking at the overall accuracy is a very bad idea when dealing with imbalanced data. There are other measures that are much better suited:
▪️ Precision
▪️ Recall
▪️ F1 score

I wrote a whole thread on that

 \n\n---\n\n 2️⃣ Undersampling

The idea is to throw away samples of the overrepresented classes.

One way to do this is to randomly throw away samples. However, ideally, we want to make sure we are only throwing away samples that look similar.

Here is a strategy to achieve that 👇  \n\n---\n\n Clever Undersampling

▪️ Compute image features for each sample using a pre-trained CNN
▪️ Cluster images by visual appearance using k-means, DBSCAN etc.
▪️ Remove similar samples from the clusters (check out for example the Near-Miss or the Tomek Links strategies)

👇 \n\n---\n\n 3️⃣ Oversampling

The idea here is to generate new samples from underrepresented classes. The easiest way to do this is of course to repeat the samples. However, we are not gaining any new information with this.

Some better strategies 👇  \n\n---\n\n Data Augmentation

Create new samples by modifying the existing ones. You can apply many different transformations like for example:

▪️ Rotation
▪️ Flipping 
▪️ Zooming
▪️ Skewing
▪️ Color changing

We can do some even more advanced stuff 👇  \n\n---\n\n SMOTE

The idea is to create new samples by combining two existing ones.

This technique is more common when working with tabular data, but can be used for images as well. For that, we can combine the images in feature space and reconstruct them using an autoencoder.  \n\n---\n\n Synthetic Data

Another option is to generate synthetic data to add to our dataset. This can be done either using a GAN or using a realistic simulation to render new images.

There are even companies that specialize in this, like  (not affiliated)

👇  \n\n---\n\n 4️⃣ Adapting the loss function

Finally, an easy way to improve the balance is directly in your loss function. We can specify that samples of the underrepresented class to have more weight and contribute more to the loss function.

Here is an example of how to do it in the code.  \n\n---\n\n So, let's recap the main ideas when dealing with imbalanced data:

▪️ Make sure you are using the right evaluation metric
▪️ Use undersampling and oversampling techniques to improve your dataset
▪️ Use class weights in your loss function \n\n---\n\n I regularly write threads like this to help people get started with Machine Learning.

Did you ever want to learn how to read ROC curves? 📈🤔

This is something you will encounter a lot when analyzing the performance of machine learning models.

Let me help you understand them 👇  \n\n---\n\n What does ROC mean?

ROC stands for Receiver Operating Characteristic but just forget about it. This is a military term from the 1940s and doesn't make much sense today.

Think about these curves as True Positive Rate vs. False Positive Rate plots.

Now, let's dive in 👇 \n\n---\n\n The ROC curve visualizes the trade-offs that a binary classifier makes between True Positives and False Positives.

This may sound too abstract for you so let's look at an example. After that, I encourage you to come back and read the previous sentence again!

Now the example 👇 \n\n---\n\n We are building a self-driving car and want it to stop at red traffic lights 🚦

(You saw this coming, right 😁?)

We build a classifier to determine if the car should STOP (light is 🔴 or 🟡) or PASS (light is 🟢). I'm using just 2 classes here to make the example simpler.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Now we ask the model - should the car stop at the 🚦?

There are 4 possible cases
▪️ Light is 🔴, model says STOP - True Positive
▪️ Light is 🔴, model says PASS - False Negative
▪️ Light is 🟢, model says PASS - True Negative
▪️ Light is 🟢, model says STOP - False Positive

👇 \n\n---\n\n Given many examples from our validation/test set, we can compute the following metrics:

▪️ True Positive Rate (TPR) - how good is our model telling us correctly to stop.
▪️ False Positive Rate (FPR) - how often does our model tell us wrongly to stop

To get a feeling for it 👇  \n\n---\n\n A high TPR means that we stop at most 🔴 lights.
A low TPR means that we often miss 🔴 lights and pass.

A high FPR means that we often confuse 🟢 lights for 🔴 and wrongly stop.
A low FPR means that we don't have many false stops.

So, we want a high TPR and low FPR, right? 👇 \n\n---\n\n Evaluating a model on a validation/test dataset will give us exactly one TPR and FPR value. Here an example of a (not so good) classifier:
▪️ TPR = 95%
▪️ FPR = 1%

Wait, but this is just one point on the TPR vs. FPR plot above. So, how do we get the curve now?

👇 \n\n---\n\n Machine learning classifiers usually don't simply output a class, but they tell you the probability of each class being the correct one.

You can then define a threshold based on which you decide. For example, stop at a light only if the classifier is 99% sure. Or 90%? 80%?

👇 \n\n---\n\n We can now try many different values of the threshold and evaluate on our validation/test dataset. 

Every time we will get different values for TPR and FPR and we can put them on the ROC plot. This is how we get our curve!

So let's look at different thresholds 👇 \n\n---\n\n Here is an example plot. Look at the 3 points I marked on it to see the fundamental trade-off between FPR and TPR.

1️⃣ TPR = 20%, FPR = 2% - setting a high threshold (we want to be really sure before stopping), we won't have many FPs, but we will also miss many real 🔴.

👇  \n\n---\n\n 2️⃣ TPR = 81%, FPR = 33% - decreasing the threshold improves the detection rate, but now we also have many false detections of 🔴.

3️⃣ TPR = 99%, FPR = 90% - a model with a very low threshold will detect almost all 🔴, but will wrongly classify most 🟢 as 🔴 as well.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Changing the threshold will only change the trade-off not make our model better.

However, this is still an important step when you are tuning the model for a specific application. For self-driving cars, it is **very** Important to not run the red lights - you need high TPR!

👇 \n\n---\n\n We can, however, train another model using more data, more parameters, better optimization. But how do we tell that it is really better and not just finding a different trade-off point?

The new ROC curve should be closer to the upper left corner of the graph! 👇  \n\n---\n\n A better ROC curve means that we can choose thresholds that give us the same TPR for both classifiers, but the better one will have less FPR.

Alternatively, for the same FPR, the better classifier will have a higher TPR.

👇 \n\n---\n\n There is one problem, though - in the reality, ROC curves are much noisier. At some points, the curve of one model may be higher, but at others lower. So which one is better in this case?

See this image from a real evaluation (credit to Wikipedia). Which one is best?

👇  \n\n---\n\n To get a single number summarizing the whole ROC curve, we can compute the Area under the Curve (AOC).

This will again be a number between 0 and 1 and expresses the probability of the model to rank a random positive example higher than a random negative example.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁

To recap quickly:

▪️ ROC curves visualize the trade-off between TPR and FPR
▪️ The curve is created by varying an internal decision threshold
▪️ Models with a curve closer to the upper left corner are better
▪️ Use the Area under the Curve to get a single metric \n\n---\n\n I regularly write threads like this to help people get started with Machine Learning.

Do you know the car that didn't like vanilla ice cream? 🍦

A man went to the store every night after dinner to buy ice cream. If he bought vanilla 🍦 his new Pontiac wouldn't start. If he bought any other kind the car would start fine.

A story about correlation vs causation 👇 

---

 The man wrote to Pontiac about the problem acknowledging how crazy it sounds. Pontiac sent an engineer to check it out and sure enough, the problem happened every time the man bought vanilla 🍦.

However, the engineer knew - the ice cream was not *causing* the problem... 👇 

---

 What did he do? He gathered statistics! He visited every day and took notes about other things that could have an impact: time of day, type of fuel, time to drive to the store, etc.

This helped him find another correlation that actually caused the problem 👇 

---

 It took the man less time to buy the vanilla 🍦 compared to any other kind. The reason was that the store had the popular vanilla 🍦 at the front and all other kinds at the back. So it took longer to fetch the chocolate ice cream for example.

Time was the problem 👇 

---

 The cause was vapor lock. This happens when the liquid fuel is heated by the engine so much that it turns into gas in the fuel system. This causes problems with the fuel pump.

Waiting longer allowed the engine to cool down and the fuel to become liquid again...

Lesson 👇 

---

 Sometimes we observe two effects at the same time - vanilla 🍦 and car not starting. This is called correlation.

This doesn't mean one causes the other. It is often the case that there is another unobserved effect (timing) that causes the first two effects. This is causation.

There are two problems with ROC curves

❌ They don't work for imbalanced datasets
❌ They don't work for object detection problems

So what do we do to evaluate our machine learning models properly in these cases?

We use a Precision-Recall curve.

Another one of my threads 👇  \n\n---\n\n Last week I wrote another detailed thread on ROC curves. I recommend that you read it first if you don't know what they are.



Then go on 👇 \n\n---\n\n ❌ Problem 1 - Imbalanced Data

ROC curves measure the True Positive Rate (also known as Accuracy). So, if you have an imbalanced dataset, the ROC curve will not tell you if your classifier completely ignores the underrepresented class.

More details: 

👇 \n\n---\n\n ❌ Problem 2 - Object Detection Problems

ROC curves measure the False Positive Rate (FPR) according to the following formula.

In object detection problems the True Negatives don't make sense. There are so many possibilities to detect the background class.

Let's dive deeper 👇  \n\n---\n\n I'll use my favorite example again - traffic lights detection (for a self-driving car 🧠🚗).

We want to detect the presence and location (using a bounding box) of traffic lights in images. This is a typical Object Detection problem - an important class of CV problems.

👇  \n\n---\n\n The typical way to solve this is to design a neural network that will check many locations in the image and classify them as being a traffic light or not (background).

For more details, check out this thread: 

Now on the actual problem 👇 \n\n---\n\n There is no (practical) way to define True Negatives

These would be all locations in the image that don't contain a traffic light and where our model correctly predicted no traffic lights as well.

Imagine now going through all possible bounding box sizes for every pixel...

👇 \n\n---\n\n Common evaluation metrics for this are Precision and Recall.

▪️ Precision - the percentage of traffic lights the model detected that are indeed real traffic lights
▪️ Recall - the percentage of real traffic lights that the model detected

Confusing? Let's see some examples 👇  \n\n---\n\n High Precision, Low Recall

In this example, the Precision is 100% (all detected lights are correct), but the Recall is only 50% (2 out of 4 lights missed).

👇  \n\n---\n\n Low Precision, High Recall

In this example, the Precision is 67% (4 out of 6 detected lights are correct), while the Recall is 100% (all 4 real lights are detected).

👇  \n\n---\n\n Precision and Recall give us a way to measure both types of errors (FPs and FNs), without requiring us to count TNs.

By the way, that's why they work better for imbalanced data! Object Detection is imbalanced - there is much more background than objects.

Now the curve 👇 \n\n---\n\n For every candidate the network classifies, it gives us the probability of it being a traffic light. We need to choose a threshold on the probability to consider it a detected light.

It could be 50% if we don't want to miss many lights or 99% if we want to be really sure.

👇 \n\n---\n\n For every value of the threshold, we will get different Precision and Recall when evaluating our test dataset.

▪️ High thresholds - high Precision, low Recall
▪️ Low thresholds - low Precision, high Recall

Plotting these values gives us the Precision-Recall curve. \n\n---\n\n The Precision-Recall Curve visualizes the trade-off between making False Positives and False Negatives.

Similar to ROC curves, we can also compare different models. If the curve of one model is closer to the upper right corner than another one, then it is a better model.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁

To recap:
▪️ ROC curves don't work for imbalanced data
▪️ ROC curves don't work for object detection (can't count TNs)
▪️ Prevision-Recall curves are computed in a similar way to ROC curves
▪️ Prevision-Recall curves visualize the trade-off between FNs and FPs \n\n---\n\n I regularly write threads like this to help people get started with Machine Learning.

Why are ROC curves not suitable for imbalanced datasets? 🤔

I wrote a thread on ROC curves vs. Precision-Recall curves yesterday, but I didn't articulate this point well enough.

Let's take an example - look at the confusion matrix below and let's dive in... 👇  \n\n---\n\n First, if you want to have the background of the discussion or learn how to read ROC curves and Precision-Recall curves, checkout out my previous thread:



Now back to the example 👇 \n\n---\n\n We are obviously dealing with a severely imbalanced dataset - 1000 samples for class 0 and only 10 for class 1. This is not uncommon in practice, though.

The classifier is also not particularly good, because it has a lot of false positives.

Let's compute some metrics 👇 \n\n---\n\n ROC

To draw a ROC curve we need to compute the True Positive Rate (TPR) and the False Positive Rate (FPR). In this case:

TPR = 90%
FPR = 5%

Remember, a good classifier has high TPR and low FPR (upper left corner on the ROC curve). This looks quite OK.

Or is it? 👇  \n\n---\n\n Precision-Recall

Let's compute the metrics for the Precision-Recall curve.

Precision = 15%
Recall = 90% (same as TPR)

Now, this is a different story. We want both precision and recall to be high (upper right corner of the curve), so this classifier clearly isn't good!

👇  \n\n---\n\n A better way to understand this is to visually look at what is computed. Look at the image.

You see how in the case of Precision-Recall, we don't look at the True Negatives at all. So it doesn't matter if they are as much as the positive classes or much more!  \n\n---\n\n And by the way, this is also the reason that we can use Precision-Recall for Object Detection with a practically infinite background class, but we can't use ROC 😉 \n\n---\n\n This is a great point! I was implicitly assuming a constant distribution during training and test time, but if it changes it is trickier.

Last week I did a small quiz about the Gambler's Fallacy 🎰

Most people got it right - the probability of getting heads after we got tails 4 times in a row is still 50%.



I find it interesting to compare two ways to look at this 👇 \n\n---\n\n Independent events

The key here is that every flip of the coin is independent of the others. The outcome of the previous flip doesn't have any influence on the next one.

In contrast, if you are pulling cards from a deck without returning them, then these are not independent. \n\n---\n\n In mathematical terms, we can write this like:

P(Y | X) = P(Y)

Here X and Y denote the outcome of one flip. You read this formula like:

The probability of getting Y given X is the same as the probability of getting Y - because X and Y are independent. \n\n---\n\n Getting tails 5 times in a row

You can ask, what is the probability of getting tails 5 times in a row and it's small - 3.1%.

If we denote P(T) as the probability to get tails (50%), then:

P(T,T,T,T,T) = P(T)P(T)P(T)P(T)P(T) = 0.03125

This is because each flip is independent. \n\n---\n\n Getting heads after 4 tails

The key difference now is that we are not asking how likely it is to get TTTTH. We are asking how likely is it to get H, *given* TTTT.

Mathematically, we can use the formula from above:

P(H | T,T,T,T) = P(H) = 50% \n\n---\n\n The lesson is that in statistics, it's very important how you formulate your problem, because you may get very different results

▪️What is the probability to get TTTT and then H?      3.1%

▪️What is the probability to get H given TTTT?           50.0%

The Gambler's Fallacy 🤷‍♂️ \n\n---\n\n One more note - this is different than the Monty Hall problem! The Gambler's Fallacy is a much simpler one coming directly from the different ways to look at independent events.

Optimizing the weights of a model is too mainstream, let's optimize the features! 🤗

Why the hell do we want to do that? We are going to hide a secret image in our data using machine learning techniques! 

Let me show you 👇  \n\n---\n\n What do we do?

We want to have a bunch of points that look random on the first look. We can then enter codes that will change the sizes of the points.

Only if we enter the right code, we will see one of the several images hidden in the points.

Demo 👇 \n\n---\n\n I created one and uploaded it on my website here:



Try out the following codes:
▪️ 8198399457
▪️ 6674004952
▪️ 0856561979

There are 3 more images hidden in there, can you find them?

This is created using linear regression! Let's dive into it 👇 \n\n---\n\n The Secret Images

I first created a black image containing white pixels at the positions where each point should be.

This can be done in any image editor (I use Photoshop) by overlaying a black layer on top of a photo and tracing the contour with white pixels.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Creating the point cloud

A Python script reads every image and creates a point for each white pixel. We store the index of the image as the class of each point. This will be used later to distinguish between the points of different images.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Random points

After that, new random points are generated. We make sure that the new points fall into a circle around the center of the image and that they are not too close to other points. The class is now 255.

Here are the points visualized with Plotly. 

👇  \n\n---\n\n Linear Regression

Typically, we have a feature vector X describing some properties of every data point and weights W that define our classifier and that are optimized during training.

To predict the class of each data point, we simply compute the dot product of X and W.

👇  \n\n---\n\n "Inverted" Linear Regression

Here, we do it differently:
▪️ Fix a set of weights W for every hidden image - this will be our secret code
▪️ Change the features X during training
▪️ The prediction is the size of each point - size of 0 means the point is not visible

👇 \n\n---\n\n The Training

For each hidden image, we have a different fixed vector W - a different classifier.

We use gradient descent to optimize the features X of all points. so that for a given vector W, the points of the corresponding image get size 1 and all others get size 0.

👇 \n\n---\n\n The Weights

We initialize the weights in a random manner and convert them in a way that they can be mapped to the digits from 0 to 9.

▪️ 0 → -1.0
▪️ 1 → -0.8
▪️ 2 → -0.6
...
▪️ 8 → 0.6
▪️ 9 → 0.8

👇  \n\n---\n\n The Optimization

The optimization step is similar to linear regression using gradient descent, but we compute the gradients with respect to X and not W. We use the Mean Squared Error loss.

I won't explain details, but make sure to check out the last tweet for more info.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Putting it all together

In the end, we have a feature vector X for each point. 

If we multiply it with the weights of the corresponding hidden image we will get a number close to 1

If we multiply it with the weights of another hidden image we will get a number close to 0

👇 \n\n---\n\n The Interface

We can use plotly and some JavaScript to build a simple web page displaying the points and show a single field to enter a code.

Here is the link once more: 

Give it a try and feel free to poke around the code.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Behind the scenes

What happens is that after a code is entered, the digits are converted back to weights between -1 and 1. 

The features of each point are multiplied by the weights and the size of the points is changed correspondingly. That's it!
