Machine Learning Formulas Explained! 👨‍🏫

This is the formula for the Binary Cross Entropy Loss. This loss function is commonly used for binary classification problems.

It may look super confusing, but I promise you that it is actually quite simple!

Let's go step by step 👇  \n\n---\n\n The Cross-Entropy Loss function is one of the most used losses for classification problems. It tells us how well a machine learning model classifies a dataset compared to the ground truth labels.

The Binary Cross-Entropy Loss is a special case when we have only 2 classes.

👇 \n\n---\n\n The most important part to understand is this one - this is the core of the whole formula!

Here, Y denotes the ground-truth label, while Ŷ is the predicted probability of the classifier.

Let's look at a simple example before we talk about the logarithm... 👇  \n\n---\n\n Imagine we have a bunch of photos and we want to classify each one as being a photo of a bird or not.

All photos are manually so that Y=1 for all bird photos and Y=0 for the rest.

The classifier (say a NN) outputs a probability of the photo containing a bird, like Ŷ=0.9

👇 \n\n---\n\n Now, let's look a the logarithm.

Since Ŷ is a number between 0 and 1, log Ŷ will be a negative number increasing up to 0.

Let's take an example of a bird photo (Y=1):
▪️ Classifier predicts 99% bird, so we get -0.01
▪️ Classifier predicts 5% bird, so we get -3

That's weird 👇  \n\n---\n\n For a loss, we want a value close to 0 if the classifier is right and a large value when the classifier is wrong. In the example above it was the opposite!

Fortunately, this is easy to fix - we just need to multiply the value by -1 and can interpret the value as an error 🤷‍♂️

👇 \n\n---\n\n If the photo is labeled as no being a bird, then we have Y=0 and so the whole term becomes 0.

That's why we have the second part - the negative case. Here we just take 1-Y and 1-Ŷ for the probabilities. We are interested in the probability of the photo not being a bird.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Combining both we get the error for one data sample (one photo). Note that one of the terms will always be 0, depending on how the photo is labeled.

This is actually the case if we have more than 2 classes as well when using one-hot encoding!

OK, almost done with that part 👇  \n\n---\n\n Now, you should have a feeling of how the core of the formula works, but why do we use a logarithm?

I won't go into detail, but let's just say this is a common way to formulate optimization problems in math - the logarithm makes all multiplications to sums.

Now the rest 👇 \n\n---\n\n We know how to compute the loss for one sample, so now we just take the mean over all samples in our dataset (or minibatch) to compute the loss.

Remember - we need to multiply everything by -1 so that we can invert the value and interpret it as a loss (low good, high bad).

👇  \n\n---\n\n Where to find it in your ML framework?

The Cross-Entropy Loss is sometimes also called Log Loss or Negative Log Loss. 

▪️ PyTorch - torch.nn.NLLLoss 
▪️ TensorFlow - tf.keras.losses.BinaryCrossentropy and CategoricalCrossentropy
▪️ Scikit-learn - sklearn.metrics.log_loss \n\n---\n\n And if it is easier for you to read code than formulas, here is a simple implementation and two examples of a good (low loss) and a bad classifier (high loss).  \n\n---\n\n I regularly post threads like this on topics like machine learning and self-driving cars.

Follow me @haltakov for more! \n\n---\n\n Yes, this is a good point! The input to the loss needs to be probabilities!

For classifiers that don't necessarily output probabilities (for example a NN with ReLU), you usually add a softmax layer.

Or use torch.nn.CrossEntropyLoss in PyTorch.

 \n\n---\n\n This is actually interesting! There are two very different ways to arrive at the same formula. One is what you mention using the log loss, but the other comes from information theory. They happen to be the same in this context.

▪️ Reduce overfitting

▪️ Ensembles

How would you curate a dataset for classifying photos of birds as in the @xkcd below?

I asked you this question the other day and again, there were many great answers! Most people seem to be overcomplicating this, though...

Let me explain 👇

 \n\n---\n\n The process of curating a good dataset involves several stages:

1️⃣ Collect images
2️⃣ Pre-label images
3️⃣ Label images
4️⃣ Evaluate problem categories
5️⃣ Monitor deployed model

Let's look into these in details 👇 \n\n---\n\n 1️⃣ Collect images

The first step is to collect many images both containing birds (positive example) and not containing birds (negative example). At this stage, we only care about collecting a lot of photos with as much variability as possible.

There are various sources 👇 \n\n---\n\n Existing datasets

There are already several public datasets that have labeled images of birds, like PASCAL VOC, MS COCO, ImageNet. We can take these and train our model with them already.

This may not be enough, but it will surely provide a good starting point.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Internet

There are many public sources where we can get photos, that may contain birds:
▪️ Unsplash
▪️ Pexels
▪️ Flickr
▪️ Reddit /r/itookapicture/
▪️ Google Images

These provide APIs and in some cases even curated datasets.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Create Yourself

Birds are a very common subject, so this is probably overkilled. However, for some projects, you need to go out and take the photos yourself (or hire people to do that).

👇 \n\n---\n\n 2️⃣ Pre-label images

Before jumping into labeling, we usually want to have a step where we can already filter out the easy cases. This means that we can create some pre-labels that will speed up the actual labeling process.

Let's see how 👇 \n\n---\n\n Text descriptions

Many photos come with some kind of a text description - either in a dedicated description field in the API, the title of the photo, or the ALT attribute. This text can be used to classify photos of birds and others. It won't be perfect, but it is a start.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Pre-trained models

We can use a pre-trained model like YOLO or Mask R-CNN to detect objects in the images and look for birds. Some labeling tools (like CVAT) even have this option integrated. Again, not perfect, but will help speed up the process.



👇 \n\n---\n\n Train your own model

If you have labeled some part of the data, you can also train a simple model yourself. This is helpful in the case when you are interested in a class that is not supported by existing pre-trained models.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Use a zero-shot model

A special case of pre-trained models is the so-called zero-shot models, like for example CLIP by OpenAI. The idea is that you provide a text prompt describing what you want to classify and the model does it. Figuring out the right prompt is critical!

👇 \n\n---\n\n 3️⃣ Label images

The hard part - the actual labeling. The pre-labels will help you sort through them faster, but still, there is some work to do, especially in the cases where the model wasn't very confident.

You need a good labeling tool or you can hire a labeling company.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Labeling tools

Here is a fantastic repository with links to different label tools. Take one that is designed for your particular use case. I've had some good experience with CVAT - an open-source tool created by Intel.



👇 \n\n---\n\n 4️⃣ Evaluate problem categories

After you have the first version of the dataset, you will train and evaluate a model. You need to analyze the issues it has and come back to your dataset to:
▪️ Correct wrong labels
▪️ Balance the dataset
▪️ Add more data for problematic cases

👇 \n\n---\n\n 5️⃣ Monitor deployed model

Finally, when you deploy your model, you need to monitor its performance and be prepared to react in case of a problem. Maybe some specific birds species doesn't work? You will need to collect more data and retrain your model.

Example 👇 \n\n---\n\n In the bird identifying app, for example, you can add a "Report problem" button. This will allow you to collect feedback and data from your users and continue improving your dataset and model over time. \n\n---\n\n I regularly write threads like this to help people get started with Machine Learning.

How to create art with Machine Learning? 🎨

You've probably seen these strangely beautiful AI-generated images on Twitter. Have you wondered how they are created?

In this thread, I'll tell you about a method for generating art with ML known as VQGAN+CLIP.

Let's jump in 👇  \n\n---\n\n Short History 📜

In January @OpenAI publicly released CLIP, which is a model that allows matching text to images.

Just days after that, some people like @advadnoun, @RiversHaveWings, and @quasimondo started experimenting using CLIP to guide the output of a GAN using text.

👇 \n\n---\n\n OpenAI published an image generation model together with CLIP, called DALL-E, but without the full code and the pre-trained models. 

The results from guiding StyleGAN2 or BigGAN with CLIP aren't as accurate as DALL-E, but they are weirdly artistic.



👇 \n\n---\n\n When CLIP was paired with a recent model released by the University of Heidelberg in December 2020 called VQGAN, the quality of the generated images improved dramatically.

VQGAN+CLIP is one of the most commonly used methods today.



👇 \n\n---\n\n If you are interested in more details about the history of these projects, check out this fantastic article by @sea_snell!



We are now going to explore how this method works and how you can use it yourself 👇 \n\n---\n\n For the experiments below I'm using this Colab notebook by @jbusted1, which itself is based on one of the original notebooks by @RiversHaveWings.

I only did some modifications on my side to speed up making different experiments.



👇 \n\n---\n\n The text prompt

To start you need to specify how the final image should look like - the text prompt. You can use natural language for this and you can define several prompts as well.

Let's try the following prompt:

"a car driving on a beautiful mountain road"

Not bad!

👇  \n\n---\n\n However, let's say we want to see some sky on the top and we want the car to be nicer. We can add 2 more prompts describing the scene better.

"a car driving on a beautiful mountain road" 
"sky on the top mountains on the sides"
"a beautiful sports car"

Much better!

👇  \n\n---\n\n You can now apply some tricks to improve the visual style of the image. For example, you can use the so-called "unreal engine trick" found by @arankomatsuzaki. You just add another prompt saying "unreal engine" and you will get a more realistic-looking image!

Nice! 👇  \n\n---\n\n The process of tuning the text description is called prompt engineering. CLIP is a very powerful model, but you need to ask it in the right way to get the best results. Try out different things!

Here is an example of the styles you can achieve with different prompts.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Start image

By default, the generation will start from a random noise image. However, you can provide your own image to start the process. This will make the final image look much more like it, so it is a way to guide the model.

Example with the same text prompt

👇  \n\n---\n\n Now, let's look a bit under the hood. What happens is the following:

1️⃣ VQGAN generates an image
2️⃣ CLIP evaluates how well the image fits the text prompt
3️⃣ Do a backpropagation pass to the VQGAN
4️⃣ Go back to 1️⃣

👇 \n\n---\n\n CLIP

The really cool thing about CLIP is that it can take an image or some text end encode them in an intermediate (latent) space.  This space is the same for both, so you can then compare how similar an image is to a sentence. This itself is a 🤯 achievement.

👇 \n\n---\n\n VQGANs

VQGAN is also an interesting method because for the first time it allows the powerful vision transformers to be efficiently used on high-resolution images by decomposing the image into an ordered list of entries from a codebook.

👇 \n\n---\n\n So, we are basically training the VQGAN to produce images that will fit the text prompts. CLIP is used as a powerful judge to guide the GAN in the right direction in order to achieve good results.

The expressive power comes from the vast knowledge CLIP contains and can use.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Unfortunately, this also means that the whole process is rather slow and needs a powerful GPU with lots of RAM. The experiments above were done in a Google Colab Pro notebook with an Nvidia P100 GPU and each image (1000 iterations) takes about 15 minutes to create.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Another interesting feature is that you can take all the intermediate images and create a cool-looking video!

"a scary orange jack-o-lantern"
"red fire background"

Why is AI bad at math? 📐

Machine learning models today are good at generating realistic-looking text (see GPT-3), images (VQGAN+CLIP), or even code (GitHub Co-Pilot/Codex).

However, these models only learn to imitate, so the results often contain logical errors.

Thread 👇  

---

 Simple math problems, like the ones 10-year-old kids solve, usually require several logical steps involving simple arithmetics.

The problem is that, if the ML model makes a logical mistake anywhere along the way, it will not be able to recover the correct answer.

👇  

---

 @OpenAI is now working on tackling this issue. 

In their latest paper, they introduce the so-called verifiers. The generative model generates 100 solutions, but the verifiers select the one that has the highest chance of being factually correct.



👇 

---

 This strategy helps them get much better at solving simple math problems - almost on par with kids aged 9-12. However, they still achieve only 55% correct answers, so there is still some way to go.

It is an interesting research field though, so great to see progress there.

Can you detect COVID-19 using Machine Learning? 🤔

You have an X-ray or CT scan and the task is to detect if the patient has COVID-19 or not. Sounds doable, right?

None of the 415 ML papers published on the subject in 2020 was usable. Not a single one!

Let's see why 👇  \n\n---\n\n Researchers from Cambridge took all papers on the topic published from January to October 2020.

▪️ 2212 papers
▪️ 415 after initial screening
▪️ 62 chosen for detailed analysis
▪️ 0 with potential for clinical use



There are important lessons here 👇 \n\n---\n\n Small datasets 🐁 

Getting medical data is hard, because of privacy concerns, and at the beginning of the pandemic, there was just not much data in general.

Many papers were using very small datasets often collected from a single hospital - not enough for real evaluation.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Biased datasets 🧒🧑‍🦲

Some papers used a dataset that contained non-COVID images from children and COVID images from adults. These methods probably learned to distinguish children from adults... 🤷‍♂️

👇 \n\n---\n\n Training and testing on the same data ❌

OK, you just never do that! Never!

👇 \n\n---\n\n Unbalanced datasets ⚖️

There are much more non-COVID scans than real COVID cases, but not all papers managed to adequately balance their dataset to account for that.

Check out this thread for more details on how to deal with imbalanced data:


👇 \n\n---\n\n Unclear evaluation methodology ⁉️

Many papers failed to disclose the amount of data they were tested or important aspects of how their models work leading to poor reproducibility and biased results.

👇 \n\n---\n\n The problem is in the data 💽

The big problem for most methods was the availability of high-quality data and a deep understanding of the problem - many papers didn't even consult with radiologists.

A high-quality and diverse dataset is more important than your fancy model!

Machine Learning in the Real World 🧠 🤖

ML for real-world applications is much more than designing fancy networks and fine-tuning parameters.

In fact, you will spend most of your time curating a good dataset.

Let's go through the steps of the process together 👇  \n\n---\n\n Collect Data 💽

We need to represent the real world as accurately as possible. If some situations are underrepresented we are introducing Sampling Bias.

Sampling Bias is nasty because we'll have high test accuracy, but our model will perform badly when deployed.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Traffic Lights 🚦

Let's build a model to recognize traffic lights for a self-driving car. We need to collect data for different:

▪️ Lighting conditions
▪️ Weather conditions
▪️ Distances and viewpoints
▪️ Strange variants

And if we sample only 🚦 we won't detect 🚥  🤷‍♂️

👇  \n\n---\n\n Data Cleaning 🧹

Now we need to clean all corrupted and irrelevant samples. We need to remove:

▪️ Overexposed or underexposed images
▪️ Images in irrelevant situations
▪️ Faulty images

Leaving them in the dataset will hurt our model's performance!

👇  \n\n---\n\n Preprocess Data ⚙️

Most ML models like their data nicely normalized and properly scaled. Bad normalization can also lead to worse performance (I have a nice story for another time...)

▪️ Crop and resize all images
▪️ Normalize all values (usually 0 mean and 1 std. dev.)

👇 \n\n---\n\n Label Data 🏷️

Manual labeling is expensive. Try to be clever and automate as much as possible:

▪️ Generate labels from the input data
▪️ Use slow, but accurate algorithms offline
▪️ Pre-label data during collection
▪️ Develop good labeling tools
▪️ Use synthetic data?

👇 \n\n---\n\n Label Correction ❌

You will always have errors in the labels - humans make mistakes. Review and iterate!

▪️ Spot checks to find systematic problems
▪️ Improve labeling guidelines and tools
▪️ Review test results and fix labels
▪️ Label samples multiple times

👇 \n\n---\n\n The danger of label errors 🧑‍🏫

A recent study by MIT found that 10 of the most popular public datasets had 3.4% label errors on average (ImageNet had 5.8%).

This even lead authors to choose the wrong (and more complex) model as their best one!



👇 \n\n---\n\n Balance Dataset ⚖️ 

Dealing with imbalanced data can be tricky...

Let's classify the color of the 🚦 - we can get 97% just by learning to recognize 🟢 and 🔴, just because 🟡 is severely underrepresented.

I have a separate thread on this topic:


👇 \n\n---\n\n Train and Evaluate Model 💪📏

This is the part that is usually covered by ML courses. Now is the time to try out different features, network architectures, fine-tune parameters etc.

But we are not done yet... 👇 \n\n---\n\n Iterative Process 🔄

In most real-world applications the bottleneck is not the model itself, but the data. After having a first model, we need to review where it has problems and go back to:

▪️ Collecting and labeling more data
▪️ Correcting labels
▪️ Balancing the data

👇 \n\n---\n\n Deploy Model 🚢

Deploying the model in production poses some additional constraints:

▪️ Speed
▪️ Cost
▪️ Stability
▪️ Privacy
▪️ Hardware availability and integration

We have to find a good trade-off between these factors and accuracy.

Now we are done, right? No...👇 \n\n---\n\n Monitoring 🖥️

The performance of the model will start degrading over time because the world keeps changing:

▪️ Concept drift - the real-world distribution changes
▪️ Data drift - the properties of the data change

We need to detect this, retrain, and deploy again.

Example 👇 \n\n---\n\n Drift ➡️

We now have a trained model to recognize 🚦, but people keep inventing new variants - see what some creative people in Munich came up with 😄

We need a way to detect that we have a problem, collect data, label, and retrain our model.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁 

This is how a typical ML pipeline for real-world applications looks like. Please remember this:

▪️ Curating a good dataset is the most important thing
▪️ Dataset curation is an iterative process
▪️ Monitoring is critical to ensure good performance over time  \n\n---\n\n This week I'm reposting some of my best threads from the past months, so I can focus on creating my machine learning course.

Let's talk about a common problem in ML - imbalanced data ⚖️ 

Imagine we want to detect all pixels belonging to a traffic light from a self-driving car's camera. We train a model with 99.88% performance. Pretty cool, right?

Actually, this model is useless ❌

Let me explain 👇  \n\n---\n\n The problem is the data is severely imbalanced - the ratio between traffic light pixels and background pixels is 800:1.

If we don't take any measures, our model will learn to classify each pixel as background giving us 99.88% accuracy. But it's useless!

What can we do? 👇 \n\n---\n\n Let me tell you about 3 ways of dealing with imbalanced data:

▪️ Choose the right evaluation metric
▪️ Undersampling your dataset
▪️ Oversampling your dataset
▪️ Adapting the loss

Let's dive in 👇 \n\n---\n\n 1️⃣ Evaluation metrics 

Looking at the overall accuracy is a very bad idea when dealing with imbalanced data. There are other measures that are much better suited:
▪️ Precision
▪️ Recall
▪️ F1 score

I wrote a whole thread on that

 \n\n---\n\n 2️⃣ Undersampling

The idea is to throw away samples of the overrepresented classes.

One way to do this is to randomly throw away samples. However, ideally, we want to make sure we are only throwing away samples that look similar.

Here is a strategy to achieve that 👇  \n\n---\n\n Clever Undersampling

▪️ Compute image features for each sample using a pre-trained CNN
▪️ Cluster images by visual appearance using k-means, DBSCAN etc.
▪️ Remove similar samples from the clusters (check out for example the Near-Miss or the Tomek Links strategies)

👇 \n\n---\n\n 3️⃣ Oversampling

The idea here is to generate new samples from underrepresented classes. The easiest way to do this is of course to repeat the samples. However, we are not gaining any new information with this.

Some better strategies 👇  \n\n---\n\n Data Augmentation

Create new samples by modifying the existing ones. You can apply many different transformations like for example:

▪️ Rotation
▪️ Flipping 
▪️ Zooming
▪️ Skewing
▪️ Color changing

We can do some even more advanced stuff 👇  \n\n---\n\n SMOTE

The idea is to create new samples by combining two existing ones.

This technique is more common when working with tabular data, but can be used for images as well. For that, we can combine the images in feature space and reconstruct them using an autoencoder.  \n\n---\n\n Synthetic Data

Another option is to generate synthetic data to add to our dataset. This can be done either using a GAN or using a realistic simulation to render new images.

There are even companies that specialize in this, like  (not affiliated)

👇  \n\n---\n\n 4️⃣ Adapting the loss function

Finally, an easy way to improve the balance is directly in your loss function. We can specify that samples of the underrepresented class to have more weight and contribute more to the loss function.

Here is an example of how to do it in the code.  \n\n---\n\n So, let's recap the main ideas when dealing with imbalanced data:

▪️ Make sure you are using the right evaluation metric
▪️ Use undersampling and oversampling techniques to improve your dataset

Machine Learning Formulas Explained 👨‍🏫

This is the formula for Mean Squared Error (MSE) as defined in WikiPedia. It represents a very simple concept, but may not be easy to read if you are just starting with ML.

Read below and it will be a piece of cake! 🍰

Thread 👇  \n\n---\n\n The core ⚫

Let's unpack from the inside out. MSE calculates how close are your model's predictions Ŷ to the ground truth labels Y. You want the error to go to 0.

If you are predicting house prices, the error could be the difference between the predicted and the actual price.  \n\n---\n\n Why squared? 2️⃣

Subtracting the prediction from the label won't work. The error may be negative or positive, which is a problem when summing up samples.

You can take the absolute value or the square of the error. The square has the property that it punished bigger errors more.  \n\n---\n\n Why squared? Example 2️⃣

Imagine your pediction for the price of two houses is like this:

🏡 House 1: actual 120K, predicted 100K -> error 20K
🏠 House 2: actual 60K, predicted 80K -> error -20K

If you sum these up the error will be 0, which is obviously wrong... \n\n---\n\n Summing up all samples ➕

When training your model you will have many samples (n) in your batch. We need to calculate the error for each one and sum it up.

Again, having the error be always ≥ 0 is important here.  \n\n---\n\n Taking the average ➗

You are good to go how!

However, if you want to compare the errors of batches of different sizes, you need to normalize for the number of samples - you take the average.

For example, you may want to see which batch size produces a lower error.  \n\n---\n\n Mean Squared Error 📉

Now it should be easier to understand the formula!

MSE is a commonly used statistical measure and loss function in ML regression models (e.g. linear regression).

You should look into the Mean Absolute Error (MAE) as well, which handles outliers better.  \n\n---\n\n You can also see the explanation of this formula, as well as other machine learning concepts here:

Your ML model training code is full of print statements? You are doing it wrong... 🛑

I can't count the number of times that a good visualization has saved me hours debugging my ML model. And as they say, "a picture is worth a 1000 words"!

We can do better than print 👇 \n\n---\n\n Real-world example 👨‍🏫

I was training a semantic segmentation model and the results were horrible. Not completely random, because the model was detecting some objects, but the performance was very bad.

I started looking at my data, hyperparameters, features...

But then 👇 \n\n---\n\n I had a custom visualization showing the probability distribution over all classes on mouseover.

I immediately saw that the output of the model wasn't normalized so I got raw classifier scores, but interpreted them as probabilities! The model and the training were fine!

👇  \n\n---\n\n Btw. this was 2012 - much before all the fancy visualization tools we have today were created. So we had to do most visualizations by ourselves then.

Speaking of modern tools, let's see what we've got! 👇 \n\n---\n\n TensorBoard

One of the most popular tools is TensorBoard. It allows you to display important internals of your model during development:
▪️ Evaluation metrics
▪️ Images
▪️ Embeddings
▪️ Weights histograms
▪️ Model graph
▪️ Experiment management
▪️ ...

How to evaluate your ML model? 📏

Your accuracy is 97%, so this is pretty good, right? Right? No! ❌

Just looking at the model accuracy is not enough. Let me tell you about some other metrics:
▪️ Recall
▪️ Precision
▪️ F1 score
▪️ Confusion matrix

Let's go 👇

#RepostFriday \n\n---\n\n We'll use this example in the whole thread - classifying traffic light colors (e.g. for a self-driving car).

Yellow traffic lights appear much less often, so our dataset may look like this.

This means our model could reach 97% accuracy, by ignoring all 🟡 lights. Not good!

👇  \n\n---\n\n Let's assume now that we trained our model and we get the following predictions.

Do you think this model is good? How can we quantitatively evaluate its performance? How should it be improved?

Let's first discuss the possible error types 👇  \n\n---\n\n Let's evaluate how well our model classifies 🟡  lights. There are 3 possible cases:

✅ True Positive - our model correctly classifies the 🟡
❌ False Negative - our model classifies 🟡  as another color
❌ False Positive - our model classifies another color as 🟡 

👇  \n\n---\n\n Accuracy

We can now just take the percentage of correctly classified samples - this is called the accuracy. In this case, it is 75%.

What is the problem? 🤔 

We have no idea in which cases the model has problems and needs to be improved.

We need to look at other metrics 👇  \n\n---\n\n Recall

The recall is computed separately for each color as the percentage of samples of the color classified correctly (per class accuracy).

We now see that we have a big problem with 🟡 and we should also improve 🟢. 

On the other hand 🔴 looks perfect. But it isn't... 👇  \n\n---\n\n Precision

The precision tells us how many of the model's predictions for a certain class were correct. The precision for 🔴 is low because the model wrongly classifies 🟢 and 🟡 lights as 🔴. 

The 🟢 looks much better, while 🟡 is bad again.

Now, let's combine both 👇  \n\n---\n\n F1 Score

The problem with Recall is that it ignores False Positives (FPs), while Precision ignores False Negatives. The F1 score is another metric that considers both.

We can see that 🟡 is indeed quite bad, but we also see that both 🔴 and 🟢 need to be improved.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Confusion Matrix

We can also get an overview of both FPs and FNs by looking at the Confusion Matrix. It breaks down for each class, how it was classified.

For example, looking at the 🟡 row, we see that 67% of the 🟡 lights were classified as 🔴 , 33% as 🟡 and none as 🟢 

👇  \n\n---\n\n If you look closely, you'll see that the diagonal of the matrix is exactly the Recall.

However, in the Confusion Matrix we can also see where we have FPs - for example, the 🟡 and 🟢 lights that are classified as 🔴.

That's why I like to use the Confusion Matrix.

👇 \n\n---\n\n So, let's summarize:

▪️ Accuracy - doesn't tell us where the problems are
▪️ Recall - ignores FPs
▪️ Precision - ignores FNs
▪️ F1 score - combines Recall and Precision
▪️ Confusion matrix - overview overall error types

You need to choose the best metrics for your application! \n\n---\n\n I'm reposting some of my best threads over the year every Friday. On the other days, I regularly write threads like this to help people get started with Machine Learning and web3.

You think you know what is an NFT? Well, think again...

You are doing it wrong if you think about NFTs as pixelated images of punks, toads, or apes. It is not about the JPEG!

A better mental model for thinking about NFTs 👇 \n\n---\n\n Forget the images for now. Owning an NFT means that your wallet address is listed as the owner of a specific digital asset on the blockchain.

Digital assets are organized in collections and an NFT is one specific piece of this collection.

Let's look at an example 👇 \n\n---\n\n I own an NFT from the @underfittedio membership collection - a membership card.

You can now check the collection on the blockchain and can see that my wallet address is the owner of token ID 4.

Everybody can check this. Nobody can change it - except me!

How is this useful? 👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio I get access to members-only communication channels

In the @underfittedio community, we use Discord for communication (chat, audio, and video). Only people that own a membership NFT get access to the members-only area. Ownership is verified on the blockchain by a bot.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio I can vote on decisions for the development of the community

All important decisions in the community are done using voting. To vote, you need to prove that you own a membership NFT. The voting platform (Snapshot) verifies this on the blockchain.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio I can participate in the development of community projects

Only members holding the NFT are allowed to participate in building community projects and earn a share of their profit. Again, who is allowed to participate is verified on the blockchain.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio Now, let's finally talk about the images!

Every NFT has some additional information (metadata) associated with it. This information is usually not stored directly on the blockchain, but you can get the link to this information from the blockchain (the so-called tokenURI).

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio The metadata can contain information about different properties on the NFT like a name, description, image, video, 3D model, website... it can really be anything!

Many NFT projects use IPFS as decentralized storage for the metadata.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio What do you do with the metadata then? NFT exchanges like OpenSea read the metadata and display it in a nice way on their website, including the image.

So this is how my @underfittedio NFT looks like 🐸



👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio But wait, the image itself doesn't play any role when I'm using the community Discord or voting on Snapshot?

Exactly!

The image, the JPEG is only a *visualization* of the information stored on the blockchain - it doesn't mean anything by itself.

And how could it... 👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio Think about this for a second! JPEGs are digital assets, so they can be reproduced infinitely at zero cost. You don't own the JPEG, because everybody can copy it. Or as they say "right-click save-as" the image.

What we really care about is the information stored on the chain 👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio The information on the blockchain is what unlocks the utility of an NFT, not the JPEG.

Different NFT projects offer different utilities and you need to decide which is useful for you and which is not when buying an NFT. Additionally, NFTs can be easily traded on exchanges.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio NFT utilities are worth a whole thread, but here are some quick examples:

🎫 Membership cards
🎟️ Event tickets (both in the digital and physical world)
🎨 Digital art ownership
🕹️ Virtual objects in games
🌐 Crypto domain names (like ENS)
🎖️ Achievement badges
...

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio With this mental model, some of the NFT critiques become very easy to answer. 

"I can just right-click and save your NFT"

Yes, you can, but you will only save the image, the metadata. The information on the blockchain is unchanged and this is what gives the whole utility!

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio "Buying an NFT is not like buying the Mona Lisa, but like buying a receipt for the Mona Lisa"

Sure, digital assets can be copied and distributed at no cost. What I care about is what I can do with the receipt. What if it allowed me to have dinner with Leonardo Da Vinci? 😀

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio "I can take your image and mint it as an NFT myself"

Sure, but you can't do this in the original collection, so you still can't use the utility. You can't sell it.

That's like writing a check to send money from my bank account, but signing it yourself - it's worthless.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio "It makes no sense to pay thousands of dollars for a JPEG"

It may not matter to you, but it matters to some people to have access to the community and events behind projects like Bored Apes.

It's like buying an expensive watch when a $20 one will do the same job 🤷‍♂️

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio "All NFTs are a scam"

There are many scam projects, but there are many genuine ones. The utility of a project may be worthless to you (and this is fine), but this doesn't automatically make it a scam.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio "NFTs are used to sell stolen artist's works"

Yes, some people do this. Technology is amoral - it amplifies people's abilities. Unfortunately, there are both good and bad people in the world.

Same thing happens with torrents, fake watches, and Adibas sneakers.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @underfittedio Let's summarize

Think of NFTs as proving you own a piece of a digital collection. This proof gives you access to the utility associated with the particular project.

The image is just a simple visualization of the proof.

It's not about the JPEG! \n\n---\n\n I'll be sharing more thoughts about crypto, NFTs, and web3 in the future, along with my regular machine learning content.

Programming smart contracts and self-driving cars… same thing! 🤷‍♂️

Wait what? Smart Contracts and Self-driving cars? 😳

They are so different on the first look - digital vs physical, assets vs transportation, rules vs AI.

However, programming smart contracts and safety-critical features of self-driving cars have a lot in common!

Thread 👇  \n\n---\n\n They are similar in that bugs can have disastrous consequences in both cases. We are not talking about your app crashing or a button on your website not working.

A bug in your smart contract can lose you millions of $.

A bug in your self-driving car can kill somebody.

👇 \n\n---\n\n We need to take extra care of code quality, testing, and programming approach. Some things we strive for in both cases:

▪️ Code is simple
▪️ Code is well documented
▪️ Code is well tested
▪️ Code analysis
▪️ Code auditing
▪️ Code is efficient

👇 \n\n---\n\n Wait a minute! Aren't self-driving cars driven all by AI? 🤔

Yes and no.

Many of the functions of a self-driving car like perception, prediction, and planning are nowadays done by complex machine learning models.

However, for safety-critical code there are monitors.

👇 \n\n---\n\n It is common to have the ML model drive the car but to have simple pieces of code called monitors that implement redundant plausibility checks.

For example, the ML model steers, but a monitor could look at the lidar and make sure the car never drives into the side barrier.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Monitors are simple, written according to strict conventions, and rigorously tested. In some cases can even formally verified.

They are also important for detecting faults in hardware systems and sensors and making sure the car doesn't go crazy.

Let's dive into the details👇 \n\n---\n\n 1. Code is simple 🤏

Code complexity can hide a lot of bugs and edge cases. Writing simple and understandable code is very important when writing mission-critical code.

Don't be a smart ass - stick to a simple and understandable style.

👇 \n\n---\n\n 2. Code is well documented 📁

Every dev hates writing documentation. However, in mission-critical code, it is important to document not only the behavior of the code but also why some decisions were taken and trade-offs were made.

👇 \n\n---\n\n 3. Code is well tested ⚙️

Since the code is fairly simple, there is no excuse to not have high test coverage (and not only line coverage ☝️). It is not the time to move fast when writing the code that will hit the car brake in an emergency or transfer millions of $.

👇 \n\n---\n\n 4. Code analysis 🔬

Devs cannot always think about all edge cases. This is where automatic code analysis comes into play. There are two main types:
▪️ Static analysis
▪️ Dynamic analysis

👇 \n\n---\n\n Static code analysis 🧍

Static analysis tools go over your code and look for patterns that are known to be a frequent cause of problems or inefficiencies.

For example, having unused variables is not bad in general, but it is an indication that the dev forgot something.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Dynamic code analysis 🏃

Dynamic analysis tools run your application and provide input attempting to find bugs. This is often called fuzzing.

Running fuzzing tools on many of the popular libs will quickly reveal many unnoticed bugs!

👇 \n\n---\n\n 5. Code auditing 🕵️

Another common practice is to hire people specializing in analyzing mission-critical software, assess the quality, and recommend changes if needed.

For cars, there are also standards like ISO 26262 (ASIL) that require you to perform an audit.

👇 \n\n---\n\n 6. Code is efficient 🐇

Efficiency is always important in embedded systems, where we typically have lots of constraints like integration space, temperature, cooling, and cost.

For smart contracts every operation costs gas, so it is critical to be efficient as well.

👇 \n\n---\n\n OK, I hope now you believe me that the development of smart contracts and safety-critical code for self-driving cars is similar in many aspects.

In both cases bugs can have disastrous consequences, so we strive for simple, well-tested, and efficient code.

How decentralized is web3 really?

While there is a lot of hype around web3, NFTs, and decentralized apps (dApps), there is also a lot of criticism. Today, I'll focus on the critique that web3 is actually too centralized.

Let's try to have an honest discussion 👇 \n\n---\n\n These are the main arguments I see regularly. Please add more in the comments.

1️⃣ The Internet is already decentralized
2️⃣ It is inefficient
3️⃣ Everything can be implemented better using a centralized approach
4️⃣ Important services are centralized

👇 \n\n---\n\n I was inspired to write this in part after reading this great article by @moxie pointing some of the problems with the current state of web3. If you've been living under a rock in the last weeks, make sure you check it out:

But before we start, let's establish some basic terms.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @moxie What are web3/decentralized apps?

When building a web3 app we are storing important data on the blockchain instead of a centralized database.

Additionally, all code that modified the data in the blockchain runs in smart contracts that are also deployed on the blockchain.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @moxie The key features of the blockchain we are interested in here are:

▪️ All data is public
▪️ Transactions are permanent
▪️ Transactions need to be signed with the private key of the wallet that creates them
▪️ Data is modified by creating a transaction with a smart contract

👇 \n\n---\n\n @moxie And smart contracts:

▪️ Smart contracts store data on-chain
▪️ Once deployed, the code of the smart contract cannot be changed
▪️ Smart contracts cannot be destructed
▪️ Reading data from a contract is free
▪️ Changing data in a contract requires a transaction and has a fee

The Internet is already decentralized, why do we need web3? 🤔

This is a common critique of web3. However, decentralization on its own is not always enough - sometimes we need to agree on a set of facts.

Blockchains give us a consensus mechanism for that!

Thread 🧵

1/12 \n\n---\n\n The Internet is built of servers that communicate using open protocols like HTTP, SMTP, WebRTC etc. Everybody can set up a server and participate. It is decentralized!

However, if two servers distribute contradicting information, how do you know which one is right?

2/12 \n\n---\n\n This is what blockchains give us, a way for decentralized parties to agree on one set of facts. They offer a consensus mechanism!

Imagine the blockchain as a global public database that anybody can read and nobody can falsify - every transaction/change needs to be signed.

3/12 \n\n---\n\n Consensus mechanisms like Proof-of-Work (Bitcoin, Ethereum) and Proof-of-Stake (Tezos, Polygon, Ethereum 2.0) allow all participants in the blockchain network to verify all changes and guarantee that nobody is cheating (for example by double-spending coins).

4/12 \n\n---\n\n Of course, many applications don't need that, and supporting this database is not easy (more on that tomorrow).

However, when talking about ownership of digital assets, I really don't want to be dependent on a single company. Let me give you an example...

5/12 \n\n---\n\n Hic Et Nunc is the biggest NFT marketplace on the Tezos blockchain. The founder decided to destroy it and did as much damage as possible.

The website was down, but all ownership information is on the blockchain, so he couldn't delete it. People didn't lose their NFTs.

6/12 \n\n---\n\n Because the website was open source, the community got new forked versions up and running in less than 24 hours. Everything was there. No assets were lost.

Now imagine what will happen if the founder of your favorite startup decides to destroy it...

7/12 \n\n---\n\n Another example - many people in the Ethereum community are not happy with the largest exchange OpenSea. So they build new exchanges - we see new launches all the time!

They trade the same NFTs, because they are stored on the blockchain, not in the OpenSea database.

8/12 \n\n---\n\n You are not happy with Facebook?

Well, good luck setting up a competing website reusing the social graph of Facebook. The data is stored in the centralized Facebook database. And if they decide to close down your account - you are again out of luck.

9/12 \n\n---\n\n Another point against web3 is that it is too difficult for people to run their own node validating the blockchain and that people don't want to run their own servers.

This is true and this is fine. As a web 2.0 app user you also don't need to run your servers, right?

10/12 \n\n---\n\n There are different layers. While it is important that some parties (miners, bakers) take care of validating the blockchain. There are people that want to do that and that can profit from it.

People building and using web3 apps don't need to worry about that.

11/12 \n\n---\n\n To summarize, web3 gives us more than decentralization - it gives us a way to agree on a common set of facts, like who owns which token.

And you don't need to do everything yourself - you need to make sure the really important information is stored on-chain!

How inefficient is web3? 🤔

Another common critique of blockchain technology is that it is inefficient and it destroys the planet.

Blockchains using Proof-of-Work consensus are very energy-intensive and this is a real problem. There are alternatives, though.

Thread 🧵

1/13 \n\n---\n\n If we don't want to trust a central authority to handle the data, we need a decentralized system that provides consensus. 

And creating this consensus has a very real cost. This is a trade-off we need to be aware of when deciding if we want decentralization or not.

2/13 \n\n---\n\n Proof-of-Work is a problem and the two most popular blockchains currently are using Proof-of-Work - Bitcoin and Ethereum 1.0. PoW requires a huge amount of mathematical computations to validate the chain.

Before discussing the alternatives, let's talk about some numbers.

3/13 \n\n---\n\n This website has a good overview of the annual energy consumption of different blockchains. Here are some of the numbers:

▪️ Bitcoin: around 130 TWh
▪️ Ethereum 1.0: 75 TWh
▪️ Polygon (@0xPolygon): <0.001 TWh
▪️ Tezos (@tezos): <0.0001 TWh



4/13 \n\n---\n\n @0xPolygon @tezos Now, to put this into perspective, an average US home consumes about 10 KWh per year. Let's convert the numbers:

▪️ Bitcoin: 13,000,000 households
▪️ Ethereum 1.0: 7,500,000 households
▪️ Polygon: 100 households
▪️ Tezos: 10 households

Source: 

5/13 \n\n---\n\n @0xPolygon @tezos Wow, the difference is huge 🤯 (I just did the numbers myself and I'm surprised as well).

Even more, Tezos is not a small chain that nobody uses. It does roughly the same amount of transactions per day as Bitcoin (300,000) and about 25% of Ethereum (1,200,000).

6/13 \n\n---\n\n @0xPolygon @tezos Anybody that claims that the energy consumption of 10 average homes per year is too much energy to validate 300,000 transactions per day is not serious.

On the other hand, I agree with the arguments against the energy consumption of PoW chains

7/13 \n\n---\n\n @0xPolygon @tezos How do Polygon and Tezos manage to be so much more efficient than Bitcoin and Ethereum 1.0?

They use a different consensus mechanism, called Proof-of-Stake. Instead of doing lots of computations, PoS validators stake coins as proof that they are telling the truth.

8/13 \n\n---\n\n @0xPolygon @tezos In PoW, validators that attack the network waste energy which costs them money. In PoS, validators will lose their staked coins if they misbehave.

PoS is also more robust against 51% attacks because it is even less profitable than for PoW chains.

9/13 \n\n---\n\n @0xPolygon @tezos Currently, Ethereum uses Proof-of-Work, but there are plans to transition soon to Ethereum 2.0 which uses Proof-of-Stake.

To be honest, though, this plan is being postponed for several years now, so the word "soon" needs to be taken with a grain of salt.

10/13 \n\n---\n\n @0xPolygon @tezos There are also some critiques regarding the trade-offs that Proof-of-Stake requires in comparison to Proof-of-Work.

I'm not deep enough into the topic and I don't fully understand the argument in the following paper, but wanted to mention it.



11/13 \n\n---\n\n @0xPolygon @tezos The fact is, however, that Proof-of-Stake chains have been operating and flourishing for years now. I plan to understand the topics in more detail and comment on it in the future - stay tuned 😉

12/13 \n\n---\n\n @0xPolygon @tezos Time for a summary!

We established that decentralization has some penalties because we need to establish consensus. This is a trade-off to be aware of.

We also saw that PoW chains require immense amounts of energy, but we also saw that PoS chains can solve this problem.

Can you do everything better with Web 2.0 than web3? 🤔

Another common critique of web3 is that things can be implemented in a cheaper and more efficient way using Web 2.0 tech.

This is indeed true in many cases, but not always. We need to talk trade-offs!

Thread 🧵

1/17 \n\n---\n\n Yesterday, we talked about the energy efficiency of different consensus mechanisms and established that while Proof-of-Work chains consume too much energy, the problem can be solved using Proof-of-Stake.



However, there is more...

2/17 \n\n---\n\n Energy is not the only cost of decentralization. Using the blockchain to store data or run code increases the complexity of an application and adds latency in the process (waiting for the transaction to be validated).

It's a trade-off, but not as big as you think...

3/17 \n\n---\n\n First, if you are only reading data from the blockchain, the complexity is not higher than using a managed database service!

You need to register with a node service, get your API key and you need to use a small lib in your app to interact with it.

4/17 \n\n---\n\n The node service providers like Alchemy or Infura run full Ethereum nodes so you don't need to do it. Same as AWS running classical servers.

They have generous free tiers that give you access to the blockchain. On the client, you can use a lib like ethers.js or web3.js

5/17 \n\n---\n\n And most importantly, reading from the blockchain is free! Even more, running smart contract functions that only read and not write is free as well. No transactions, no gas fees needed!

If you want to change something on the blockchain you need to pay a transaction fee

6/17 \n\n---\n\n What is important to understand, though, is that you don't need to store everything on the blockchain!

What you need there is the most critical information of your app, especially information on who owns what. The rest doesn't need to be stored there!

7/17 \n\n---\n\n For example, many NFT projects don't store the actual images on the blockchain, but on IPFS.

IPFS is a distributed file system that stores images. If you want to make sure, your files will not be deleted, you can pin them (or use a pinning service, most offer free tiers).

8/17 \n\n---\n\n Now, distributed systems on their own don't offer consensus. IPFS doesn't know who owns the image NFT or which image is the right one. This is what you need to store on the blockchain!

The NFT smart contract then contains a permanent link from your token to the image.

9/17 \n\n---\n\n Having said that, there are NFT projects that store images on centralized servers like AWS or allow the owner to change the image URLs in the contract.

These are bad practices that defeat the purpose of the blockchain. Reputable collections, though, don't do that.

10/17 \n\n---\n\n We need to build better tools to help people easily check such things. We cannot expect everybody to be able to jump in the smart contract and read it to make sure everything is fine.

These tools will be built!

11/17 \n\n---\n\n Another example with a blog. It will be a terrible idea to put the content on the blockchain. Instead, you can put it on IPFS, GitHub, or somewhere where people can make a copy if they want.

Then store a hash of the content on the chain, so everybody can verify it.

12/17 \n\n---\n\n So, now we established that Proof-of-Stake blockchains can vastly reduce the cost of transactions and the environmental impact and that we don't need to store everything on the blockchain.

Now you need to think about what tradeoffs you want to make in your app.

13/17 \n\n---\n\n If you are building an app for people to upload funny cat images, using web3 is a bad idea. The cost and complexity are not worth it.

And this is fine - web3 is a layer in addition to Web 2.0 that is suitable for some use-cases, not a replacement of Web 2.0

14/17 \n\n---\n\n However, if you want to give people ownership of digital assets (art, memberships, game assets, certificates), using the blockchain is a small cost to pay in comparison to your assets being locked up in the central database controlled by a single company.

15/17 \n\n---\n\n Of course, if you don't see value in this particular asset (and many people often don't), the cost will still be too high and you may think the blockchain is still not needed.

However, I'm sure digital assets will grow more important and allow us to do many new things.

16/17 \n\n---\n\n Finally, I just want to repeat myself, but I think this is key.

You don't need to store everything on the blockchain!

And remember, reading from the blockchain is completely free!

👇 \n\n---\n\n Open Neural Network Exchange (ONNX)

ONNX is an open format to define machine learning models. All popular frameworks like TensorFlow or PyTorch allow you to export your model in ONNX. You can then run inference using the ONNX runtime lib for your language and platform.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Custom web app

In some cases, even a web app that loads your model using TensorFlow or PyTorch and runs inference is sufficient.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Embedded platforms

Embedded platforms usually come with their own SDK like Apple Core ML or Qualcomm Neural Processing SDK. They usually offer the possibility to deploy models from popular frameworks or at least ONNX.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Specialized services

There are also many specialized services to deploy and serve your models on. They usually offer advantages in some specific use-cases.

A thread about Sampling Bias 👇 \n\n---\n\n There is a lot of information about rules you need to follow when evaluating your machine learning model:

▪️ Balance your dataset
▪️ Use the right metric
▪️ Use high-quality labels
▪️ Split your training and test data
▪️ Perform cross-validation

But this may not be enough 👇 \n\n---\n\n A common problem when evaluating an ML model is the Sampling Bias.

This means that your dataset contains more samples of some part of the underlying distribution than others.

Some examples 👇 \n\n---\n\n You are training a computer vision model for traffic light detection.

You have many samples of vertical traffic lights, but you don't include any horizontal traffic lights.

👇 \n\n---\n\n You are training a natural language processing model.

You have samples from many people, but you have no samples from a particular language dialect.

👇 \n\n---\n\n You are training a model to predict housing prices.

You have data from the market for the last 10 years, but you don't have any data after the COVID-19 pandemic started.

👇 \n\n---\n\n What is the problem?

The biggest problem is that you usually don't know you have a problem while evaluating your model.

Your data is correctly split for training and testing, but neither dataset contains the problematic examples.

👇 \n\n---\n\n This means that you will be able to reach high accuracy on your test dataset and even on cross-validation.

However, when you encounter the underrepresented or missing samples in production, your model will fail.

So, what can we do about that? 👇 \n\n---\n\n Know your domain

You need to know your domain very well. You need to understand where the data is coming from, how is it collected, what variations exist in the underlying distribution.

You need to think of ways how to get samples covering all cases.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Be prepared to detect problems in the production

Even with the best preparation, there will be cases you didn't think about. Accept that!

Make sure you have good monitoring of your model to detect when it fails and inspect these cases.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Be prepared to retrain your model

You need to be prepared to iterate. Make sure you can collect additional data from the problematic situations, retrain your model and deploy again. \n\n---\n\n If you liked this thread you will also like the other things I post too. I regularly tweet about similar topics.

Did you ever want to learn how to read ROC curves? 📈🤔

This is something you will encounter a lot when analyzing the performance of machine learning models.

Let me help you understand them 👇

#RepostFriday  \n\n---\n\n What does ROC mean?

ROC stands for Receiver Operating Characteristic but just forget about it. This is a military term from the 1940s and doesn't make much sense today.

Think about these curves as True Positive Rate vs. False Positive Rate plots.

Now, let's dive in 👇 \n\n---\n\n The ROC curve visualizes the trade-offs that a binary classifier makes between True Positives and False Positives.

This may sound too abstract for you so let's look at an example. After that, I encourage you to come back and read the previous sentence again!

Now the example 👇 \n\n---\n\n We are building a self-driving car and want it to stop at red traffic lights 🚦

(You saw this coming, right 😁?)

We build a classifier to determine if the car should STOP (light is 🔴 or 🟡) or PASS (light is 🟢). I'm using just 2 classes here to make the example simpler.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Now we ask the model - should the car stop at the 🚦?

There are 4 possible cases
▪️ Light is 🔴, model says STOP - True Positive
▪️ Light is 🔴, model says PASS - False Negative
▪️ Light is 🟢, model says PASS - True Negative
▪️ Light is 🟢, model says STOP - False Positive

👇 \n\n---\n\n Given many examples from our validation/test set, we can compute the following metrics:

▪️ True Positive Rate (TPR) - how good is our model telling us correctly to stop.
▪️ False Positive Rate (FPR) - how often does our model tell us wrongly to stop

To get a feeling for it 👇  \n\n---\n\n A high TPR means that we stop at most 🔴 lights.
A low TPR means that we often miss 🔴 lights and pass.

A high FPR means that we often confuse 🟢 lights for 🔴 and wrongly stop.
A low FPR means that we don't have many false stops.

So, we want a high TPR and low FPR, right? 👇 \n\n---\n\n Evaluating a model on a validation/test dataset will give us exactly one TPR and FPR value. Here an example of a (not so good) classifier:
▪️ TPR = 95%
▪️ FPR = 1%

Wait, but this is just one point on the TPR vs. FPR plot above. So, how do we get the curve now?

👇 \n\n---\n\n Machine learning classifiers usually don't simply output a class, but they tell you the probability of each class being the correct one.

You can then define a threshold based on which you decide. For example, stop at a light only if the classifier is 99% sure. Or 90%? 80%?

👇 \n\n---\n\n We can now try many different values of the threshold and evaluate on our validation/test dataset. 

Every time we will get different values for TPR and FPR and we can put them on the ROC plot. This is how we get our curve!

So let's look at different thresholds 👇 \n\n---\n\n Here is an example plot. Look at the 3 points I marked on it to see the fundamental trade-off between FPR and TPR.

1️⃣ TPR = 20%, FPR = 2% - setting a high threshold (we want to be really sure before stopping), we won't have many FPs, but we will also miss many real 🔴.

👇  \n\n---\n\n 2️⃣ TPR = 81%, FPR = 33% - decreasing the threshold improves the detection rate, but now we also have many false detections of 🔴.

3️⃣ TPR = 99%, FPR = 90% - a model with a very low threshold will detect almost all 🔴, but will wrongly classify most 🟢 as 🔴 as well.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Changing the threshold will only change the trade-off not make our model better.

However, this is still an important step when you are tuning the model for a specific application. For self-driving cars, it is **very** Important to not run the red lights - you need high TPR!

👇 \n\n---\n\n We can, however, train another model using more data, more parameters, better optimization. But how do we tell that it is really better and not just finding a different trade-off point?

The new ROC curve should be closer to the upper left corner of the graph! 👇  \n\n---\n\n A better ROC curve means that we can choose thresholds that give us the same TPR for both classifiers, but the better one will have less FPR.

Alternatively, for the same FPR, the better classifier will have a higher TPR.

👇 \n\n---\n\n There is one problem, though - in the reality, ROC curves are much noisier. At some points, the curve of one model may be higher, but at others lower. So which one is better in this case?

See this image from a real evaluation (credit to Wikipedia). Which one is best?

👇  \n\n---\n\n To get a single number summarizing the whole ROC curve, we can compute the Area under the Curve (AOC).

This will again be a number between 0 and 1 and expresses the probability of the model to rank a random positive example higher than a random negative example.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁

To recap quickly:

▪️ ROC curves visualize the trade-off between TPR and FPR
▪️ The curve is created by varying an internal decision threshold
▪️ Models with a curve closer to the upper left corner are better

Is your machine learning model performing well? What about in 6 months? 🤔

If you are wondering why I'm asking this, you need to learn about 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘁 and 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘁.

Let me explain this to you using two real world examples.

Thread 👇 \n\n---\n\n Imagine you are developing a model for a self-driving car to detect other vehicles at night. 

Well, this is not too difficult, since vehicles have two red tail lights and it is easy to get a lot of data. You model works great!

But then... 👇  \n\n---\n\n Car companies decide to experiment with red horizontal bars instead of two individual lights.

Now your model fails to detect these cars because it has never seen this kind of tail light.

Your model is suffering from 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗽𝘁 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘁

👇  \n\n---\n\n Concept drift happens when the objects you are trying to model change over time.

In the case above, cars changed and you now need to adapt your model.

Another example 👇 \n\n---\n\n You are now dealing with the detection of traffic sights. Again, at night things are pretty easy because signs reflect the lights from the car's headlights and are very well visible in the image. Easy!

And again something happens... 👇  \n\n---\n\n New cars start getting more powerful laser high beams and now suddenly the signs reflect so much light that there are overexposed in the image.

The problem now is 𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗮 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗳𝘁.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Data drift happens when the object you are modeling stays the same, but the environment changes in a way that affects how the object is perceived.

In this case, the signs are exactly the same, but they appear different because of the lighting.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Since we talked about Sampling Bias last week, we can connect it with the concept of drift. Since the underlying distribution of your data changed, even if your sampling was good in the beginning it isn't anymore

You now have a Sampling Bias problem



👇 \n\n---\n\n What can we do about it?

While there are some methods like online learning to continue improving the model and some others to detect the drift, usually the solution is just to retrain your model.

This is something you need to be prepared about in your pipeline!

👇 \n\n---\n\n Follow me @haltakov for more intuitive explanations of machine learning and web 3 topics. \n\n---\n\n This depends on your application and how much error you can tolerate. You first need to monitor the model and detect that it is getting worse. Then collect data and retrain.

You can also keep the data collection ongoing and retrain periodically.

There are two problems with ROC curves

❌ They don't work for imbalanced datasets
❌ They don't work for object detection problems

So what do we do to evaluate our machine learning models properly in these cases?

We use a Precision-Recall curve.

Thread 👇

#RepostFriday  \n\n---\n\n Last week I wrote another detailed thread on ROC curves. I recommend that you read it first if you don't know what they are.



Then go on 👇 \n\n---\n\n ❌ Problem 1 - Imbalanced Data

ROC curves measure the True Positive Rate (also known as Accuracy). So, if you have an imbalanced dataset, the ROC curve will not tell you if your classifier completely ignores the underrepresented class.

Let's take an example confusion matrix 👇  \n\n---\n\n We are obviously dealing with a severely imbalanced dataset - 1000 samples for class 0 and only 10 for class 1. This is not uncommon in practice, though.

The classifier is also not particularly good, because it has a lot of false positives.

Let's compute some metrics 👇 \n\n---\n\n ROC

To draw a ROC curve we need to compute the True Positive Rate (TPR) and the False Positive Rate (FPR). In this case:

TPR = 90%
FPR = 5%

Remember, a good classifier has high TPR and low FPR (upper left corner on the ROC curve). This looks quite OK.
Or is it?  👇  \n\n---\n\n Precision-Recall

Let's compute the metrics for the Precision-Recall curve.

Precision = 15%
Recall = 90% (same as TPR)

Now, this is a different story. We want both precision and recall to be high (upper right corner of the curve), so this classifier clearly isn't good!

👇  \n\n---\n\n A better way to understand this is to visually look at what is computed. Look at the image.

You see how in the case of Precision-Recall, we don't look at the True Negatives at all. So it doesn't matter if they are as much as the positive classes or much more!  \n\n---\n\n ❌ Problem 2 - Object Detection Problems

ROC curves measure the False Positive Rate (FPR) according to the following formula.

In object detection problems the True Negatives don't make sense. There are so many possibilities to detect the background class.

Let's dive deeper 👇  \n\n---\n\n I'll use my favorite example again - traffic lights detection (for a self-driving car 🧠🚗).

We want to detect the presence and location (using a bounding box) of traffic lights in images. This is a typical Object Detection problem - an important class of CV problems.

👇  \n\n---\n\n The typical way to solve this is to design a neural network that will check many locations in the image and classify them as being a traffic light or not (background).

For more details, check out this thread: 

Now on the actual problem 👇 \n\n---\n\n There is no (practical) way to define True Negatives

These would be all locations in the image that don't contain a traffic light and where our model correctly predicted no traffic lights as well.

Imagine now going through all possible bounding box sizes for every pixel...

👇 \n\n---\n\n Common evaluation metrics for this are Precision and Recall.

▪️ Precision - the percentage of traffic lights the model detected that are indeed real traffic lights
▪️ Recall - the percentage of real traffic lights that the model detected

Confusing? Let's see some examples 👇  \n\n---\n\n High Precision, Low Recall

In this example, the Precision is 100% (all detected lights are correct), but the Recall is only 50% (2 out of 4 lights missed).

👇  \n\n---\n\n Low Precision, High Recall

In this example, the Precision is 67% (4 out of 6 detected lights are correct), while the Recall is 100% (all 4 real lights are detected).

👇  \n\n---\n\n Precision and Recall give us a way to measure both types of errors (FPs and FNs), without requiring us to count TNs.

By the way, that's why they work better for imbalanced data! Object Detection is imbalanced - there is much more background than objects.

Now the curve 👇 \n\n---\n\n For every candidate the network classifies, it gives us the probability of it being a traffic light. We need to choose a threshold on the probability to consider it a detected light.

It could be 50% if we don't want to miss many lights or 99% if we want to be really sure.

👇 \n\n---\n\n For every value of the threshold, we will get different Precision and Recall when evaluating our test dataset.

▪️ High thresholds - high Precision, low Recall
▪️ Low thresholds - low Precision, high Recall

Plotting these values gives us the Precision-Recall curve. \n\n---\n\n The Precision-Recall Curve visualizes the trade-off between making False Positives and False Negatives.

Similar to ROC curves, we can also compare different models. If the curve of one model is closer to the upper right corner than another one, then it is a better model.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁

To recap:
▪️ ROC curves don't work for imbalanced data
▪️ ROC curves don't work for object detection (can't count TNs)
▪️ Prevision-Recall curves are computed in a similar way to ROC curves
▪️ Prevision-Recall curves visualize the trade-off between FNs and FPs \n\n---\n\n Every Friday I repost one of my old threads so more people get the chance to see them. During the rest of the week, I post new content on machine learning and web3.

Machine Learning Formulas Explained! 👨‍🏫

This is the formula for the Binary Cross Entropy Loss. It is commonly used for binary classification problems.

It may look super confusing, but I promise you that it is actually quite simple!

Let's go step by step 👇

#RepostFriday  \n\n---\n\n The Cross-Entropy Loss function is one of the most used losses for classification problems. It tells us how well a machine learning model classifies a dataset compared to the ground truth labels.

The Binary Cross-Entropy Loss is a special case when we have only 2 classes.

👇 \n\n---\n\n The most important part to understand is this one - this is the core of the whole formula!

Here, Y denotes the ground-truth label, while Ŷ is the predicted probability of the classifier.

Let's look at a simple example before we talk about the logarithm... 👇  \n\n---\n\n Imagine we have a bunch of photos and we want to classify each one as being a photo of a bird or not.

All photos are manually so that Y=1 for all bird photos and Y=0 for the rest.

The classifier (say a NN) outputs a probability of the photo containing a bird, like Ŷ=0.9

👇 \n\n---\n\n Now, let's look a the logarithm.

Since Ŷ is a number between 0 and 1, log Ŷ will be a negative number increasing up to 0.

Let's take an example of a bird photo (Y=1):
▪️ Classifier predicts 99% bird, so we get -0.01
▪️ Classifier predicts 5% bird, so we get -3

That's weird 👇  \n\n---\n\n For a loss, we want a value close to 0 if the classifier is right and a large value when the classifier is wrong. In the example above it was the opposite!

Fortunately, this is easy to fix - we just need to multiply the value by -1 and can interpret the value as an error 🤷‍♂️

👇 \n\n---\n\n If the photo is labeled as no being a bird, then we have Y=0 and so the whole term becomes 0.

That's why we have the second part - the negative case. Here we just take 1-Y and 1-Ŷ for the probabilities. We are interested in the probability of the photo not being a bird.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Combining both we get the error for one data sample (one photo). Note that one of the terms will always be 0, depending on how the photo is labeled.

This is actually the case if we have more than 2 classes as well when using one-hot encoding!

OK, almost done with that part 👇  \n\n---\n\n Now, you should have a feeling of how the core of the formula works, but why do we use a logarithm?

I won't go into detail, but let's just say this is a common way to formulate optimization problems in math - the logarithm makes all multiplications to sums.

Now the rest 👇 \n\n---\n\n We know how to compute the loss for one sample, so now we just take the mean over all samples in our dataset (or minibatch) to compute the loss.

Remember - we need to multiply everything by -1 so that we can invert the value and interpret it as a loss (low good, high bad).

👇  \n\n---\n\n Where to find it in your ML framework?

The Cross-Entropy Loss is sometimes also called Log Loss or Negative Log Loss. 

▪️ PyTorch - torch.nn.NLLLoss 
▪️ TensorFlow - tf.keras.losses.BinaryCrossentropy and CategoricalCrossentropy
▪️ Scikit-learn - sklearn.metrics.log_loss \n\n---\n\n And if it is easier for you to read code than formulas, here is a simple implementation and two examples of a good (low loss) and a bad classifier (high loss).  \n\n---\n\n Every Friday I repost one of my old threads so more people get the chance to see them. Machine Learning Formulas Explained 👨‍🏫

This is the Huber loss - another complicated-looking formula... 

Yet again, if you break it down and understand the individual, it becomes really easy.

Let me show you 👇  \n\n---\n\n Background

The Huber loss is a loss function that is similar to the Mean Squared Error (MSE) but it is designed to be more robust to outliers.

MSE suffers from the problem that if there is a small number of severe outliers they can dominate the whole loss

How does it work? 👇 \n\n---\n\n The key to understanding math formulas is not to try to understand everything at the same time. 

Try looking at the terms inside the formula. Try to understand them from the inside to the outside...

Here, we can quickly see that one term is repeated several times...

👇  \n\n---\n\n Here y is the ground truth value we compare to and f(x) is the result provided by our model.

You can think for example about estimating house prices. Then y is the real prices and f(x) is the price our machine learning model predicted.

We can then simplify the formula a bit 👇  \n\n---\n\n The next thing we see is that the formula has two parts.

The first part is a simple quadratic term α^2 (with a constant of 0.5).

The second part is a bit convoluted with a couple of constants, but it is an absolute (linear) term - |α|.

Let's simplify further...  \n\n---\n\n The parameter δ determines when we choose one part and when the other. Let's try to set to a fixed value for now, so that we can simplify things. Setting δ = 1 gives us the simplest form.

OK, now if you ignore the constants (I'll come back to them later), it is quite simple

👇  \n\n---\n\n What the formula now tells us is that we take the square of α close to 0 and the absolute value otherwise.

Let's quickly implement the function in Python and plot it for δ = 1.

Take a look at the plot - do you see the quadratic and the linear part?

👇  \n\n---\n\n Alright, let me annotate the image a little bit.

You can clearly see how the Huber loss behaves like a quadratic function close to 0 and like the absolute value further away.

OK, now we understand the core of the formula. Let's go back and undo the simplifications...

👇  \n\n---\n\n First, what's with these deltas?

We want our loss function to be continuous, so at the border between the two parts (when α = δ) they need to have the same value.

What the constants in the linear term do is just make sure that it equals the quadratic term when α = δ!

👇  \n\n---\n\n Finally, why is this constant 0.5 everywhere? Do we really need it?

The thing is that we typically use a loss function to compute its derivative and optimize our weights. And the derivative of 0.5*α^2 is... simply α.

We use the 0.5 just to make the derivative simpler 🤷‍♂️

👇 \n\n---\n\n And if you want to use the Huber loss, you probably don't need to implement it yourself - popular ML libraries already have it implemented:

▪️ PyTorch: torch.nn.HuberLoss
▪️ TensorFlow: tf.keras.losses.Huber
▪️scikit-learn: sklearn.linear_model.HuberRegressor \n\n---\n\n Summary

The Huber loss takes the form of a quadratic function (like MSE) close to 0 and of a linear function (like MAE) away from zero. This makes it more robust to outliers while keeping it smooth around 0. You control the balance with the parameter δ.

Simple, right? 😁  \n\n---\n\n I regularly write threads to explain complex concepts in machine learning and web3 in a simple manner.

Follow me @haltakov for more \n\n---\n\n Good question! When you do want to avoid having big outliers it is better to use MSE. It depends on the application.

I'll write another thread on that.

 \n\n---\n\n It really depends on the use-case and how much you want to penalize outliers and when do you count a sample as an outlier. Consider this another hyperparameter that you need to tune.
