Machine Learning in the Real World 🧠 🤖

ML for real-world applications is much more than designing fancy networks and fine-tuning parameters.

In fact, you will spend most of your time curating a good dataset.

Let's go through the process together 👇

#RepostFriday  \n\n---\n\n Collect Data 💽

We need to represent the real world as accurately as possible. If some situations are underrepresented we are introducing Sampling Bias.

Sampling Bias is nasty because we'll have high test accuracy, but our model will perform badly when deployed.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Traffic Lights 🚦

Let's build a model to recognize traffic lights for a self-driving car. We need to collect data for different:

▪️ Lighting conditions
▪️ Weather conditions
▪️ Distances and viewpoints
▪️ Strange variants

And if we sample only 🚦 we won't detect 🚥  🤷‍♂️

👇  \n\n---\n\n Data Cleaning 🧹

Now we need to clean all corrupted and irrelevant samples. We need to remove:

▪️ Overexposed or underexposed images
▪️ Images in irrelevant situations
▪️ Faulty images

Leaving them in the dataset will hurt our model's performance!

👇  \n\n---\n\n Preprocess Data ⚙️

Most ML models like their data nicely normalized and properly scaled. Bad normalization can also lead to worse performance (I have a nice story for another time...)

▪️ Crop and resize all images
▪️ Normalize all values (usually 0 mean and 1 std. dev.)

👇 \n\n---\n\n Label Data 🏷️

Manual labeling is expensive. Try to be clever and automate as much as possible:

▪️ Generate labels from the input data
▪️ Use slow, but accurate algorithms offline
▪️ Pre-label data during collection
▪️ Develop good labeling tools
▪️ Use synthetic data?

👇 \n\n---\n\n Label Correction ❌

You will always have errors in the labels - humans make mistakes. Review and iterate!

▪️ Spot checks to find systematic problems
▪️ Improve labeling guidelines and tools
▪️ Review test results and fix labels
▪️ Label samples multiple times

👇 \n\n---\n\n The danger of label errors 🧑‍🏫

A recent study by MIT found that 10 of the most popular public datasets had 3.4% label errors on average (ImageNet had 5.8%).

This even lead authors to choose the wrong (and more complex) model as their best one!



👇 \n\n---\n\n Balance Dataset ⚖️ 

Dealing with imbalanced data can be tricky...

Let's classify the color of the 🚦 - we can get 97% just by learning to recognize 🟢 and 🔴, just because 🟡 is severely underrepresented.

I have a separate thread on this topic:


👇 \n\n---\n\n Train and Evaluate Model 💪📏

This is the part that is usually covered by ML courses. Now is the time to try out different features, network architectures, fine-tune parameters etc.

But we are not done yet... 👇 \n\n---\n\n Iterative Process 🔄

In most real-world applications the bottleneck is not the model itself, but the data. After having a first model, we need to review where it has problems and go back to:

▪️ Collecting and labeling more data
▪️ Correcting labels
▪️ Balancing the data

👇 \n\n---\n\n Deploy Model 🚢

Deploying the model in production poses some additional constraints:

▪️ Speed
▪️ Cost
▪️ Stability
▪️ Privacy
▪️ Hardware availability and integration

We have to find a good trade-off between these factors and accuracy.

Now we are done, right? No...👇 \n\n---\n\n Monitoring 🖥️

The performance of the model will start degrading over time because the world keeps changing:

▪️ Concept drift - the real-world distribution changes
▪️ Data drift - the properties of the data change

We need to detect this, retrain, and deploy again.

Example 👇 \n\n---\n\n Drift ➡️

We now have a trained model to recognize 🚦, but people keep inventing new variants - see what some creative people in Munich came up with 😄

We need a way to detect that we have a problem, collect data, label, and retrain our model.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁 

This is how a typical ML pipeline for real-world applications looks like. Please remember this:

▪️ Curating a good dataset is the most important thing
▪️ Dataset curation is an iterative process

Machine Learning Formulas Explained 👨‍🏫

For regression problems you can use one of several loss functions:
▪️ MSE
▪️ MAE
▪️ Huber loss

But which one is best? When should you prefer one instead of the other?

Thread 🧵  \n\n---\n\n Let's first quickly recap what each of the loss functions does. After that, we can compare them and see the differences based on some examples.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Mean Square Error (MSE)

For every sample, MSE takes the difference between the ground truth and the model's prediction and computes its square. Then, the average over all samples is computed.

For details, check out this thread:


👇 \n\n---\n\n Mean Absolute Error (MAE)

MAE is very similar to MSE, but instead of taking the square of the difference between the ground truth and the model's prediction, it takes the absolute value.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Huber Loss

The Huber loss is a combination of both ideas. It behaves like a square function (MSE) for small differences and like a linear function (MAE) for large differences.

I've written in detail about the Huber loss here:


👇 \n\n---\n\n Alright, these loss functions are very similar in some aspects:

▪️ They are always positive or 0
▪️ The loss function increases if our model makes worse predictions
▪️ They can be used for training machine learning models for regression

But there are important differences 👇 \n\n---\n\n Handling outliers

Big differences between the ground truth and the prediction of the model are amplified by MSE much more than the others.

Imagine predicting a house price of 100K, while the real price is 50K. MSE will give us 2500K, while MAE and Huber loss only 50K.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Therefore, a model trained with MSE as a loss function will focus on removing the large outliers because they will dominate the loss function. Samples with a smaller error will practically be ignored. 

This can be problematic if we don't care about big outliers.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Behavior around 0

MSE and the Huber loss are smooth around 0. This means that their derivative gets gradually smaller, which allows the optimization to converge nicely.

👇 \n\n---\n\n MAE on the other hand has completely different gradients on both sides of the 0. This means that the optimization process may start oscillating when the error becomes small.

👇 \n\n---\n\n OK, but which one is best?

Well, there is no universal answer to this question (you saw that coming, don't you 😉). It really depends on your application and especially how you want to handle outliers.

Let's discuss two examples:
▪️ House price predictor
▪️ Trading bot

👇 \n\n---\n\n House prices

Imagine you are a real estate agent. You want an ML model that can estimate the price of a house given properties like its size, location, age etc. You want your model to predict the price so you can compare it with the listing price and find good deals.

👇 \n\n---\n\n You will run your model over many listings and let it filter out potential good deals, which you will then review manually before taking a decision to buy.

A big outlier is not a problem there - if the model makes a very wrong prediction you will spot it and ignore it.

👇 \n\n---\n\n In this case, it is probably a good idea to use MAE or the Huber loss, because you don't want to avoid huge errors in the model at any cost.

On the other hand, you want to model to be fairly accurate for most predictions, so you don't waste your time reviewing bad deals.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Automatic trading bot

Now imagine you are programming an ML model to predict stock prices and automatically buy and sell.

Things are different now - a big error of the model may lead to huge losses in a single trade! You don't want that.

👇 \n\n---\n\n In this case, you should rather use MSE, because it will penalize these huge errors. There may be more cases where the model makes smaller mistakes, but as long as it is profitable, this will not matter that much.

👇 \n\n---\n\n So, you see? Two different applications where we need different approaches. Sometimes MSE is better and sometimes MAE is better.

👇 \n\n---\n\n And the Huber loss?

It kind of combines the advantages of MAE for outliers and MSE for smoothness. However, it adds complexity with the additional hyperparameter δ. It essentially defines which errors are counted as outliers.

It is one more parameter you need to tune...

👇 \n\n---\n\n Let me summarize

▪️ MSE is good to avoid having large outliers
▪️ MAE is better if you don't care about the outliers too much
▪️ The Huber loss behaves like MAE for outliers but is smooth like MSE around 0
▪️ The Huber loss comes with an additional hyperparameter to tune

This is the formula for Gradient Descent with Momentum as presented in Wikipedia. 

It may look intimidating at first, but I promise you that by the end of this thread it will be easy to understand!

Thread 👇

#RepostFriday  \n\n---\n\n The Basis ◻️

Let's break it down! The basis is this simple formula describing an iterative optimization method.

We have some weights (parameters) and we iteratively update them in some way to reach a goal

Iterative methods are used when we cannot compute the solution directly  \n\n---\n\n Gradient Decent Update 📉

We define a loss function describing how good our model is. We want to find the weights that minimize the loss (make the model better).

We compute the gradient of the loss and update the weights by a small amount (learning rate) against the gradient.  \n\n---\n\n Here is an illustration of how it works. 

The gradient tells us if the loss will decrease (negative gradient) or increase (positive gradient) if we increase the weight.

The learning rate defines how far along the gradient we will jump in the current step of the optimization.  \n\n---\n\n Momentum ⚽️

Now we add the momentum. It is defined as the weight update in the previous step times a decay factor.

The decay factor is just a number between 0 and 1 defining how much of the previous update will be taken into account. α = 0 means no momentum and α = 1 is a lot.  \n\n---\n\n A useful analogy is a ball rolling down a hill. If the hill is steep, the ball will accelerate (we update the weights more)

This will help the ball jump over small local minima and continue down the hill (to a smaller loss).

More momentum means a heavier ball with high inertia  \n\n---\n\n Putting it all together 🏁

So, in the original formula we update the weights using two terms.

The *gradient descent* term pushes us down the slope of the loss function.

The *momentum* term helps us accelerate and jump over small local minima.

PCA

Principal Component Analysis is a commonly used method for dimensionality reduction.

It's a good example of how fairly complex math can have an intuitive explanation and be easy to use in practice.

Let's start from the application of PCA 👇  \n\n---\n\n Dimensionality Reduction

This is one of the common uses of PCA in machine learning.

Imagine you want to predict house prices. You get a large table of many houses and different features for them like size, number of rooms, location, age, etc.

Some features seem correlated 👇 \n\n---\n\n Correlated features

For example, the size of the house is correlated with the number of rooms. Bigger houses tend to have more rooms.

Another example could be the age and the year the house was built - they give us pretty much the same information.

We don't want that 👇 \n\n---\n\n Curse of Dimensionality

In general, we want to have fewer features, because of the Curse of Dimensionality.

The amount of data required to fit a model increases exponentially with the number of features. Therefore, having many features telling us the same thing is bad.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Remove features

Then, let's remove the features we don't need. But how do you select these?

Take a look at the code. Using scikit-learn and PCA you can take a dataset containing many features and transform it into a dataset with fewer features (5 in the example).

👇  \n\n---\n\n What you can use PCA for is to essentially create new features that will "compress" the data of the full feature set as well as possible.

In this way, redundant features will effectively be removed. This is what we call dimensionality reduction.

Why does it work 👇 \n\n---\n\n To understand better what happens, let's look at a specific example using the awesome visualization by @vicapow.

I'll post images and videos in this thread, but I encourage you to click the link and experiment yourself a bit.



Let's start in 3D 👇 \n\n---\n\n @vicapow Take a look at this 3D model

Guess what, you are now doing dimensionality reduction!

You see, you are looking at a 3D model on a screen that is 2D. While every point in the model is defined by 3 features (coordinates), you only select 2 features to look at it.

👇  \n\n---\n\n @vicapow As the model is rotating, you can observe that some views are better at displaying the data than others.

Look at the screenshots I did below. On the first one, you can clearly see that there are 3 clusters in the data, while on the second you only see 2.

Can PCA help? 👇  \n\n---\n\n @vicapow I wrote above that PCA will find a new reduced set of features that optimally encodes the full dataset.

So, if we apply it to the 3D model, we get the following view of the data, which clearly shows the 3 clusters. The optimal view!

👇  \n\n---\n\n @vicapow Now you can imagine that on the 3 dimensions you have features describing a house.

And the good thing is that PCA doesn't care how many dimensions you have and how many you want to reduce your dataset.

Now a bit about the math 👇 \n\n---\n\n @vicapow What happens is that PCA will rotate your dataset in a way that in the first dimension (first principal component) you have the highest variability of the data, on the second dimension - the second-highest, and so on.

The reduction happens by removing the last dimensions.

👇  \n\n---\n\n @vicapow Now, go back to the visualization and play with the 2D example.

Move the points in the left around and observe how the PCA plot changes. Put all points on a diagonal like (highly correlated) and you will see that after PCA the second dimension almost disappears.

👇  \n\n---\n\n @vicapow The math

You saw how you can use PCA in practice and got an intuition of why it works and you haven't seen a single formula!

To perform PCA you need to perform Singular Value Decomposition of the covariance matrix, but I won't go into detail here.

👇 \n\n---\n\n @vicapow If you are interested in math let me know and I can write another thread.

However, I really want to stress that you can understand PCA and use it in practice even without understanding the internals of how it works.

Dealing with imbalanced datasets 🐁 ⚖️ 🐘

Real world datasets are often imbalanced - some of the classes appear much more often than others.

The problem? You ML model will likely learn to only predict the dominant classes.

What can you do about it? 🤔

Thread 🧵 #RepostFriday \n\n---\n\n Example 🚦

We will be dealing with an ML model to detect traffic lights for a self-driving car 🤖🚗

Traffic lights are small so you will have much more parts of the image that are not traffic lights. 

Furthermore, yellow lights 🟡 are much rarer than green 🟢 or red 🔴. \n\n---\n\n The problem ⚡

Imagine we train a model to classify the color of the traffic light. A typical distribution will be:
🔴 - 56%
🟡 -    3%
🟢 -  41%

So, your model can get to 97% accuracy just by learning to distinguish red from green.

How can we deal with this? \n\n---\n\n Evaluation measures 📐

First, you need to start using a different evaluation measure than accuracy:
- Precision per class
- Recall per class
- F1 score per class

I also like to look at the confusion matrix to get an overview. Always look at examples from the data as well! \n\n---\n\n In the traffic lights example above, we will see very poor recall for 🟡 (most real examples were not recognized), while precision will likely be high.

At the same time, the precision of 🟢 and 🔴 will be lower (🟡 will be classified as 🟢 or 🔴). \n\n---\n\n Get more data 🔢

The best thing you can do is to collect more data of the underrepresented classes. This may be hard or even impossible...

You can imagine ways to record more yellow lights, but imagine you want to detect a very rare disease in CT images? \n\n---\n\n Balance your data 🔀

The idea is to resample your dataset so it is better balanced.

▪️Undersampling - throw away some examples of the dominant classes

▪️ Oversampling - get more samples of the underrepresented class \n\n---\n\n Undersampling ⏬

The easiest way is to just randomly throw away samples from the dominant class.

Even better, you can use some unsupervised clustering method and throw out only samples from the big clusters.

The problem of course is that you are throwing out valuable data... \n\n---\n\n Oversampling ⏫

This is more difficult. You can just repeat sample, but it won't work very good.

You can use methods like SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique) to generate new samples interpolating between existing ones. This may not be easy for complex images. \n\n---\n\n Oversampling ⏫

If you are dealing with images, you can use data augmentation techniques to create new samples by modifying the existing ones (rotation, flipping, skewing, color filters...)

You can also use GANs or simulation the synthesize completely new images. \n\n---\n\n Adapting your loss 📉

Another strategy is to modify your loss function to penalize misclassification of the underrepresented classes more than the dominant ones.

In the 🚦 example we can set them like this (proportionally to the distribution)
🔴 -   1.8
🟡 - 33.3
🟢 -  2.4 \n\n---\n\n If you are training a neural network with TensorFlow or PyTorch you can do this very easily:

▪️ TensorFlow - use the class_weights parameter in the fit() function ()

▪️PyTorch - use the weight parameter in the CrossEntropyLoss () \n\n---\n\n Summary 🏁

In practice, you will likely need to combine all of the strategies above to achieve good performance.

How can I prove to you that I know a secret, without revealing any information about the secret itself?

This is called a zero-knowledge proof and it is a super interesting area of cryptography! But how does it work?

Thread 🧵 \n\n---\n\n Let's start with an example

Peggie and Victor travel between cities A and B. There are two paths - a long path and a short path. The problem is that there is a gate on the short path for which you need a password.

Peggie knows the password, but Victor doesn't.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Victor wants to buy the password from Peggie so he can use the short path.

But what if Victor pays Peggie, but she lied and she didn't know the password? How can Peggie prove to Victor she knows the password, without actually revealing it?

They use a zero-knowledge proof 👇 \n\n---\n\n Victor turns around and Peggie starts walking from A towards B on one of the roads.

After some time, Victor calls Peggie and asks her to come back on either the short path or the long path.

If Peggie took the same path Victor asked her to use she can just come back.

👇  \n\n---\n\n However, if Peggie took the other path, the only way she can fulfill Victor's request is to go through the gate.

For example, if she took the short path, but Victor asked her to come back on the long path, Peggie needs to pass the gate, go to B and then come back.

👇  \n\n---\n\n Now, doing this a single time is not enough - there is 50% chance that Peggie chose the same path that Victor asked her to come back on.

However, if they repeat the experiment many times, Victor can gain confidence (exponentially), that Peggie indeed knows the password.

👇 \n\n---\n\n This is not a mathematical proof, because there is still a tiny chance that Peggie got lucky, even after repeating the experiment many times. However, for practical applications, it is enough.

For example, repeating 20 times gives Victor confidence of 99.9999%.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Now let's see what are the 3 important properties of zero-knowledge proofs:

1️⃣ Completeness
2️⃣ Soundness
3️⃣ Zero-knowledge

👇 \n\n---\n\n 1️⃣ Completeness

If the statement to be proven is true, an honest verifier can be convinced that it is true indeed (100% true positive rate).

In the example above, the experiment is enough to convince Victor that Peggy really knows the password.

👇 \n\n---\n\n 2️⃣ Soundness

If the statement is false, with a very high probability the prover cannot cheat and deceive an honest verifier (a very, very low false-positive rate).

In the example, there Peggie has no way to cheat about knowing the password.

👇 \n\n---\n\n 3️⃣ Zero-knowledge

The proof doesn't reveal any information about the secret.

Indeed, Peggie doesn't need to tell anything about the password to Victor. Even more, Victor even cannot prove to anybody else, that Peggie knows the password.

👇 \n\n---\n\n The last point is interesting. Imagine Victor recording the whole process and publishing the video on YouTube.

Watching the video alone is not convincing enough, because Peggie and Victor may have cheated by agreeing on which path to call every time.

👇 \n\n---\n\n More examples 

There are many other examples of zero-knowledge proof. In this thread, I repurposed the famous cave example, but you can find more on Wikipedia .

👇 \n\n---\n\n Applications

There are also many applications of zero-knowledge proofs, for example in authentication systems. In my opinion, one of the most usages is in scaling blockchains.

👇 \n\n---\n\n Blockchain

Blockchains usually rely on the so-called non-interactive zero-knowledge proofs, like ZK-SNARK or ZK-STARK, where there is no need for the prover and the verifier to interact.

👇 \n\n---\n\n The intuition here is that zero-knowledge proofs allow somebody to perform the (expensive) validation of a bunch of transactions and write the proof on the blockchain.

Using zero-knowledge, anybody can verify the proof, without the need to actually verify all transactions.

👇 \n\n---\n\n This method can significantly increase the efficiency of the blockchain allowing for faster execution and lower transaction fees, without compromising security and decentralization.

👇 \n\n---\n\n And while these methods are fairly new (especially the non-interactive proofs), there are already real applications using them.

For example, @Immutable is a carbon-neutral blockchain optimized for NFTs and games without transaction costs. And zk-proofs make this possible.

@TiffanyAndCo launched an expensive, custom-made jewelry collection limited to the owners of a prestigious art collection.

You pay $50K for a pendant that is customized to look like the art piece you own.

This is how they use the blockchain to make this happen

1/8 🧵  \n\n---\n\n @TiffanyAndCo First, $50K may sound like a whole lot of money for a pendant (and it is), but this is nothing new...

Luxus jewelry brands have much more expensive pieces. There are currently 17 more expensive necklaces in the @TiffanyAndCo store. This one is $115K for example. 🤷‍♂️

2/8  \n\n---\n\n @TiffanyAndCo Now, @TiffanyAndCo want to make the new collection more special, so they want to only offer it to people that own a piece of another art collection.

However, imagine how difficult this is to verify this...

3/8 \n\n---\n\n @TiffanyAndCo Let's say they want to sell only to people that own a Picasso painting.

You log into the online store and you need to prove that they own a Picasso.

Do you submit a certificate? Online or per mail? Do you get somebody to come by your house and inspect the painting?

4/8 \n\n---\n\n @TiffanyAndCo Or let's say they want to offer the new collection only to Ferrari owners.

Again, how do you prove you own a Ferrari? You upload your car registration? Oh, it is registered to your company... now you upload the company registration? Who reviews this? Who approves this?

5/8 \n\n---\n\n @TiffanyAndCo @TiffanyAndCo, however, chose to limit their sale to owners of a Crypto Punk NFT (@cryptopunksnfts).

The ownership information of NFTs is stored on the blockchain, which is a public database. Therefore, everybody can easily verify which wallet owns which punk.

6/8 \n\n---\n\n @TiffanyAndCo @cryptopunksnfts Now, in their online store, @TiffanyAndCo only needs to verify that the one who wants to buy their piece is the one that owns this wallet address.

This is again, trivial - the user just needs to sign a message using their crypto wallet.

7/8 \n\n---\n\n @TiffanyAndCo @cryptopunksnfts Many people are mocking @TiffanyAndCo that they are selling an NFT for $50K, but they miss the point...

This is a case of a luxury brand using the blockchain to enable a new use-case - sell limited, custom jewelry to owners of another art collection.

Permissionless.

Outsmarted the Domain Name Hustlers!

I once owned haltakov-dot-com but foolishly let it expire. It was quickly snapped up by someone who then offered to sell it back to me at a much higher price. This happened about 10 years ago.

This continued...👇 \n\n---\n\n Over the years, I've been contacted twice by some very shady companies that bought the domain and offered it to me for about $500. I just hate the idea of giving my money to these types of companies.

Biggest lessons from the Presentation Zen book

- Keep it simple
- There is only one message the audience will remember
- Don't put too many words on the slides
- Slides support the presentation, they are not the goal
- Practice  

---

 Keep it simple

Avoid overcomplicating your slides and message, avoid clutter. 

---

 There is only one message the audience will remember

Most people int he audience don't care about your presentation. Think about the single most important thing you want to convey and make sure you make that message stick. 

---

 Don't put too many words on the slides

People are not good at reading and listening at the same time. Keep the text minimal - not more than 7 bullet points with not more than 7 words each. 

---

 Slides support the presentation, they are not the goal

The slides should support your presentation, not be self-contained. You don't need to put everything you say on the slides. 

---

 Practice

Practice your presentation many times. This helps me a lot as my brain has more capacity to look at the audience and see their reactions when I give a well rehearsed presentation. Helps with stage fever as well.

I vibe coded a game for #vibejam with Cursor as an experienced developer.

Here are 6 lessons I learned 👇 

---

 1. Vibe coding is great for problems that are narrowed down

Try to ask Cursor Agent a very specific thing to do. Ideally already open the related file so it takes it in the context. Then it usually works well. If the task spans multiple files it often creates a mess. 

---

 2. Commit often

Before every new feature, make sure you have commited your work. Often you need to test the code before you can decide if it works or not. git reset --hard is your friend if it goes wrong. 

---

 3. Clean the context

For new features, open a new Agent window. Otherwise you risk Cursor continuing fiddling with the code of the previous feature, sometimes even undoing manual changes you made 

---

 4. Check the code for duplications

Always check the code the Agent produces, especially for duplications. Several times it added a component a second time or implemented functionality that already exists. 

---

 5. Check useEffect dependencies

Another thing that happens often in React is that Agent will add more dependencies to useEffects that may have catastrophic effects of performance and even functionality. Make sure to check that extra carefully 

---

 6. Use 2 instances in parallel

It worked very well for me to checkout the repo twice in different folders, run 2 instances of Cursor and work in parallel on 2 features on separate branches. Much more effective, just make sure you merge properly. 

---

 7. Refactor the structure

Cursor Agent (with Claude 3.7 Sonnet thinking) is still very bad at overall architecture. Take some time to refactor things, extract components and functions, introduce a better file structure. Cursor will have a much easier time after that as well. 

---

 8. Don't ask it to do too much at once

This always creates a mess. Break the problem down in smaller pieces. That being said, you can give it hard problems to solve and usually it works fine if the complexity is contained. 

---
